c-at-m1-cores.text: The M1 has four Firestorm performance cores, four Icestorm efficiency cores and an eight-core GPU
c-at-m1-cores.quote: With four large performance cores, four efficiency cores, and an 8-GPU core GPU
c-at-m1-cores.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech

c-at-m1-transistors.text: The M1 has 16 billion transistors on a 5 nm process, 35% more than the A14
c-at-m1-transistors.quote: it features 16 billion transistors on a 5nm process node ... which is 35% more than the A14 inside of the newest iPhones
c-at-m1-transistors.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech

c-at-m1-die-size.text: AnandTech estimates the M1 die at about 120 mm² if its transistor density matches the A14's
c-at-m1-die-size.quote: If Apple was able to keep the transistor density between the two chips similar, we should expect a die size of around 120mm²
c-at-m1-die-size.hedge: If Apple was able to keep the transistor density between the two chips similar

c-at-m1-dram-package.text: The M1 package carries the DRAM beside the compute die inside the organic package, not stacked on top of it
c-at-m1-dram-package.quote: This packaging style with DRAM embedded within the organic packaging isn't new for Apple

c-at-m1-dram-bus.text: AnandTech expects a 128-bit DRAM bus on the M1, as on earlier A-X chips
c-at-m1-dram-bus.quote: we're almost certainly looking at a 128-bit DRAM bus on the new chip

c-at-m1-l2-size.text: The M1's performance-cluster L2 is 12 MB, shared by the four Firestorm cores
c-at-m1-l2-size.quote: the 12MB cache was one of the surprise reveals of the event ... it is after all now being used by 4 cores instead of 2
c-at-m1-l2-size.notes: Apple's announcement as relayed by AnandTech; the A14's L2 is 8 MB for two cores

c-at-m1-l2-blocks.text: On the M1 die shot the 12 MB L2 appears to be split into three large blocks
c-at-m1-l2-blocks.quote: The new cache here looks to be portioned into 3 larger blocks

c-at-m1-slc-shared.text: The M1's system level cache sits near the Icestorm cores and is shared by all IP blocks on the SoC
c-at-m1-slc-shared.quote: above which we find the SoC's system level cache, which is shared across all IP blocks
c-at-m1-slc-shared.notes: from AnandTech's die-shot annotation; no M1 SLC size is given in the article

c-at-a14-l2-size.text: The A14's L2 is an 8 MB cache shared by its two Firestorm cores
c-at-a14-l2-size.quote: Apple has been employing an 8MB structure that's shared between their two big cores

c-at-a14-l2-latency.text: The A14's big-core L2 latency is 16 cycles, up from 14 cycles on the A13
c-at-a14-l2-latency.quote: the A14 saw the L2 of the big cores make a regression in terms of access latency, going back from 14 cycles to 16 cycles

c-at-a14-slc.text: The A14's last-level (system level) cache appears to be 16 MB, serving all IP blocks on the SoC
c-at-a14-slc.quote: On the A14 this appears to be again a 16MB cache that is serving all the IP blocks on the SoC

c-at-a14-clock.text: On the A14 a single Firestorm core runs at 2998 MHz, dropping to 2890 MHz with two cores active
c-at-a14-clock.quote: Performance 1 | 2998 | 2890 ... clocking down to 2.89GHz when there's two cores active

c-at-decode-8.text: Firestorm decodes eight instructions per cycle
c-at-decode-8.quote: Featuring an 8-wide decode block, Apple's Firestorm is by far the current widest commercialized design in the industry
c-at-decode-8.notes: measured on the A14 (AnandTech's figures are estimated from testing the A14 in the iPhone 12 Pro)

c-at-rob-630.text: Veedrac's test exposes an out-of-order window of about 630 instructions on Firestorm, which AnandTech calls the ROB while noting it may not be a traditional ROB
c-at-rob-630.quote: we can seemingly confirm that Firestorm's ROB is in the 630 instruction range deep
c-at-rob-630.hedge: seemingly confirm ... in the 630 instruction range
c-at-rob-630.notes: measured on the A14 with Veedrac's microarchitecturometer test; the filler is not described. The A13 measured 560.

c-at-int-prf.text: Firestorm's integer in-flight and rename physical register capacity is estimated at about 354 entries
c-at-int-prf.quote: whose in-flight instructions and renaming physical register file capacity we estimate at around 354 entries

c-at-int-units.text: Firestorm has at least seven integer execution ports: four simple ALUs, two complex units that also multiply, and what appears to be a dedicated divide unit
c-at-int-units.quote: we find at least 7 execution ports for actual arithmetic operations. These include 4 simple ALUs capable of ADD instructions, 2 complex units which feature also MUL (multiply) capabilities
c-at-int-units.hedge: at least 7 ... what appears to be a dedicated integer division unit

c-at-branches.text: Firestorm executes two branches per cycle; the author thinks one or two dedicated branch ports do this but could not confirm the layout
c-at-branches.quote: The core is able to handle 2 branches per cycle, which I think is enabled by also one or two dedicated branch forwarding ports
c-at-branches.hedge: I think ... I wasn't able to 100% confirm the layout of the design here
c-at-branches.notes: measured on the A14; branch execution rate, not taken branches fetched per cycle

c-at-fp-pipes.text: Firestorm has four 128-bit FP/NEON pipelines, a fourth pipeline added over the A13
c-at-fp-pipes.quote: enabled by Apple's addition of a fourth execution pipeline ... The four 128-bit NEON pipelines thus on paper match

c-at-fp-prf.text: Firestorm's FP rename registers appear to number 384
c-at-fp-prf.quote: The FP rename registers here seem to land at 384 entries, which is again comparatively massive

c-at-fp-throughput.text: FP throughput matches the pipe count, so Firestorm sustains four FADDs and four FMULs per cycle
c-at-fp-throughput.quote: Floating-point operations throughput here is 1:1 with the pipeline count, meaning Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle

c-at-fadd-latency.text: FADD latency on Firestorm is 3 cycles
c-at-fadd-latency.quote: Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle with respectively 3 and 4 cycles latency

c-at-fmul-latency.text: FMUL latency on Firestorm is 4 cycles
c-at-fmul-latency.quote: Firestorm can do 4 FADDs and 4 FMULs per cycle with respectively 3 and 4 cycles latency

c-at-fp-div-one-pipe.text: The four FP/vector pipes appear identical except that FP divide, reciprocal and square root run on only one of them
c-at-fp-div-one-pipe.quote: Vector abilities of the 4 pipelines seem to be identical, with the only instructions that see lower throughput being FP divisions, reciprocals and square-root operations that only have an throughput of 1, on one of the four pipes

c-at-ls-ports.text: Firestorm appears to have four load-store ports, one load/store, one store-only and two load-only
c-at-ls-ports.quote: we're seeing what appears to be four execution ports: One load/store, one dedicated store and two dedicated load units

c-at-loads-per-cycle.text: Firestorm executes at most three loads per cycle, and at most two loads alongside two stores
c-at-loads-per-cycle.quote: The core can do at max 3 loads per cycle and two stores per cycle, but a maximum of only 2 loads and 2 stores concurrently

c-at-stores-per-cycle.text: Firestorm executes at most two stores per cycle, and at most two stores alongside two loads
c-at-stores-per-cycle.quote: The core can do at max 3 loads per cycle and two stores per cycle, but a maximum of only 2 loads and 2 stores concurrently

c-at-lq.text: Up to about 148-154 loads can be outstanding on Firestorm, taken as the load queue size
c-at-lq.quote: We're measuring up to around 148-154 outstanding loads and around 106 outstanding stores, which should be the equivalent figures of the load-queues and store-queues
c-at-lq.hedge: up to around ... should be the equivalent figures
c-at-lq.notes: range 148-154 (midpoint given); measured on the A14, probe not described

c-at-sq.text: About 106 stores can be outstanding on Firestorm, taken as the store queue size
c-at-sq.quote: We're measuring up to around 148-154 outstanding loads and around 106 outstanding stores, which should be the equivalent figures of the load-queues and store-queues
c-at-sq.hedge: around ... should be the equivalent figures
c-at-sq.notes: measured on the A14, probe not described

c-at-l1-tlb.text: Firestorm's L1 TLB holds 256 pages, double the A13's 128
c-at-l1-tlb.quote: One large improvement on the part of the Firestorm cores this generation has been on the side of the TLBs. The L1 TLB has been doubled from 128 pages to 256 pages
c-at-l1-tlb.notes: measured on the A14; the article does not say data or instruction TLB

c-at-l2-tlb.text: Firestorm's L2 TLB holds 3072 pages, up from 2048 on the A13
c-at-l2-tlb.quote: the L2 TLB goes up from 2048 pages to 3072 pages
c-at-l2-tlb.notes: measured on the A14; the article adds that with 16 KB pages this covers 48 MB

c-at-l1i.text: The A13's L1 instruction cache is 192 KB per Apple's Darwin kernel sources, not the 128 KB AnandTech had assumed; the article says the A14 Firestorm continues the large-cache trend but gives no Firestorm L1I size
c-at-l1i.quote: Last year we had speculated that the A13 had 128KB L1 Instruction cache ... following Darwin kernel source dumps Apple has confirmed that it's actually a massive 192KB instruction cache
c-at-l1i.notes: The sentence is about the A13 (Lightning), not Firestorm. Firestorm's 192 KB comes from 7-cpu (c-7cpu-l1i).

c-at-l1d-latency.text: Firestorm's L1D load-use latency is 3 cycles
c-at-l1d-latency.quote: The huge caches also appear to be extremely fast – the L1D lands in at a 3-cycle load-use latency
c-at-l1d-latency.notes: measured on the A14; the author does not know whether load-load cascading is involved

c-at-streaming-stores.text: New relative to the A13, the core turns streaming stores into non-temporal stores automatically, using Arm's relaxed memory model, as the Cortex-A76 and Exynos M4 do
c-at-streaming-stores.quote: the new design now also makes usage of Arm's more relaxed memory model in that the design is able to optimise streaming stores into non-temporal stores automatically
c-at-streaming-stores.notes: measured on the A14; the test is not described

c-at-pointer-prefetch.text: AnandTech has seen signs that Apple's designs may use some kind of pointer-chase prefetcher, which would help sparse-memory workloads such as 429.mcf and 471.omnetpp
c-at-pointer-prefetch.quote: In our microarchitectural investigations we've seen signs of ... where we might believe they're using some sort of pointer-chase prefetching mechanism
c-at-pointer-prefetch.hedge: we might believe they're using some sort of
c-at-pointer-prefetch.notes: said of Apple's designs in general, in the A14 SPEC discussion

c-7cpu-cores.text: The M1 tested has four Firestorm cores and four Icestorm cores
c-7cpu-cores.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)

c-7cpu-clock.text: The M1's Firestorm cores run at 3200 MHz
c-7cpu-clock.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)
c-7cpu-clock.notes: The page gives 3200 MHz; its single-thread 7-Zip run reports 3196-3202 MHz

c-7cpu-ice-clock.text: The M1's Icestorm cores run at 2064 MHz
c-7cpu-ice-clock.quote: Apple M1 (4x Firestorm 3200 MHz + 4x Icestorm 2064 MHz)

c-7cpu-memory.text: The M1 tested has 16 GB of LPDDR4X-4266 on eight 16-bit channels

c-7cpu-ice-l1d.text: Icestorm's L1 data cache is 64 KB; line size and associativity not determined
c-7cpu-ice-l1d.quote: Icestorm (Small Core): ... L1 Data cache = 64 KB, ? B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-ice-l1i.text: Icestorm's L1 instruction cache is 128 KB

c-7cpu-ice-l2.text: The Icestorm cluster's L2 is 4 MB, shared by its four cores

c-7cpu-l1d-size.text: Firestorm's L1 data cache is 128 KB
c-7cpu-l1d-size.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L1 Data cache = 128 KB, 64 B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-l1d-line.text: Firestorm's L1 data cache has 64-byte lines
c-7cpu-l1d-line.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L1 Data cache = 128 KB, 64 B/line, ?-WAY.

c-7cpu-l1i.text: Firestorm's L1 instruction cache is 192 KB; line size and associativity not determined

c-7cpu-l2-size.text: The Firestorm cluster's L2 is 12 MB, shared by its four cores

c-7cpu-l2-line.text: 7-cpu gives the Firestorm L2 line as 128 bytes, marked uncertain
c-7cpu-l2-line.notes: 7-cpu marks the value with a question mark and does not say how it was obtained

c-7cpu-l1d.text: Firestorm's L1D latency is 3 cycles for a simple pointer access
c-7cpu-l1d.quote: L1 Data Cache Latency = 3 cycles for simple access via pointer
c-7cpu-l1d.notes: the 128 KB size and the 4-cycle complex-address latency are c-7cpu-l1d-size and c-7cpu-l1d-complex

c-7cpu-l1d-complex.text: Firestorm's L1D latency is 4 cycles when the address needs a complex calculation (indexed pointer chase)
c-7cpu-l1d-complex.quote: L1 Data Cache Latency = 4 cycles for access with complex address calculation (size_t n, *p; n = p[n])

c-7cpu-l2-latency.quote: Firestorm (Big Core): ... L2 Cache Latency = 18 cycles
c-7cpu-l2-latency.notes: The page lists the 12 MB L2 at 18 cycles; its "L3" is the 8 MB SLC (c-7cpu-slc-latency). The page names pointer access only for the L1 lines.

c-7cpu-slc-size.text: The M1's system level cache (7-cpu's L3) is 8 MB, shared by all clusters
c-7cpu-slc-size.quote: L3 Cache = 8 MB (shared for all clusters)

c-7cpu-slc-line.text: 7-cpu gives the SLC line as 128 bytes, marked uncertain
c-7cpu-slc-line.quote: L3 Cache = 8 MB (shared for all clusters), 128 ? B/line

c-7cpu-slc-exclusive.text: 7-cpu suggests, with a question mark, that the SLC is exclusive of the L2

c-7cpu-slc-latency.text: From a Firestorm core, an SLC hit costs the 18-cycle L2 latency plus 10-15 ns
c-7cpu-slc-latency.quote: L3 Cache Latency = 18 cycles + (10-15 ns) : for Firestorm - Big Core
c-7cpu-slc-latency.notes: stated as 18 cycles + (10-15 ns), so not a cycle count without a clock; value is the midpoint of the ns part

c-7cpu-dram-latency.text: From a Firestorm core, DRAM latency is the 18-cycle L2 latency plus 91 ns
c-7cpu-dram-latency.quote: RAM Latency = 18 cycles + 91 ns : for Firestorm - Big Core
c-7cpu-dram-latency.notes: stated as 18 cycles + 91 ns; the value is the time beyond the 18-cycle L2 latency

c-7cpu-dtlb-l1.text: Firestorm's L1 data TLB holds 160 entries; associativity not determined

c-7cpu-dtlb-l1-miss.text: An L1 dTLB miss costs 6 cycles; overlapped misses cost 1.35 cycles per access
c-7cpu-dtlb-l1-miss.quote: Data TLB L1: 160 items. ?-way? Miss penalty = 6 cycles. Parallel miss: 1.35 cycles per access

c-7cpu-dtlb-l2.text: Firestorm's L2 data TLB holds about 3K entries

c-7cpu-dtlb-l2-miss.text: An L2 TLB miss costs 26 cycles, probably a page walk to the L2 cache; overlapped misses cost 6.4 cycles per access including the data access
c-7cpu-dtlb-l2-miss.quote: Miss penalty = 26 cycles (page walk to L2 cache ? ). Parallel miss: 6.4 cycles per access (including L2 cache access for data and page walk).

c-7cpu-walk-cache.text: A page directory cache of 24 entries, each covering a 32 MB block, covers 768 MB; a miss costs about 24 cycles
c-7cpu-walk-cache.quote: page directory cache: cover 768 MB = (24 items * 32 MB block). Miss penalty = 24 ? cycles (page walk to L2 cache ? ).

c-7cpu-latency-curve-l2.text: In the latency sweep, latency is 3 cycles at 128 KB, 11 at 256 KB (where the L2 adds 15), 15 at 512 KB, 16 at 1 MB, 17 at 2 MB, 20 at 4 MB (L1 TLB miss, +6) and 23 at 8 MB

c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.text: Beyond 8 MB the sweep reads 24 cycles + 9 ns at 16 MB, 24 + 44 ns at 32 MB (RAM, +91 ns), 32 + 66 ns at 64 MB (L2 TLB miss, +26), 55 + 90 ns at 1 GB (directory cache miss, +24) and 64 + 91 ns at 2 GB
c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.quote: 16 M 24 + 9 ns 1 + 9 ns 32 M 24 + 44 ns 0 + 35 ns + 91 ns (RAM) 64 M 32 + 66 ns 8 + 22 ns + 26 (L2 TLB miss)
c-7cpu-latency-curve-dram.notes: 16 KB pages; the 1 GB and 2 GB rows come from the same table

c-7cpu-mispredict.text: Firestorm's branch misprediction penalty is 13 cycles

c-7cpu-8b-cross.text: An access that crosses an 8-byte range pays a 1-cycle penalty

c-7cpu-l1-read-tput.text: Parallel random L1 reads take 0.34 cycles per access
c-7cpu-l1-read-tput.quote: L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 0.34 cycles per one access

c-7cpu-l1-write-tput.text: L1 write throughput is 0.5 cycles per write
c-7cpu-l1-write-tput.quote: L1 Write throughput = 0.5 cycles per one write

c-7cpu-l2-read-bw.text: L2-to-L1 reads take 2.0 cycles per cache line, for both parallel random reads and 64-byte-step reads
c-7cpu-l2-read-bw.quote: L2->L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 2.0 cycles per cache line - L2->L1 B/W (Read, 64 bytes step) = 2.0 cycles per cache line

c-7cpu-l2-write-bw.text: Writes to the L2 with a 64-byte step take 2.0 cycles per write
c-7cpu-l2-write-bw.quote: L2 Write (Write, 64 bytes step) = 2.0 cycles per write

c-7cpu-slc-read-bw.text: Parallel random reads from the SLC (7-cpu's L3) into L1 take 5 cycles per cache line
c-7cpu-slc-read-bw.quote: L3->L1 B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 5 cycles per cache line

c-7cpu-ram-random-read.text: Parallel random DRAM reads take 4 ns per line, the line probably being 128 bytes
c-7cpu-ram-random-read.quote: RAM Read B/W (Parallel Random Read) = 4 ns / access line (128 bytes ?)

c-7cpu-ram-read-bw.text: Sequential DRAM read bandwidth from one Firestorm core is 64 GB/s with 16-64 byte steps
c-7cpu-ram-read-bw.quote: RAM Read B/W (Read, 16-64 Bytes step) = 64 GB/s

c-7cpu-ram-chase-bw.text: A pointer chase through DRAM with a 64-byte step reaches 52 GB/s thanks to hardware prefetch
c-7cpu-ram-chase-bw.quote: RAM Read B/W (Read, 64 Bytes step - pointer chasing) = 52 GB/s (HW prefetch)

c-7cpu-ram-write-bw.text: Full DRAM writes with an 8-byte step reach 32-63 GB/s
c-7cpu-ram-write-bw.quote: RAM Write B/W (Write, full, 8 Bytes step) = 32-63 GB/s

c-7cpu-ram-partial-write-bw.text: Partial DRAM writes with a 16-64 byte step reach 29 GB/s
c-7cpu-ram-partial-write-bw.quote: RAM Write B/W (Write, partial, 16-64 Bytes step) = 29 GB/s

c-7cpu-clock-multi.text: 7-Zip's clock estimate is about 3200 MHz with one thread, 3092 MHz with two threads and 2983 MHz with four
c-7cpu-clock-multi.notes: value is the four-thread figure; the page does not say which cores ran the threads

c-pat-us20210064376a1-last-reference.text: Each mapping update writes a history-file entry naming the replaced physical register, marked as the last reference when no other mapping points to it; at retirement only last references go back to the free list

c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.text: Handley identifies the shared ~620-entry structure that limits register-writing instructions with the history file of Apple's last-physical-register-reference patent
c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.quote: What are these unknown shared ~620 resources?
c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent.hedge: the real answer appears to be in this patent

c-mh-v1-virtual-lsq.text: Apparent load/store queue sizes change with the probe's delay (~330, ~125/~100, ~188/~118); Handley explains this as a virtual queue: ordering IDs at rename, queue slots allocated at issue

c-pat-us20200394039a1-two-load-queues.text: An executing load gets an entry in a load execution queue, held until its data is forwarded and used for replay, and in a larger load retirement queue, held until it retires and used for ordering

c-mh-v1-lsq-patent-reading.text: Handley reads the multiple-load-queue patent as allocating load-execution-queue entries at issue and leaving retirement- and store-queue allocation open, and concludes that by the A14/M1 all are allocated at issue

c-mh-v1-early-load-release.text: With no older stores pending, loads give up their load-queue slots early, so the plain FSQRT-delay probe reaches the ~330 retire-row limit instead of the load queue
c-mh-v1-early-load-release.hedge: Apple appears to be doing this

c-pat-us9535695b2-early-load-completion.text: A load may leave the load queue once it is known not to conflict with any older store still in the store queue

c-mh-v1-store-early-release.text: Once a store is non-speculative its data can go to the L1 and its store-queue entry be reused, however far it is from retirement
c-mh-v1-store-early-release.hedge: there's a patent confirming this hypothesis

c-pat-us10228951b1-ooo-store-commit.text: A store may commit to the memory hierarchy ahead of older stores once every older store in the store queue is non-speculative

c-mh-v1-register-security-tag.text: Code that reads registers it has not itself written pays a substantial extra cost; Handley's guess is a security tag on each register mapping, checked on access, like the context tags on branch predictor entries
c-mh-v1-register-security-tag.notes: Handley later says the tag "does appear to be implemented"

c-pat-us20200192673a1-context-encrypted-.text: Indirect branch predictor entries hold target addresses encrypted with machine context, including the branch's program counter, and are decrypted with the current context when read
c-pat-us20200192673a1-context-encrypted-.notes: The predictor-side analogue Handley points to for the register tag (vol 4)

c-pat-us10747539b1-scan-on-fill.text: A next-fetch predictor built by scanning instruction-cache fills for basic-block exits whose targets resolve in one cycle; it supplies the next fetch address, and the main branch predictor checks it later
c-pat-us10747539b1-scan-on-fill.notes: Handley uses it to describe the fetch pipeline (vol 4)

c-pat-us10642618b1-callgraph-prefetch.text: An instruction prefetcher keyed on a signature of recent call and return targets: misses are recorded under the signature, and a later match triggers a prefetch
c-pat-us10642618b1-callgraph-prefetch.notes: Handley calls it Apple's second instruction prefetcher after FDIP (vol 4)

c-tm-tage.text: The M1 cores' conditional branch predictor is taken to be a TAGE variant, a hypothesis drawn from Apple patent filings that the authors say they confirm experimentally
c-tm-tage.quote: Our analysis assumes that M1 cores employ a TAGE conditional branch predictor (§ 2.3). This hypothesis is based on Apple patent filings [2, 42] and we confirm it experimentally.
c-tm-tage.notes: Patents cited are US 10,719,327 B1 and US 11,321,095 B2. No separate experiment, only that the TAGE-based 25 % aliasing signature and last-provider-component primitive behave as predicted (c-tm-lpc). Both cores.

c-tm-bruteforce.text: Brute-force out-of-place mistraining of a conditional branch on Firestorm succeeded once in about a billion attempts, implying a search space near 2^30
c-tm-bruteforce.quote: We empirically find that brute-force out-of-place mistraining on the M1 can take 1 B attempts to succeed.
c-tm-bruteforce.notes: A 26-hour run of BHI's code adapted to conditional branches; Icestorm had 4 successes in 650 M (2^27). The authors blame the TAGE multi-component structure, against 2^14-2^17 reported by BHI for Intel cores.

c-tm-lpc.text: Forcing every mistraining attempt into the last (longest-history) TAGE component cuts the brute-force attempts needed on Firestorm 32-fold
c-tm-lpc.quote: a brute force search employing our LPC primitive succeeds with 32× and 16× fewer attempts on the Firestorm and Icestorm microarchitectures, respectively
c-tm-lpc.notes: Table 2: Firestorm 33 successes in 1.1 B trials, search space about 2^25. The primitive trains the branch both ways with histories that differ only in their oldest bit, so only the full-history component can separate them.

c-tm-ice-lpc.text: Forcing mistraining into the last TAGE component cuts the brute-force attempts needed on Icestorm 16-fold
c-tm-ice-lpc.quote: a brute force search employing our LPC primitive succeeds with 32× and 16× fewer attempts on the Firestorm and Icestorm microarchitectures, respectively
c-tm-ice-lpc.notes: Table 2: Icestorm 61 successes in 565 M trials, about 2^23; plain brute force gave 4 in 650 M, about 2^27 (Table 1).

c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.text: In a slide of history-length + 1 branches, moving the first branch 4 bytes (changing PC bit 2) flips the oldest bit of the history register seen by the last branch
c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.quote: flipping the last bit of the BHR value can be achieved by moving the first branch in the branch slide 4 bytes ahead or behind in memory
c-tm-lpc-pc-bit2.notes: The paper's M1 implementation of its last-provider-component primitive (c-tm-lpc).

c-tm-counter-3bit.text: The direction predictor's saturating prediction counters are 3 bits wide
c-tm-counter-3bit.quote: finding the width of the M1 BPU’s saturating prediction counters, which we find is c = 3
c-tm-counter-3bit.notes: Appendix A.2: a branch with a fixed history whose outcome flips every N iterations mispredicts at 4/N, i.e. 2^(c-1) = 4 mispredictions per flip. Core not named; stated for both cores by default.

c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.text: PMC5 with event encoding 0xc5 counts conditional branch mispredictions
c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.quote: Overall, we identify PMC5 event 0xc5 as counting conditional branch mispredictions.
c-tm-pmc-cond-mispredict.notes: Found by sweeping event encodings against a random-outcome branch (50 %) and an N-iteration loop branch (1/N); 0xcb and 0xcd gave similar results. Counters PMC2-PMC9 are selected through PMESR0/PMESR1.

c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.text: PMC5 with event encoding 0xc6 counts indirect branch mispredictions, exclusive of the conditional event 0xc5
c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.quote: Using analogous experiments, we find that PMC5 event 0xc6 counts indirect branch mispredictions.
c-tm-pmc-ind-mispredict.notes: The authors verify 0xc5 and 0xc6 never count the same event. 0xcb and 0xce gave similar results.

c-tm-history-inputs.text: The history register takes conditional-branch PC bits 2-24, all 19 bits of the conditional branch offset, indirect-branch PC bits 2-5 and 25-30, and indirect-branch target bits 2-30
c-tm-history-inputs.quote: only bits 2–24 in a conditional branch’s PC address affect the BHR ... only bits 2–5 and 25–30 affect the BHR ... every bit 2–30 affects the BHR ... signed 19-bit field ... all these bits affect the BHR
c-tm-history-inputs.value: cond PC bits 2-24, cond offset (all 19 bits), indirect PC bits 2-5 and 25-30, indirect target bits 2-30
c-tm-history-inputs.notes: Firestorm, H = 0 (the tested branch right before the spy branch). Bits above 30 could not be swept this way; bits 32-46 are excluded separately (c-tm-high-bits-ignored) and bit 31 is left undetermined.

c-tm-high-bits-ignored.text: Bits 32-46 of branch PC and target addresses do not affect the history register
c-tm-high-bits-ignored.quote: Figure 7 shows the results for the Firestorm microarchitecture, which show that bits 32–46 do not affect the BHR.
c-tm-high-bits-ignored.notes: Tested for conditional and indirect branch PC and target bits 26-46. User and kernel addresses differ in these high bits, so a user-space shadow of a kernel path matching it in the low 32 bits reproduces its history.

c-tm-history-100.text: Firestorm's branch history length is 100 branches
c-tm-history-100.quote: We conclude that the Firestorm’s branch history length is 100.
c-tm-history-100.notes: PC bit 2 still affects the history 99 branches back, no PC bit does at 100. Distance counts branches that shift the history; not-taken conditional branches do not (c-tm-history-update).

c-tm-ice-history-60.text: Icestorm's branch history length is 60 branches
c-tm-ice-history-60.quote: Icestorm results (not shown) indicate that its history length is 60.

c-tm-bhr-width.text: Firestorm's branch history register is 100 bits wide, one bit of shift per history update over 100 branches
c-tm-bhr-width.quote: It follows from the results of § 6.3.6 and § 6.3.5 that the BHR width of Firestorm and Icestorm cores is 100 and 60 bits, respectively.
c-tm-bhr-width.notes: The authors derive width = shift per update (1 bit) x history length (100); the history length is in c-tm-history-100.

c-tm-ice-bhr-width.text: Icestorm's branch history register is 60 bits wide
c-tm-ice-bhr-width.quote: It follows from the results of § 6.3.6 and § 6.3.5 that the BHR width of Firestorm and Icestorm cores is 100 and 60 bits, respectively.
c-tm-ice-bhr-width.notes: Width = 1-bit shift x 60-branch history length, as the authors derive it.

c-tm-history-update.text: Each history update shifts the register by one bit and XORs in the branch's bits; direct unconditional branches shift it, not-taken conditional branches do not
c-tm-history-update.quote: demonstrating that non-taken conditional branches do not shift the BHR ... which shows that direct (unconditional) branches do shift the BHR ... all the immediate offset bits except 2 are XORed to the shifted (by one bit) BHR
c-tm-history-update.value: shift 1 bit and XOR in branch bits per update; not-taken conditional branches do not shift
c-tm-history-update.notes: Firestorm figures (Fig. 10, 11). Taken conditional and indirect branches also shift by one bit (c-tm-pc-shift-xor, c-tm-target-shift-xor).

c-tm-imm-shift-xor.text: Bits 0-1 and 3-16 of a conditional branch's offset are XORed, unshifted, into the history register after it shifts by one bit
c-tm-imm-shift-xor.quote: We find that bits 0–1 and 3–16 of a conditional branch’s immediate jump offset use a shift-and-XOR1 update policy.
c-tm-imm-shift-xor.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 10). The bits are not shifted before the XOR: offset bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - i (Fig. 19). Offset bit 2 does not follow the pattern.

c-tm-pc-shift-xor.text: Taken conditional branches XOR their PC bits into the history register after shifting it by one bit
c-tm-pc-shift-xor.quote: BHR update policy of taken conditional branch PC address bits is shift-and-XOR with a shift value of 1.
c-tm-pc-shift-xor.notes: Table 3 lists conditional PC bits 2-4 and 6-24 as following this policy, unshifted. PC bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - (i - 2) (Fig. 21). Firestorm.

c-tm-target-shift-xor.text: Indirect branches XOR their target bits into the history register after shifting it by one bit
c-tm-target-shift-xor.quote: BHR update policy of indirect branch target address bits is shift-and-XOR with a shift value of 1.
c-tm-target-shift-xor.notes: Table 3 lists target bits 2-20 as following this policy, unshifted. Target bit i stops affecting the history at H = 100 - (i - 2) (Fig. 24). Firestorm.

c-tm-ind-pc-position.text: An indirect branch's PC bit i stops affecting the history register at distance H = 100 - (72 - (i - 2)), much sooner than conditional-branch PC or indirect target bits, which last about 100 branches
c-tm-ind-pc-position.quote: Effect of indirect branch PC address bit i on the BHR is lost at distance H = 100 − (72 − (i − 2)) from the spy branch
c-tm-ind-pc-position.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 22, which shows bit 2 at H = 27 and H = 28).

c-tm-not-taken-updates.text: A not-taken conditional branch, though it does not shift the history register, still changes it in some undetermined way
c-tm-not-taken-updates.quote: The results of the experiment (Figure 13) confirm that a non-taken conditional branch does update the BHR in some undetermined manner.
c-tm-not-taken-updates.notes: Firestorm (Fig. 13); test uses 100 taken conditional branches spaced 2^32 or more bytes apart so only the switch branch's outcome differs.

c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.text: Firestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between user space and kernel: a user process can mistrain a kernel branch, and did so to exploit a Spectre v1 gadget in a kext
c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.quote: userspace/kernel isolation appears to exist on the Icestorm microarchitecture, but it does not exist on Firestorm ... we also successfully use userspace out-of-space mistraining on a Firestorm core to exploit an in-kext Spectre v1 gadget
c-tm-no-user-kernel-isolation.notes: Victim branch in a kext reached by sysctl; the attacker trains a user-space shadow of its branch slide matching the kernel addresses in the low 32 bits. Victim misprediction rate 25 % on Firestorm (Fig. 14).

c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.text: Icestorm appears to isolate conditional-predictor state between user space and kernel
c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.quote: Figure 14 shows the results, indicating that userspace/kernel isolation appears to exist on the Icestorm microarchitecture
c-tm-ice-user-kernel-isolation.notes: Footnote 6 says a different mistraining technique might still succeed.

c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.text: Firestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between processes: a process mistrained a branch in another process and exploited a Spectre v1 gadget there
c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.quote: Figure 15 shows the results, which indicate that cross-BPU isolation does not exist. We further validate these results by successfully using cross-process out-of-space mistraining to exploit a Spectre v1 gadget in another process
c-tm-no-cross-process-isolation.notes: Both processes bound to the same core, with an identical branch slide mapped at the same address (Fig. 15).

c-tm-ice-no-cross-process-isolation.text: Icestorm does not isolate conditional-predictor state between processes
c-tm-ice-no-cross-process-isolation.quote: We also find that no cross-process BPU isolation exists on either microarchitecture.

c-tm-patent-security-tag.text: Per the authors' reading of Apple's indirect-predictor security patent, BTB entries carry a security tag of the context that made them (exception level against cross-privilege training, a process identifier against cross-process training) and mismatched entries are ignored
c-tm-patent-security-tag.quote: Apple’s mechanism thus dynamically isolates BTB entries of different security contexts. ... Cross-privilege attacks (e.g., process vs. OS) are blocked by storing the privilege level (EL). ... blocked by storing a process identifier.
c-tm-patent-security-tag.notes: Patent US 11,321,095 B2, same title as us20200192673a1. Not tested on the M1; the paper notes Apple has no matching patent for the conditional predictor.

c-dimva-inplace-pht.text: Nine in-bounds calls train a bounds-check branch enough that the tenth, out-of-bounds call is mispredicted, giving a working in-place Spectre-PHT attack on the M1
c-dimva-inplace-pht.quote: We call the gadget with an in-bound value 9 times to bias the prediction to predict that the provided index is always in bounds. ... In the 10th call to the gadget, we provide an out-of-bounds index
c-dimva-inplace-pht.notes: M1 Mac mini, macOS 11.2.1; core type not stated. Each value is leaked 4 times to cover imperfect misprediction. Leakage 1109 B/s at 13.66 % error on the M1 (Table 3).

c-dimva-spectre-btb.text: An in-place, same-address-space Spectre-BTB attack, mistraining an indirect branch's target, works on the M1
c-dimva-spectre-btb.quote: we show a Spectre-PHT and Spectre-BTB implementation on two iPhones and an M1 Mac mini
c-dimva-spectre-btb.notes: The authors say no hardware or software mitigation exists for their same-address-space, in-place Spectre-BTB. Core type not stated.

c-dimva-csdb.text: On the M1, a CSDB barrier after the bounds check stops Spectre-PHT leakage
c-dimva-csdb.quote: the M1 Mac mini, CSDB is available and stops the leakage in our proof of concept
c-dimva-csdb.notes: On the A10 and A11 iPhones CSDB has no effect. Core type not stated.

c-dimva-isb.text: An ISB barrier prevents Spectre-PHT exploitation on the M1
c-dimva-isb.quote: The ISB instruction prevents exploitation on both iPhones and the M1 Mac mini.

c-dimva-dmb-dsb.text: DMB or DSB on its own does not stop speculative execution past the mispredicted bounds check
c-dimva-dmb-dsb.quote: Data Memory Barriers (DMB) or DSB alone do not stop speculative execution.
c-dimva-dmb-dsb.notes: Stated for the tested devices (A10, A11, M1) together.

c-ox-decode-8.text: The decoder is eight instructions wide and consumes eight per cycle when instructions arrive without delay
c-ox-decode-8.quote: M1 has a decoder with eight instruction width. As long as instructions are fed without delay, the decoder can consume eight of them per cycle.

c-ox-mov-elim-8.text: Rename eliminates register-to-register movs at up to eight per cycle, scalar and SIMD/fp combined
c-ox-mov-elim-8.quote: It can process up to eight inter-register mov instructions in total for scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-chained-mov.text: Chains of dependent movs are also eliminated, but only in the scalar domain
c-ox-chained-mov.quote: Chained movs are also eliminated, for ones in the scalar domain.

c-ox-nop-decoder.text: NOPs are removed in the decoder and use no execution unit
c-ox-nop-decoder.quote: NOP instruction is also removed in the decoder and consumes no execution unit.
c-ox-nop-decoder.notes: Johnson counts a nop as one uop (it occupies pipeline width and retire slots) with no issue

c-ox-mov-imm-8.text: Immediate-loading movs run at up to eight per cycle without using an execution unit, probably handled when they enter the reservation station
c-ox-mov-imm-8.quote: it processes up to eight immediate-loading mov instructions per cycle, probably when it enqueues them into the reservation station. This makes immediate-loading mov not consume any execution unit.
c-ox-mov-imm-8.notes: Eight per cycle on an 8-wide core is 8 per 8 instructions; Johnson gives 2 per 8 handled by renaming (c-dj-mov-imm)

c-ox-vector-zero.text: Instructions that clear a vector register run at eight per cycle without an execution unit
c-ox-vector-zero.quote: operations clearing a vector register are processed eight per cycle without any execution unit

c-ox-simd-zero-reg.text: The author takes zero-cost vector clearing to mean there is a physical zero register in the SIMD/fp domain too
c-ox-simd-zero-reg.quote: implying there is a physical zero register in the SIMD/fp domain, too

c-ox-eor-no-idiom.text: Clearing a register with EOR gets no special treatment: it executes on a unit like any other instruction and does not break the dependency on its source
c-ox-eor-no-idiom.quote: M1 does not put a special treat on clearing registers using bitwise xor operation (EOR instruction). ... Dependency breakage from source to destination is also not detected for these operations.

c-ox-mispredict.text: The branch misprediction penalty is probably 13 or 14 cycles
c-ox-mispredict.quote: The branch misprediction penalty is probably 13 or 14 cycles.

c-ox-l1i-192.text: The L1 instruction cache is 192 KB
c-ox-l1i-192.quote: The level 1 instruction (L1I) cache is 192KB large
c-ox-l1i-192.notes: No measurement given; the notes credit AnandTech for the cache configuration

c-ox-fetch-8.text: The L1I feeds eight instructions per cycle to the decoder
c-ox-fetch-8.quote: The level 1 instruction (L1I) cache ... feeds 8 instructions to the decoder per cycle.

c-ox-btb-zero-bubble.text: When a branch hits both the L1I and the first-level BTB, fetch can redirect to the predicted target every cycle with no bubble
c-ox-btb-zero-bubble.quote: When both the L1I cache and the level 1 branch target buffer (L1 BTB) hit, the instruction feeder can jump to the predicted target every cycle without delay.

c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.text: A taken branch that hits the L1I but misses the first-level BTB delays instruction feeding by two cycles
c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.quote: A branch that hits L1I but misses L1 BTB delays the instruction feeding by two clock cycles.
c-ox-btb-miss-bubble.notes: ocxtal's "L1 BTB" is the KB's zero-bubble tier (btb.l0_*); this is the bubble of the next tier, a branch that hits only the L1I

c-ox-btb-1024.text: The first-level (zero-bubble) BTB seems to have 1024 entries; its exact configuration is unclear
c-ox-btb-1024.quote: There seem 1024 entries in the first level BTB while the exact configuration is unclear.
c-ox-btb-1024.hedge: There seem ... while the exact configuration is unclear

c-ox-two-branches.text: Up to two branches per cycle are dispatched and committed, but only when one of the two is a not-taken conditional branch, probably a limit of the instruction feeder
c-ox-two-branches.quote: M1 can process (dispatch and commit) up to two branch instructions per cycle. However, this throughput is obtained only when one of the two branch instructions is a not-taken conditional one
c-ox-two-branches.hedge: probably due to the limitation in the instruction feeder

c-ox-b-no-alu.text: A plain unconditional B uses no integer unit; BL, BLR and RET each take one slot on a flag-capable integer unit
c-ox-b-no-alu.quote: The simplest unconditional branch (B instruction) does not consume integer execution units, but the others including BL, BLR, and RET consume one slot of flag-manipulating integer units.

c-ox-ls-units.text: Four load/store units, two load-only, one store-only and one for both, giving up to three loads or two stores per cycle
c-ox-ls-units.quote: M1 has four load/store units in total: two for the load, one for the store, and one for both. Thus the maximum throughput is three for load instructions and two for stores.

c-ox-ls-128bit.text: Each load/store unit has a 128-bit data path serving both the scalar and SIMD/fp register files
c-ox-ls-128bit.quote: Each load/store unit has a 128-bit data path that accesses both the scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-agu-index.text: The load/store units generate simple signed and unsigned offset addresses without an integer uop; pre- and post-index forms add a uop to write back the updated address
c-ox-agu-index.quote: processing simple signed and unsigned offset forms without integer uOP. However, pre- and post-index forms generate an additional uOP to write the updated address back.

c-ox-load-lat-int.text: Load latency is three cycles into scalar registers
c-ox-load-lat-int.quote: The latency of load operations appears to be three cycles in the scalar and five in the SIMD/fp domain.

c-ox-load-lat-simd.text: Load latency is five cycles into SIMD/fp registers
c-ox-load-lat-simd.quote: The latency of load operations appears to be three cycles in the scalar and five in the SIMD/fp domain.

c-ox-load-penalty.text: Unaligned loads, cross-cache loads and sign-extending loads each add one cycle of latency
c-ox-load-penalty.quote: Unaligned loads, cross-cache loads, and sign extensions put a penalty of one clock cycle.
c-ox-load-penalty.notes: In some cases the unaligned penalty seems hidden by the sign-extension one

c-ox-page-cross.text: A load that crosses a page boundary costs about 28 extra cycles
c-ox-page-cross.quote: The page-crossing penalty is around 28 cycles.

c-ox-store-load.text: A load from the address of a preceding store sees five or six cycles of latency, read back through the fill buffer
c-ox-store-load.quote: Turnaround latency for a load operation from the same address after a store (reading back via the fill buffer) looks like five or six cycles.
c-ox-store-load.notes: five or six cycles; midpoint given

c-ox-no-aliasing.text: No memory-aliasing mechanism was seen in the load/store path
c-ox-no-aliasing.quote: A mechanism like memory aliasing doesn't seem to exist.

c-ox-ld3-throughput.text: The pipelined permute unit in the memory path completes one three-register LD3 or ST3 per cycle
c-ox-ld3-throughput.quote: The permute unit is pipelined and can perform one three-register permute operation (LD3 or ST3) every cycle.

c-ox-ld3-latency.text: The LD3/ST3 permutation adds two or three cycles of latency
c-ox-ld3-latency.quote: The latency of the permutation looks to be two or three cycles.
c-ox-ld3-latency.notes: two or three cycles; midpoint given

c-ox-lq-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the load queue has more than 150 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-lq-anandtech.quote: I haven't investigated the depths of load queues and store queues. AnandTech's article reports that they have more than 150 and 100 entries, respectively.
c-ox-lq-anandtech.notes: A repeat of AnandTech (c-at-lq). Lower bound ("more than"); Johnson gives 130 (c-dj-loads)

c-ox-sq-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the store queue has more than 100 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-sq-anandtech.quote: I haven't investigated the depths of load queues and store queues. AnandTech's article reports that they have more than 150 and 100 entries, respectively.
c-ox-sq-anandtech.notes: A repeat of AnandTech (c-at-sq). Lower bound ("more than"); Johnson gives 60 (c-dj-stores)

c-ox-int-units.text: Six scalar integer units, all doing basic arithmetic and logic, separate from the load/store units
c-ox-int-units.quote: Table 1 shows the capability of the six execution units in the scalar domain. ... All the six units can process basic arithmetic and logical instructions.

c-ox-int-roles.text: Scalar unit roles (names arbitrary): all six do ALU ops, shifts, ctz, rev and pre/post-index address updates; X3 and X4 multiply, X3 also multiply-add, bfm and crc32, X4 also divide; X0-X2 flag-setting ops; X0-X1 branches
c-ox-int-roles.quote: It has two multiply units in X3 and X4. One of which (X3) can also handle multiply-add instructions. ... The X4 unit, the multiply unit without multiply-add capability, handles divide instructions instead.
c-ox-int-roles.notes: Table 1 marks X0-X2 for flag-setting ops (Johnson's units 1-3); the text below it says "X0, X1, and X3". X3 and X4 match Johnson's units 6 and 5

c-ox-alu-1cycle.text: Basic ALU ops, including variable shifts, bit reverse and count trailing zeros, are single-cycle on all six units
c-ox-alu-1cycle.quote: M1 can process basic arithmetic and logical instructions in all units from X0 to X5 in a single clock cycle. ... variable-width shift, bit reversal, and count trailing zeros are also single-cycle operations.

c-ox-shift-form.text: Shifted-operand ALU forms add one cycle of latency and run on all six units; the shift is not a separate uop
c-ox-shift-form.quote: Shift-form arithmetic and logical instructions increase the latency by one cycle from the base form. ... indicating the shift part is not separated into a uOP.

c-ox-madd.text: Multiply-add is a single uop on one unit, issuing every cycle with three-cycle latency
c-ox-madd.quote: The multiply-add operation seems expressed as a single uOP, dispatched to a single unit every cycle and executed in three cycles.

c-ox-div-latency.text: Integer divide latency is at least seven cycles
c-ox-div-latency.quote: The latency of divide instructions seems seven cycles at the minimum.

c-ox-div-throughput.text: Back-to-back divides issue with one dead slot between them, one divide every two cycles
c-ox-div-throughput.quote: Consecutive divides are dispatched with a dead slot of one in between, resulting in a throughput of one instruction per two cycles.

c-ox-div-pipeline.text: Divides do not hold up other instructions on their unit, so the divider is probably a separate pipeline that shares only the dispatch queue
c-ox-div-pipeline.quote: divide instructions do not seem to limit or delay the execution of non-divide instructions ... Perhaps divide instruction has a dedicated execution pipeline and shares only the dispatch queue part with others

c-ox-fp-units.text: Four SIMD/fp units, all capable of most arithmetic and logic instructions
c-ox-fp-units.quote: There are four execution ports in the SIMD/fp domain, which I denote V0 to V3. All ports are capable of most of the arithmetic and logic instructions.

c-ox-fp-roles.text: SIMD/fp unit roles (names arbitrary): only V0 does fp divide, reciprocal, square root, flag-setting fp compare, crypto and fjcvtzs; V0 and V1 do conditional select; all four do almost everything else
c-ox-fp-roles.quote: V0 is a fat unit that handles division and some special instructions. ... Conditional selection instructions are processed in two units, V0 and V1.
c-ox-fp-roles.notes: V0 and V1 match Johnson's units 14 and 13

c-ox-simd-lat-2.text: Basic SIMD arithmetic and logic ops have two-cycle latency at four per cycle
c-ox-simd-lat-2.quote: All execution units, V0~V3, processes basic arithmetic and logical operations with a latency of two cycles and a throughput of four per clock cycle.

c-ox-simd-lat-3.text: Most other SIMD ops, including saturating, rounding, horizontal, high-narrow, absolute-difference and integer multiply and multiply-accumulate, take three cycles
c-ox-simd-lat-3.quote: Most others are three-cycle instructions, such as saturating and rounding arithmetic, horizontal, high-narrow form, and absolute difference operations. It is noticeable that integer multiplication and multiply-accumulate are processed in three cycles, too.

c-ox-xfer-fwd.text: Moves from scalar to SIMD/fp registers use a load-unit slot, at up to three per cycle
c-ox-xfer-fwd.quote: The forward transfer, scalar-to-SIMD/fp direction, uses a slot in the load units ... Throughput is three instructions every cycle for the forward
c-ox-xfer-fwd.notes: A plain FMOV uses only the load slot; DUP and INS also take a SIMD/fp slot

c-ox-xfer-rev.text: Moves from SIMD/fp to scalar registers use dedicated paths, at up to two per cycle
c-ox-xfer-rev.quote: the reverse has dedicated paths ... two for the opposite direction
c-ox-xfer-rev.notes: Each takes one SIMD/fp slot and several scalar slots

c-ox-xfer-latency.text: Register transfers between the scalar and SIMD/fp domains take six cycles in either direction
c-ox-xfer-latency.quote: Latency appears to be six cycles in both directions.

c-ox-xfer-fusion.text: A cross-domain transfer can fuse with the operation right after it, hiding one cycle of latency
c-ox-xfer-fusion.quote: In either direction, a transfer instruction may fuse with an operation immediately after the transfer, where the latency for one cycle is hidden.

c-ox-cvt.text: Integer-to-fp conversion into an fp register takes one SIMD/fp slot on any of the four units, three cycles at four per cycle
c-ox-cvt.quote: If the write destination is a floating point register, a conversion instruction occupies only one slot in the SIMD/fp domain. In this case, the latency and throughput are three cycles and four per cycle
c-ox-cvt.notes: With a scalar destination latency rises by six cycles and throughput falls to three per cycle; fp-to-int conversions behave the same way

c-ox-flag-files.text: The scalar and SIMD/fp domains have separate condition-flag register files
c-ox-flag-files.quote: M1 has independent condition flag files for the scalar and SIMD/fp domains.

c-ox-flag-xfer.text: Moving flags between the two domains probably costs six cycles each time; chains within one domain cost nothing
c-ox-flag-xfer.quote: Flag transfer across domains will probably be penalized for six cycles each time, while in-domain chains have no penalty.
c-ox-flag-xfer.notes: The forward direction has a dedicated path; the reverse shares the register-transfer route

c-ox-rob-anandtech.text: Repeating AnandTech, the reorder buffer has more than 600 entries; the author did not measure it
c-ox-rob-anandtech.quote: According to the AnandTech article, the reorder buffer has more than 600 entries.
c-ox-rob-anandtech.notes: Lower bound; the KB maps AnandTech's ROB figure to the rename retire queue (c-at-rob-630)

c-cc-oryon-m1-clusters.text: M1 groups its cores in quad-core clusters that share an L2, with a hybrid (big and little) core arrangement
c-cc-oryon-m1-clusters.quote: Apple also uses quad core clusters with a shared L2. However, M1 uses a hybrid core arrangement.

c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.text: Core-to-core latency on M1 is similar to Snapdragon X Elite within a cluster; cross-cluster transfers are slow, though a bit faster than on X Elite
c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.quote: Core to core latency is similar within a cluster. Cross-cluster transfers incur high latency much like on Snapdragon X Elite, though absolute values are a bit better.
c-cc-oryon-m1-c2c.notes: Cacheline ping-pong between core pairs, run under Asahi Linux on an M1 MacBook Air; the text gives no M1 number (Zen 4's 80-90 ns cross-cluster latency is said to be better than M1's)

c-cc-oryon-m1-slc.text: M1 has a system level cache that serves several blocks on the chip, slower than a cache dedicated to one block
c-cc-oryon-m1-slc.quote: Both Snapdragon X Elite and M1 have a System Level Cache (SLC) that can service multiple blocks on the chip, at the expense of lower performance than a cache dedicated to one block.

c-cc-oryon-m1-clock.text: Unlike Oryon, M1 does not run at 4 GHz
c-cc-oryon-m1-clock.quote: But unlike Kryo and M1, Oryon can run at 4 GHz and beyond.

c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.text: M1's taken-branch latency rises as the test's code footprint passes certain sizes; single-cycle taken branches only within a 4 KB footprint
c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.quote: It also shares traits with M1, which also sees taken branch latency increase as the test exceeds certain code footprint sizes. M1 however only gets single cycle branching within 4 KB.
c-cc-oryon-m1-taken-footprint.notes: The article reads the same footprint behaviour on Oryon as a BTB tied to the instruction cache and contrasts Zen 4, Arm and Intel cores as decoupled; the M1 variant tested is not stated

c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.text: Firestorm apparently has a 50-entry return stack
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.quote: Qualcomm's strategy mirrors that of Apple M1's Firestorm architecture, which apparently has a 50 entry return stack
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-50.notes: Not measured in the article; given with a link, and the overflow result is credited to Dougall Johnson

c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.text: Johnson found a sharp rise in call+return time on M1 once the return stack overflows, as on Oryon; the article reads this as the core clearing the return stack on overflow
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.quote: When return stack capacity is exceeded, Oryon sees a sharp increase in call+return time. ... That's similar to what Dougall discovered on Apple's M1 too, and suggests the core clears the return stack when it overflows
c-cc-oryon-m1-ras-overflow.notes: The clearing reading follows the Oryon result; the article does not say it was checked on M1

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-192.text: Firestorm has a 192 KB L1 instruction cache
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-192.quote: Oryon and Apple's Firestorm cores use a very similar strategy. Both have a huge 192 KB L1 instruction cache feeding a 8-wide decoder.

c-cc-oryon-m1-decode-8.text: Firestorm's L1I feeds an eight-wide decoder
c-cc-oryon-m1-decode-8.quote: Oryon and Apple's Firestorm cores use a very similar strategy. Both have a huge 192 KB L1 instruction cache feeding a 8-wide decoder.

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.text: Code fetch bandwidth on M1 falls far lower once the code footprint misses the L1i
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.quote: Credit to Dougall for contributing the M1 Max test result. ... Oryon and M1 have much lower code fetch bandwidth after a L1i miss.
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1i-miss-fetch.notes: M1 Max result contributed by Dougall Johnson; the text gives no M1 number (Zen 4 sustains more than 12 bytes per cycle even from L3)

c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.text: Firestorm has 134 scheduler entries for basic integer operations
c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.quote: Oryon can bring an incredible 120 scheduler entries to bear for basic integer operations alone. It's just short of Firestorm's 134 entries
c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134.notes: Taken from Johnson's scheduler diagram, which the article reproduces; whether the count includes the non-scheduling dispatch queue is not stated

c-cc-oryon-m1-fp-sched.text: Firestorm's FP/vector schedulers are smaller than Oryon's 192 entries, backed by a non-scheduling queue that delays stalls at rename
c-cc-oryon-m1-fp-sched.quote: Firestorm also stands apart in using smaller (though still large in an absolute sense) schedulers, and compensating for that with a non-scheduling queue that can delay a stall at the rename stage.

c-cc-oryon-m1-agu-sched.text: Firestorm's AGU scheduling queues and non-scheduling queue together hold fewer micro-ops than Oryon's four 16-entry AGU schedulers
c-cc-oryon-m1-agu-sched.quote: four 16 entry schedulers are nothing to sneeze at. Together, those schedulers can hold more micro-ops than Firestorm's AGU scheduling and non-scheduling queues combined.

c-cc-oryon-m1-l1d-128.text: Firestorm has a 128 KB L1 data cache
c-cc-oryon-m1-l1d-128.quote: Firestorm has a bigger 128 KB L1, but Oryon's L1 is still much larger

c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.text: M1 has a 192 KB L1 instruction cache
c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.quote: Adding the 192 KB L1i and 128 KB L1D gives 320 KB of total capacity.
c-cc-gcc-l1i-192.notes: Sizes used for a ChampSim model of M1 Max's caches

c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.text: M1 has a 128 KB L1 data cache
c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.quote: Adding the 192 KB L1i and 128 KB L1D gives 320 KB of total capacity.
c-cc-gcc-l1d-128.notes: Sizes used for a ChampSim model of M1 Max's caches

c-cc-gcc-l1d-3c.quote: On top of that, M1's L1D has 3 cycle latency.

c-cc-gcc-l2-llc.text: Given its size and the system level cache's high latency, M1's L2 acts as the CPU cluster's last-level cache; its latency matches Gracemont's L2 (AnandTech data)
c-cc-gcc-l2-llc.quote: From the L2 cache's size and the system level cache's high latency, it looks like M1's L2 functions as a last level cache for the CPU cluster.

c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-48.text: M1 Max has a 48 MB system level cache
c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-48.quote: M1 Max's 48 MB system level cache seems to fill the same role as eDRAM on Intel's big iGPU SKUs

c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-gpu.text: M1 Max's SLC sits near the memory controller, with latency too high to suit CPU accesses; it looks aimed at the GPU
c-cc-gcc-m1max-slc-gpu.quote: Because it's placed close to the memory controller, it suffers high latency that makes it non-ideal for CPU accesses. Instead, it looks targeted towards M1 Max's huge integrated GPU.

c-cc-clk-m1-cores.quote: Its four Firestorm cores feature a very wide and deep architecture running at low clocks

c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.text: M1's Firestorm cores reach a maximum clock of 3.2 GHz
c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.quote: gradually increase frequency until they reach their maximum 3.2 GHz clock slightly after 100 ms.
c-cc-clk-m1-max-clock.notes: Run by Dougall Johnson on an M1 Mac Mini; the test infers clock from the time to run a known number of dependent integer adds

c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.text: From idle, Firestorm clocks start rising after about 20 ms and climb gradually to maximum slightly after 100 ms, with much run-to-run variation
c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.quote: the Firestorm cores start increasing their clocks after about 20 ms, and gradually increase frequency until they reach their maximum 3.2 GHz clock slightly after 100 ms
c-cc-clk-m1-ramp.notes: Sometimes just above 2 GHz after 20-30 ms; Mac Mini on wall power

c-cc-clk-m1max-layout.text: M1 Max adds a second quad-core Firestorm cluster and has two Icestorm cores
c-cc-clk-m1max-layout.quote: M1 Max adds another quad core Firestorm cluster, drops the little (Icestorm) core count to two, and massively increases the GPU size.

c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.text: M1 Max's Firestorm cores ramp to 3.23 GHz in High Power mode
c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.quote: After that, M1 Max stays at 2.67 GHz if it's set to "Low Power", or slowly ramps to 3.23 GHz if "High Power" is set.
c-cc-clk-m1max-max-clock.notes: M1 Max value for pcluster.clock_max; run by Dougall Johnson

c-cc-clk-m1max-low-power.text: In Low Power mode M1 Max appears capped at 2.67 GHz, with the boost behaviour otherwise unchanged
c-cc-clk-m1max-low-power.quote: M1 Max appears to be capped to 2.67 GHz, but boosting behavior doesn't change beyond stopping at 2.67 GHz.

c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.text: On its best runs M1 Max reaches 2.67 GHz in just over 10 ms from idle
c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.quote: On the best runs, it reaches 2.67 GHz in just over 10 ms.
c-cc-clk-m1max-ramp.notes: 3.23 GHz after 43 ms on one run; nearly 100 ms to 3.2 GHz on others

c-cc-clk-m1max-hw-boost.text: Apple may control boosting in hardware, since M1 Max reaches an intermediate frequency step in just over 10 ms
c-cc-clk-m1max-hw-boost.quote: Apple may have hardware control over speed boosting, since M1 Max is able to hit an intermediate frequency step in just over 10 ms.

c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.text: With an FSQRT chain as the delay, independent loads show a jump at ~330; Handley notes the limit looks like the ROB's "failable" slots rather than a load-queue size
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.quote: a jump at ~330, which would suggests that the LSQ can hold 328 loads
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-330.notes: Stores show the same jump. Handley later attributes it to ~330 ROB rows that each hold one load or store, loads having released their queue slots early

c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.text: Past the ~330 jump, both the load and the store FSQRT probes run at about four memory ops per cycle until N of about 420, then return to their unit-limited slope
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.quote: same jump at ~330, - same running at about 4-wide till N=~420
c-mh-v1-lsq-fsqrt-4wide.notes: Handley explains the 4-wide stretch by four 12-entry LS scheduling queues, each fed one op per cycle, until the store/AMX queue fills with loads it never issues

c-mh-v1-ls-units-3l-2s.text: M1 has two load units, one store unit and one unit that does either, so it runs at most 3 loads or 2 stores per cycle; this sets the different slopes of the load and store probes
c-mh-v1-ls-units-3l-2s.quote: 2 load units - 1 store unit - 1 ambidextrous unit so that it can run either 3 loads/cycle or 2 stores/cycle

c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.text: With a chain of loads that miss to DRAM as the delay, the load probe shows a discontinuity at N of about 125, which Handley takes as the load-queue size
c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.quote: there appears to be load queue, of size ~125 loads
c-mh-v1-lq-dram-125.notes: Noisy; read off a moving-median smoothed curve. The slots are genuine load-queue entries; Handley's own count of the queue is ~130 (c-mh-v1-lq-130).

c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.text: With the DRAM-miss delay, the store probe shows a discontinuity at around 100 stores
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.quote: there appears to be store queue, of size ~100 stores
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-100.notes: Not the store-queue size: Handley later explains the jump as 60 store-queue plus 48 scheduling-queue slots, 48+60=108 (c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108)

c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.text: With an FSQRT chain feeding a store's address as the delay, the load probe jumps cleanly at N=188, matching Johnson's result from a branch-based version of the probe
c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.quote: We see a clear jump at N=188 (load queue can hold 188 entries) and this matches Dougall's results
c-mh-v1-lq-storeaddr-188.notes: Handley reads 188 as ~130 genuine load-queue entries plus 58 dispatch-buffer and scheduler slots

c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.text: With the same FSQRT-to-store-address delay, the store probe jumps cleanly at ~118 stores, again matching Johnson
c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.quote: Again we see a nice clean jump, giving us ~118 store queue slots, again matching Dougall's result.
c-mh-v1-sq-storeaddr-118.notes: Read as ~60 store-queue entries plus 58 dispatch/scheduler slots. Younger stores stay speculative behind the unresolved store address even when aligned; Handley thinks Apple does not special-case that

c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.text: The ~330 jump of the plain FSQRT probe is the ROB limit: ~330 rows of up to 7 instructions, each row holding only one "failable" instruction, and loads, stores and branches are failable
c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.quote: the ROB consists of ~330 rows, each row can hold 7 instructions, but only one "failable"
c-mh-v1-rob-rows-330.notes: Restates the conclusion of Handley's ROB section (c-mh-v1-rob-rows); the same structure as Johnson's coalesced retire groups

c-mh-v1-lq-130.text: M1 has ~130 genuine load-queue (LRQ) entries, amplified for most code by early release of entries and by late, at-issue allocation
c-mh-v1-lq-130.quote: the M1 has a pool of ~130 genuine Load Queue entries (ie LRQ entries)

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.text: When the physical load or store queue slots run out, further loads or stores wait first in the 48 load-store scheduling-queue entries, then in the 10 load-store dispatch-buffer entries, before Rename stalls
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.quote: pile up, first in the 48 LS Scheduling Queue entries, then in the 10 LS Dispatch Buffer entries
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48.notes: Sizes from Johnson's diagram; the probes test only their sum, 58, the excess of the 188-load and 118-store jumps over the ~130 and ~60 genuine queues. The 48 is four 12-entry queues (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12).

c-mh-v1-late-alloc-58.text: Allocating queue slots at issue lets 58 more loads or stores in before Rename stalls than allocation at rename would: about 50% more effective load-queue and 100% more effective store-queue capacity
c-mh-v1-late-alloc-58.quote: late allocation allows us to enqueue 58 more loads or stores than traditional allocation before we have to stall

c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108.text: Under the DRAM-miss delay the store jump comes when the 60 store-queue and 48 scheduling-queue slots are full (48+60=108); a delay load parked in the dispatch buffer cannot issue, so the buffer does not count
c-mh-v1-sq-dram-108.quote: the N, number of stores, at which we should expect a jump is in fact 48+60=108, omitting the 10 storage units of the Dispatch Buffer

c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.text: The load-store dispatch buffer does not try to dispatch the oldest instruction first, so movement into the scheduling queues is somewhat stochastic once both are full
c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.quote: the Dispatch Buffer makes no serious attempt to preserve ordering and Dispatch the oldest instruction
c-mh-v1-ls-dispatch-unordered.notes: Offered to explain noise in the DRAM-delay probe; Handley later repeats that the dispatch buffer does not promise order

c-mh-v1-sq-late-alloc-60.text: Store-queue slots are allocated late as well: in both store probes many stores get past Rename while the ~60-entry store queue is full
c-mh-v1-sq-late-alloc-60.quote: many stores can progress past Rename even when the Store Queue (of size ~60 entries) is full

c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.text: In the plain FSQRT store probe the jump stays at ~330 stores whether the stores hit one address, successive addresses, or addresses 64 bytes apart, so it is not culling of overwritten stores
c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.quote: So I separated successive stores by 64 bytes and again, no change, the jump in the curve is at ~330 stores.
c-mh-v1-store-fsqrt-not-idempotent.notes: Handley's explanation is store-queue release once a store is non-speculative (c-mh-v1-store-early-release)

c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.text: Load/store has a dispatch buffer of about 10 entries; the size is read off Johnson's diagram, which Handley accepts as probably correct
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.quote: This shows a single Dispatch Buffer holding 10 entries (probably correct)
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls.notes: Handley does not measure it: his drain argument starts "Let's start by assuming the diagram is correct", and his late-allocation accounting only tests the 48+10=58 sum

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.text: The load-store scheduler drawn as one 48-entry queue is four 12-entry queues, each fed one op per cycle by the dispatch buffer and paired so a queue can issue from its partner; this explains the 4-wide stretch from N 330 to 420
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.quote: this apparently monolithic queue is actually four queues each 12 entries in size
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12.notes: Also stated earlier (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48). 4 x 12 = 48, consistent with c-mh-v1-sched-ls-48

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.text: Handley's model of the A14/M1 load-store scheduling queues is two pairs, a store/AMX queue with a load queue and a store/AMX/load queue with a load queue, the third load pipe reusing store machinery
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.quote: So we land up, finally, with a structure that looks like (SA0 L2) (SAL1 L3)
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairs.notes: Explains the drop to 3 loads/cycle at N of about 420 (the SA0 queue fills with loads that never issue). Excess buffer past the queues: 10 dispatch + 12 (one L queue) for loads, 10 + 24 (two S queues) for stores.

c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.text: Apple's 2012 dependence-predictor patent describes a 256-entry fully associative table of store/load pairs, each side keyed by a hash of PC and register (24 low PC bits folded 12 xor 12)
c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.quote: We learn that (for this implementation) the size of the LSDP table is 256 entries.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-patent-256.notes: US20130326198A1 (2012). Not the M1 size; Handley measures ~74 entries (c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data)

c-mh-v1-lsdp-arming.text: In the 2012 design a store at Rename arms every matching predictor entry; a load at Rename that matches an armed entry takes a dependency on that store and cannot execute until the store does
c-mh-v1-lsdp-arming.quote: every store, as it flows through Rename constructs the PC+register id hash, - probes the LSDP CAM, and - sets an "armed" bit on every match

c-mh-v1-lsdp-confidence.text: Each predictor entry has a confidence field, raised when a load that matched an armed entry gets its data from the store queue and lowered when it gets it from the L1D; low-confidence entries do not arm and are replaced first
c-mh-v1-lsdp-confidence.quote: If it acquires the data from the store queue, then we increment confidence ... But if the load acquires the data from the L1D, then we decrement confidence

c-mh-v1-lsdp-replay-entries.text: The predictor also trains on loads that replayed for want of store data, not only on ordering flushes; entries carry a replay-or-flush bit, and replay entries need higher confidence before they delay a load
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replay-entries.quote: So for Replay entries, we require a rather higher confidence value before we force the load to depend on the store.

c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.text: Instructions issued speculatively behind a load stay in their scheduling queue under a shifting-bit timer (the "shadow kill window") and leave only if the load succeeds; otherwise they reissue when it replays
c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.quote: when an instruction dependent on a load begins execution, it is not removed from the scheduling queue
c-mh-v1-replay-shadow-window.notes: US10514925B1 (2016); inherited by dependents of dependents

c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.text: The load execution queue that holds loads for replay has one bank per load pipe, each acting as an extension of its scheduling queue, while the larger load retirement queue holds loads for ordering checks
c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.quote: This queue inherits the structure described above, one bank per Load Pipe.
c-mh-v1-leq-bank-per-pipe.notes: Reading of US20200394039A1; the A14's third load pipe needs a third LEQ bank

c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.text: Apple's 2019 ordering-violation patent repeats the load/store address check when the load's data would reach its register, a few cycles later, so a store address that resolves in between causes a replay, not a flush
c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.quote: suppose we move the test instead to the cycle at which the data would be stored into a register
c-mh-v1-late-ordering-check-patent.notes: US10983801B2. The later check also catches aliases that only show in physical addresses

c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.text: A 2020 patent adds a small Replay Load Buffer beside the load-store reservation station that reissues a replaying load in step with its store-data op, two cycles after the store data issues instead of seven
c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.quote: Note how it's seven cycle from the IS(issue) of the StoreData till the IS of the dependent Load. With the new timeline we are able to ISsue the load only two cycles later.
c-mh-v1-rlb-patent.notes: US11175917B1 (2020); Handley does not tie it to a chip

c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.text: Independent store/load pairs to different addresses run at two pairs (two stores and two loads) per cycle, also when the load's destination is the next store's data register
c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.quote: we see a throughput of 800 store+load pairs takes essentially 400 cycles, so two pairs (four memory ops) per cycle
c-mh-v1-ls-pairs-2-per-cycle.notes: STR x10,[x2]; LDR x11,[x3]; also LDR x10 and mixed w/x widths

c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.text: Store/load pairs to the same address with different registers run about 15% below two pairs per cycle: they issue together and the load finds the store in the store queue, with occasional replays and no predictor needed
c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.quote: would be perfection (2 load/store pairs per cycle, no cycles lost to Replay or Flush) and we run about 15% slower than perfection
c-mh-v1-same-addr-no-lsdp.notes: Handley credits the in-flight store-vs-load address compare of the 2019 ordering patent for catching loads a few cycles early

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.text: With the store data delayed by FCVTAS, same-address store/load pairs run at ~1.6 pairs per cycle up to 74 pairs and ~0.8 beyond, which Handley reads as a ~74-entry dependence predictor; past it every load replays once
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.quote: that the LSDP can hold ~74 entries
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-delayed-data.notes: FCVTAS x10,d1; STR x10,[x2]; LDR x11,[x2]. Replay costs half the throughput, no more

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-chained.text: With store and load chained through both address and register, the fast regime lasts for about 70-80 pairs, again matching a ~74-entry predictor
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-chained.quote: Secondly it confirms that the size of the LSDP seems to indeed be around 74 elements.

c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.text: A store/load pair chained through the same address and register costs about 4 cycles while the predictor holds it (both issue together, meet at the store queue, data to the bypass) and about 8 once it must replay
c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.quote: The initial regime can support about 70..80 load/store pairs. While in that regime the cost of a single load/store pair is about 4 cycles
c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4.notes: STR x10,[x2]; LDR x10,[x2]. Handley's expectation is three cycles to meet at the store-queue entry plus one to the bypass bus. A different probe from the ~6-cycle pair (c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6)

c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.text: When entries are otherwise alike the predictor appears to replace round-robin, a pointer advancing from the last entry replaced, which behaves like LRU on streaming probes and like random on mixed code
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.quote: This fourth option seems to me to be what we are seeing.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-replacement.notes: Inferred from the sharp knee of the delayed-data probe vs the softer knee of the chained probe

c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-indexed.text: Varying the shared address quadratically, so no address-pattern accelerator applies, leaves the chained store/load results unchanged, as expected of a predictor keyed on store and load PCs rather than addresses
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-indexed.quote: even this quadratically varying index stream (no ZCL!) has essentially identical results

c-mh-v1-lsdp-default-no-alias.text: With the store address delayed by FCVTAS and the load to a different address, pairs run at a smooth two per cycle even beyond predictor capacity: loads are by default predicted not to alias
c-mh-v1-lsdp-default-no-alias.quote: Even when we do overflow the LSDP, as long as loads are predicted by default never to match unknown store addresses we should still see no interference ... nice smooth two pairs processed per cycle

c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.text: Once the predictor overflows, a load that runs ahead of an aliasing store with an unresolved address costs ~38 cycles per pair, which Handley splits into ~25 cycles for the ordering flush and ~13 for redoing the FCVTAS
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.quote: I think this splits into something like 25 cycles as the cost of a flush caused by a load/store aliasing
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.hedge: I think this splits into something like
c-mh-v1-ordering-flush-25.notes: FCVTAS x0,d1; STR x10,[x2,x0]; LDR x11,[x2]. Below ~50 pairs it runs at ~1.4 pairs per cycle

c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.text: In the aliasing-flush probe the knee looks like ~50 entries, but Handley fits it with 74 entries: random replacement lets a few flushes in early, and each flush costs so much that the knee appears sooner
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.quote: I added the gold line to both curves to show how we're still really dealing with ~74 entries in the LSDP.
c-mh-v1-lsdp-74-flush.notes: From the plot legend, "fit assuming 74 entries and 38 cycle flush"

c-mh-v1-delayed-both.text: When both the store and the load wait on the slow FCVTAS address, pairs run at ~1.5 per cycle up to ~70-80 pairs and ~1.2 after, mostly replays rather than flushes
c-mh-v1-delayed-both.quote: We see an initial slightly faster regime, about 1.5 pairs per cycle, for N<~70..80. Then about 1.2 pairs per cycle.

c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.text: On M1 an EOR of a register with itself is not a zeroing or dependency-breaking idiom: it takes a cycle and chains on its input
c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.quote: on M1, unlike x86, xor is not a zero'ing or dependency breaking idiom, so EOR takes one cycle
c-mh-v1-eor-not-zero-idiom.notes: Used as a one-cycle delay element in the EOR sweep (c-mh-v1-late-check-window), where each added EOR lengthens the iteration

c-mh-v1-late-check-window.text: A late load/store address check catches loads that ran two to four cycles ahead of an aliasing store's address and turns them into replays instead of flushes
c-mh-v1-late-check-window.quote: there is also late checking of whether loads might have collided with stores (catching cases where the load is two, three, even four cycles early; and converting them into Replays)
c-mh-v1-late-check-window.notes: EOR sweep: 0-3 cycles of store-address delay give ~0.8 to ~1.5 cycles per iteration; at 4 every pair replays (a little over 4 cycles); at 5 some flush (10 cycles); at 6 every pair flushes once the predictor overflows

c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.text: M1 has a load-store dependence predictor holding about 74 (store PC, load PC) pairs that delays predicted-dependent loads to avoid both ordering flushes and store-data replays
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.quote: it can hold about 74 pairs of (storePC, loadPC) - it prevents both Flushes (catastrophic) and Replays
c-mh-v1-lsdp-pc-pairs.notes: Conclusion of the "Testing the LSDP" probes

c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.text: Offsetting both addresses by 127 bytes so every access straddles a cache line leaves independent store/load throughput unchanged, four line-straddling accesses per cycle
c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.quote: Somehow we are getting four cache-line-straddling accesses per cycle
c-mh-v1-line-cross-4-per-cycle.hedge: even if we accept that Zero Cycle Loads are shouldering some of the burden

c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.text: For chained same-address pairs that straddle a line, the fast regime matches the aligned case up to ~74 pairs and the replay regime is ~8.5 rather than 8 cycles per pair, but an unexplained ~130-cycle jump separates them
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.quote: But there is a pronounced jump (by about 130 cycles!) between the two regimes.
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.hedge: I have no idea what's causing this.
c-mh-v1-line-cross-jump.notes: Handley's tentative theory, a flush draining ~60 store-queue entries split over two lines, he calls special pleading

c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.text: Forwarding from a store pair to three byte loads that each read part of it (STP x10,x11,[x2] then three LDRB) runs at one iteration per cycle
c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.quote: The basic unit involves one store and three loads, so (assuming everything is timed correctly) we should be able to perform one iteration per cycle. And that's what we see!
c-mh-v1-partial-forward-bytes.notes: Vector loads/stores and load/store pairs also behave as expected, including predictor behaviour
