c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.text: Chaining a store pair to three dependent byte loads moves the predictor knee to ~25 iterations, as if each store/load pair took its own entry, and costs 5 and 9 cycles per iteration in the two regimes instead of 4 and 8
c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.quote: The largest difference is that we move to the slower part of the curve at around N=25 rather than 74.
c-mh-v1-stp-lsdp-third.notes: With a single-register store the regimes are 4.5 and 7 cycles; the STP itself adds a cycle

c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.text: A load that must combine bytes from two store-queue entries (and the cache) takes ~1.33 cycles per store-store-load triplet instead of 1, which Handley puts down to an extra cycle for stitching the pieces
c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.quote: Now we take ~1.33 cycles per triplet, likewise if both byte stores match the LDR address.
c-mh-v1-stitch-extra-cycle.notes: Unchanged when both halves come from store-queue entries with no cache access. His guess: speculative scheduling assumes four-cycle loads

c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.text: Besides store-queue forwarding (~6 cycles, comparable to high-end x86 at 5.5-7), Apple can serve a load from the register file that held the stored value: 5 cycles store-to-load in the hardest case, 3 in the easier one
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.quote: service the store from the register file rather than the Store Queue, so that the (store to load) takes 5 cycles (in the most difficult case) and 3 cycles (in the easier case)
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.value: store queue, plus register file when store and load share an address register
c-mh-v1-forwarding-rf.notes: Measured in the zero-cycle-load probes (3 cycles, ~5-5.5 when store and load decode together). Handley knows of no other vendor doing register-based memory renaming

c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.text: Apple's 2012 zero-cycle-load patent (RF-LSDP) records which physical register a store through a given base register wrote; a later load through the same unchanged base register is renamed to it at Rename and validated later
c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.quote: In other words, just like Zero Cycle Move, the work is done at Rename, and this acts as a Zero Cycle Load.
c-mh-v1-zcl-patent-rf-lsdp.notes: US9996348B2; extended to base+immediate addresses and immediate adds to the base

c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.text: A stack-pointer variant (SP-LSDP) applies the same register forwarding to stack stores and loads, including pairs, aimed at prologue saves and epilogue restores; entries last only until the producing store or load retires
c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.quote: This specialization, called the SP-LSDP (Stack Pointer LSDP) allows the mechanism to capture load/store pairs, and to be an especially good fit to function prolog/epilogs
c-mh-v1-sp-lsdp.notes: US10838729B1 (2018), which also covers a reload from the same base register. The patent pipeline puts RF-LSDP at Decode, SP-LSDP at Map and the LSDP at Dispatch, but it is an A7-class pipeline, not M1

c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.text: A 2019 patent extends zero-cycle loads to a store and load decoded in the same cycle by comparing the address patterns of store/load pairs within a decode group
c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.quote: every appropriate possible pair of store/loads in a decode group (ie all the instructions decoded in a single cycle) is tested for matching address patterns
c-mh-v1-zcl-same-decode-group.notes: US20210173654A1. Handley credits it for the ~5.5-cycle same-group case of his DIV probe

c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.text: Forwarding from a store still in the load-store queue to a later load reportedly takes 4 to 5 cycles on M1, where some x86 designs take one; Handley argues Apple optimised the register-matched case instead
c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.quote: Some x86 designs can handle this in one cycle, whereas M1 seems to take 4 to 5 cycles.
c-mh-v1-forwarding-lam.notes: Range 4-5; from a Chester Lam tweet (twitter.com/lamchester/status/1530297321333739521). Handley adds it seems somewhat improved on M2

c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.text: A forced-sequential store/load pair to one address through different registers (STR x1,[x1]; LDR x2,[x2], x1=x2) settles at ~6 cycles per pair once the buffers fill past ~80 pairs: about three for the store, three or four for the load
c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.quote: the time to execute a store/load pair of this form seems to takes ~6 cycles (three for the store, then three, maybe four for the load)
c-mh-v1-store-load-pair-6.notes: Handley's store-queue figure ("~6 cycles"). Adding a dependent DIV gives 11 cycles per probe (3+8). A chained pair that issues together costs ~4 (c-mh-v1-forward-chained-4)

c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.text: When store and load use the same base register (STR x1,[x2]; LDR x2,[x2]; DIV), the loaded value is supplied at rename and successive DIVs overlap: ~5.5 cycles per probe in one decode group, 3 with 8 NOPs between, against 11
c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.quote: inserting 8 NOPs between the store and the load, so they decode in subsequent cycles ... now we run at 3 cycles per probe rather than about 5.5
c-mh-v1-zcl-div-probe.notes: 11 cycles is the same probe with the address in a different register. With the DIV on the store data instead, no zero-cycle load and 12 cycles

c-mh-v1-zcl-addressing.text: The register-matched zero-cycle load handles base+immediate addresses such as [x2,#8], but not register-indexed addresses or store-pair/load-pair, and Handley saw no tracking of immediate adds to the base
c-mh-v1-zcl-addressing.quote: Slightly fancy addresses like [x2, #8] are handled appropriately. But not addresses that depend on two registers, like [x2, x10]. Likewise not store pair+load pair.

c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.text: A store/load pair that reloads its own stored register runs at ~5 cycles per pair when both use the same address register (zero-cycle load) and ~7 when the same address comes through different registers
c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.quote: the first case uses ZCL and runs at ~5 cycles/load/store; the second case doesn't use ZCL and runs at ~7cycles per load/store
c-mh-v1-zcl-5-vs-7.notes: STR x1,[x2]; LDR x1,[x2] vs STR x1,[x2]; LDR x1,[x1] with x1=x2

c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.text: Zero-cycle loads do not apply to SIMD registers: STR q0,[x2]; LDR q0,[x2] runs at ~7 cycles per pair like the unmatched case, and a stack pair of SIMD registers is not accelerated either
c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.quote: then, in principle, the front-end could notice that the address registers are the same and ZCL the q0 value given to the load. But that does not happen, we get the same ~7 cycles per load/store.
c-mh-v1-zcl-no-simd.notes: Handley also says "it seems that the ZCLs are not used for NEON registers"

c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.text: Stack save/restore pairs (STP/LDP x28,x27 at [SP,#-16]) get no zero-cycle acceleration when decoded in the same cycle, 7 cycles per pair, but are accelerated when 8 NOPs separate the store and the load
c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.quote: with 8 NOPs after the store, and another 8 after the load ... That's more like it!!! Nice acceleration there!
c-mh-v1-zcl-stack.notes: The text gives no figure for the accelerated case

c-mh-v1-no-add-imm-elim.text: Apple eliminates move-immediates at rename but does not appear to special-case add-immediate
c-mh-v1-no-add-imm-elim.quote: Apple handle zero-cycle load-immediates (a case not considered by the paper), but do not appear to handle add-immediate as a special case.

c-mh-v1-redundant-mem-ops.text: Back-to-back identical stores, or identical loads, are not removed: two stores and two loads still take one cycle per probe, the same as four distinct addresses
c-mh-v1-redundant-mem-ops.quote: In theory, now, the front-end could see that one of the stores is redundant, remove it ... But (unsurprisingly) this does not happen.

c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.text: A load whose base register comes straight from the previous load runs at 3 cycles per load, also with complex addressing or a load pair; other load chains, such as the pointer used as the index, take 4
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.quote: Pointer chasing that feeds the pointer into the first argument (the base pointer) runs at 3 cycles per load, as opposed to normal load loops ... which takes 4 cycles per load
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-3.notes: LDR x2,[x2] and LDR x2,[x2,x0] vs LDR x2,[x0,x2]. Load pair works if the chased pointer is the first register

c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.text: Apple's 2013 pointer-chasing patent issues a load whose base comes from a just-issued L1-hitting load so the address arrives inside the LSU, a cycle earlier than via the bypass bus; mispredictions replay
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.quote: begins its execution one cycle earlier than it would have been if it had to wait for the value of x1 on the bypass bus
c-mh-v1-pointer-chase-patent.notes: US9116817B2; the 2014 follow-up US9710268B2 lets failures train the LSDP. The patent pipeline is A7 generation; Handley says M1 takes one cycle less

c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.text: Handley found no case where Apple's constant-address and stride load-address prediction patent shows up and tentatively concludes M1 does not have it
c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.quote: So my tentative belief is that, in spite of the patent, this is not present in M1.
c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction.notes: US20210049015A1 (2019) predicts a load's next address from a linear stream, loads early and renames the destination

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the M1 L1 data TLB has 160 entries
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.quote: Likewise for L1D TLB M1 had 160 entries, A14 had 256 entries
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-dtlb.notes: Handley relaying Apple's CPU Optimization Guide (apple-opt-guide)

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the A14 L1 data TLB has 256 entries, unlike the M1's 160
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.quote: Likewise for L1D TLB M1 had 160 entries, A14 had 256 entries (as did M2, M3, and A15)
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-dtlb.notes: Same Firestorm core, different dTLB size per Apple's guide; M2, M3 and A15 also 256

c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.text: Citing Apple's CPU Optimization Guide, the A14 has a 16 MiB system level cache
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.quote: For example the A14 had 16MiB SLC
c-mh-v1-opt-guide-a14-slc.notes: Handley relaying Apple's guide; A15 32 MiB, A16 24 MiB in the same sentence

c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.text: Claiming registers with MOV xn, xn does not avoid the slow path for reading unclaimed registers (MOV xn, #0 does), and leaving FP registers unclaimed causes no slowdown
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.quote: What if we use something like MOV xn, xn, rather than the current MOV xn, #0, to force the overwrite? That does not work! ... I can't generate the same sort of disaster by not forcing ownership of the FP registers
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.hedge: My bet is on MOV xn, xn, being mapped to NOP.
c-mh-v1-security-tag-details.notes: Handley reads the FP result as the OS or interrupt not touching FP registers; he prefers the security-tag explanation over hardware context switching

c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.text: An L2 hit takes around 15 cycles on the M1
c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.quote: the machine will not have to halt on a miss to L2 cache (around 15 cycles for M1)
c-mh-v1-l2-latency-aside.notes: Passing figure in the introductory ROB-size discussion, no method stated; 7-cpu gives 18 cycles (c-7cpu-l2-latency). Vol 2 measures the cache hierarchy.

c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.text: A hit in the system level cache takes around 90 cycles on the M1
c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.quote: will usually cover the delay to the System Cache (around 90 cycles for M1)
c-mh-v1-slc-latency-aside.notes: Passing figure in the introductory ROB-size discussion, no method stated

c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.text: Each execution unit has its own scheduling queue of 36 entries, small next to Intel's 97 but more in total
c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.quote: separate queues in front of each. Each scheduling queue may sound small (36 entries compared to say Intel's 97)
c-mh-v1-sched-queue-36.notes: From Johnson's diagram. Handley later halves the non-load/store sizes, since a queue pair looks like one queue: ~18 per FP queue, ~13 per integer queue (c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x).

c-mh-v1-14-units.text: The M1 has fourteen execution units, each with its own scheduling queue, so it can issue up to 14 per cycle, against a sustained width of 8
c-mh-v1-14-units.quote: there are fourteen units, each has an independent scheduling queue ... In the case of the M1, this is 8, not 14.
c-mh-v1-14-units.notes: Unit count taken from Johnson's Firestorm page; 6 integer + 4 FP/SIMD + 4 load/store

c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.text: Per Apple patents, operands are read from the register file at issue, not earlier, and scheduling tracks dependencies by instruction (scheduler) numbers rather than physical register numbers
c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.quote: Apple patents explicitly say that registers are read at Issue time, not early; and they strongly suggest that scheduling is based on instruction numbers (called SCH#'s)
c-mh-v1-read-at-issue.notes: Patents cited are US9940262B2 and US8555040B2

c-mh-v1-fetch-16.text: Fetch can probably bring in up to 16 instructions (one I-cache line) per cycle, one line per cycle, above the sustained width of 8
c-mh-v1-fetch-16.quote: Fetch can probably pull in a maximum width of 16 instructions (one cache line) in one cycle ... only one I-cache line is accessed per cycle
c-mh-v1-fetch-16.notes: Forward reference to the Fetch discussion in vol 4 (c-mh-v4-fetch-16), no measurement here. Johnson's 8 is a pipeline width (c-dj-width), so this may be peak versus sustained fetch. The line size in bytes is not stated.

c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.text: Both the register files and the L2 are split into independently managed pieces; the core runs from a fraction of each (e.g. a quarter of the register file, a third of the L2) and powers up the rest only when metrics show it would help
c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.quote: they are in fact split into multiple independently managed smaller pieces ... or one third of the L2, with the rest powered down and taking no energy
c-mh-v1-split-power-gating.notes: The fractions are given as examples ("eg"); see c-mh-v1-prf-banks for the four-bank register file

c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.text: The M1 neither drops NOPs at decode nor fuses them with the next instruction (as recent Arm cores do); each NOP takes its own ROB slot
c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.quote: Apple appears not to do this, at least not as of M1 ... so Apple don't do that, they apparently allocate a ROB slot to each NOP
c-mh-v1-nop-rob-slot.notes: The NOP window (c-mh-v1-nop-window) depends on this

c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.text: LLVM lists address, arithmetic-logic, CC-select and literal fusions for the A14, but whether the A14/M1 implements them is unclear: latency and throughput tests show no gain
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.quote: It's unclear whether these fusions are present in A14/M1 (or in later chips). People investigating latency or throughput report no obvious improvement from these fusions
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.hedge: It's unclear whether these fusions are present in A14/M1
c-mh-v1-llvm-fusions.notes: FeatureFuseAddress, FeatureFuseArithmeticLogic, FeatureFuseCCSelect, FeatureFuseLiterals in AArch64.td. Handley suggests they could amplify History File capacity rather than cut latency; untested

c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.text: The History File, which records destination-register allocations, is perhaps the most common limit on how far the M1 can reorder
c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.quote: perhaps the most common constraint as to how aggressively the M1 can reorder instructions is the size of the History File
c-mh-v1-hf-common-limit.notes: Handley later restates it as either the ~330 failable ROB slots or the History File limiting real code

c-mh-v1-fusion-patent.text: Per Apple's arithmetic-branch fusion patent, fusion is detected at Decode and applied at Map by rewriting one instruction (CBZ into a SUB-CBZ) and discarding the other; ROB slots are already allocated, but the pair needs one scheduler slot and gives its result in one cycle
c-mh-v1-fusion-patent.quote: fusion detection occurs at Decode and is implemented at Map ... only one Scheduling slot is required, not two, and the result is available in once cycle, not two

c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.text: A stream of NOPs runs at 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.quote: We would expect that this should run at 8 NOPs/cycle, and that's exactly what we see.
c-mh-v1-nop-throughput.notes: Handley also says NOPs take ROB slots yet run at 8/cycle, "presumably limited by Decode"

c-mh-v1-nop-window.text: Behind a chained-FSQRT delay block, NOP filler first shows a timing glitch at 2228 NOPs, between the 2178 and 2274 NOPs predicted for 21 and 22 FSQRTs, so the ROB holds about that many NOPs
c-mh-v1-nop-window.quote: We see trouble at 2228 between these two, so our ROB size is somewhere between these two.
c-mh-v1-nop-window.notes: Delay: chained FSQRT.D, 13 cycles each, 22 in the analysis. Handley concludes "The ROB is ~2274 instructions in size", ~324 rows of 7, later ~330 rows (c-mh-v1-rob-rows).

c-mh-v1-add-throughput.text: Independent integer ADDs run at 6 per cycle
c-mh-v1-add-throughput.quote: No surprises, the primary notable fact is the slope (6 independent integer adds/cycle).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.text: With a delay block, independent ADD x0, x5, x5 filler jumps at ~378-380 instructions, read as the integer physical register file size
c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.quote: there's some sort of limitation at around 380 ADDs (seems like physical registers)
c-mh-v1-int-prf-add.notes: The jump is at ~378 (=63*6) and Handley assumes "the actual physical register count is say 380". He later repeats that ADDs (register or immediate operand) "max out at around 380 physical registers".

c-mh-v1-regs-freed-at-retire.text: Integer physical registers are freed at Retire, held while the head of the ROB is blocked, not as soon as all their readers have completed
c-mh-v1-regs-freed-at-retire.quote: we've also learned that registers are deallocated at Retire (deallocation is delayed by the Head of ROB blocking) rather than some more ambitious schemes

c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.text: Independent FABS run at 4 per cycle, and an ADD+FABS mix is throttled by the four FP pipes
c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.quote: shows a slope of 4 ops/cycle. We are throttled by the 4 fp pipes.
c-mh-v1-fabs-throughput.notes: FABS alone gives the same 4/cycle slope

c-mh-v1-fp-prf.text: With an integer (UDIV) delay block, FABS filler jumps at about 432, the FP/SIMD physical register file size
c-mh-v1-fp-prf.quote: we see that the fp register file is perhaps closer to 432 or so in size.
c-mh-v1-fp-prf.notes: With an FSQRT delay block the jump spans 403-425, centred ~415, because the delay holds FP registers

c-mh-v1-shared-pool-624.text: An ADD+FABS probe jumps at about 312 pairs, short of both register files, so a pool of ~624 entries is shared by integer and FP register writes
c-mh-v1-shared-pool-624.quote: There's an additional resource that constrains us, a pool of ~624 somethings that's shared by int and fp registers.

c-mh-v1-flags-prf.text: CMP filler exhausts the flags physical register file at about 124-128 entries
c-mh-v1-flags-prf.quote: However the jump is at ~124 (128?) physical flags registers.
c-mh-v1-flags-prf.notes: Jump measured at ~124; Handley uses ~128 from then on

c-mh-v1-cmp-throughput.text: Independent CMP x0, x0 run at 3 per cycle
c-mh-v1-cmp-throughput.quote: So no real surprises. This time the slope of the lines is 3 instructions per cycle

c-mh-v1-frontend-8.text: CMP+ADD+FABS triplets with no delay run at 8 instructions per cycle (600 triplets in 225 cycles), limited by the 8-wide Decode/Map front end
c-mh-v1-frontend-8.quote: The limiting point is the 8-wide front end (Decode, Map) of the machine.

c-mh-v1-history-file.text: A unit of ADD + FABS + 1/3 CMP jumps after 266 units, about 620 register allocations, with none of the int, FP or flags files exhausted, so a communal structure of ~620 entries is used by every register-writing instruction
c-mh-v1-history-file.quote: 266*(2+1/3) =620 register allocations! ... there is some communal structure related to the allocation of registers, of size ~620 entries
c-mh-v1-history-file.notes: Measured in the "Register File Size (All Registers)" test. At the jump 266 int, 266 FP and 87 flags registers are in use. Handley names it the History File (see c-mh-v1-620-history-file-patent).

c-mh-v1-hf-walk.text: Recovery rewinds a History File of register-mapping changes (Akkary's HBMAP+WALK) kept apart from the ROB and sized separately, with ROB entries pointing to History File entries
c-mh-v1-hf-walk.quote: HBMAP+WALK is essentially what Apple uses ... Apple separates those changes from the ROB into a separately sized History File, with a pointer in each ROB entry pointing to a History File entry
c-mh-v1-hf-walk.notes: The History File also marks when physical registers can be freed; Apple is the only company Handley knows of using one

c-mh-v1-adds-two-hf.text: A FABS + ADD + 1/2 ADDS probe jumps at about 208 units (620/3 = 206), so flag-setting ALU instructions such as ADDS take two History File slots
c-mh-v1-adds-two-hf.quote: Instructions that both perform some other calculation and set the flags register (ie have two destination registers) require two HF slots.

c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.text: History File slots are taken one per register rename: none for stores, PRFM or most special-register writes, one for a load, two for a load pair
c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.quote: zero HF slots for stores ... one HF slot for standard loads ... two HF slots slots for load pair (which takes two destination registers). These are all confirmed.
c-mh-v1-hf-slot-rule.notes: Agrees with Johnson's rename retire queue costs (c-dj-rename-cost); special registers "somewhat", some are renamed

c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.text: Per Apple's patent, flags moves are handled near the rename map, and other special-register writes proceed out of order into speculative storage and become permanent at retire, avoiding serialization
c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.quote: Some easy cases (most obviously moving data to and from the flags register) are treated via machinery close to the Rename Mapping machinery.
c-mh-v1-spr-speculative-writes.notes: US10838723B1 (2019); not tested on the M1 here

c-mh-v1-crack-merge.text: Per Apple's patent, ADDS and LDP count as two for rename and the History File but execute as one, while ADD (shifted) counts as one for allocation and retire but executes as two, the shift result taken off the bypass without a register
c-mh-v1-crack-merge.quote: an ADDS or a LDP (load pair) want to be treated as two instructions for the purposes of register allocation (Rename) and deallocation (History File) but as a single instruction for the purposes of execute.
c-mh-v1-crack-merge.notes: US9223577B2 (2012). Handley says register-free bypass is used today only for a few cracked instructions (US10691457B1)

c-mh-v1-extr-intermediate.text: EXTR, unlike ADD (shifted), allocates a physical register for its intermediate result
c-mh-v1-extr-intermediate.quote: the EXTR instruction ... does allocate a genuine intermediate register

c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.text: For eliminated moves the M1 appears to use the last-physical-register-reference scheme rather than the older register duplication array or reference counts, with no limit on how many registers are duplicated
c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.quote: The M1 appears to implements this more elegant scheme, and appears to show none of the limits one might expect from the two prior schemes.
c-mh-v1-mov-last-reference.notes: US20210064376A1 (2019) over US20130275720A1 (RDA, ~8 entries) and US20160026463A1 (free-list counts). Handley guesses the mapping lookup is a bit matrix, not a CAM.

c-mh-v1-no-width-split.text: Apple's first 64-bit cores split the integer register file into about 40% 32-bit and 60% 64-bit registers; Handley finds no sign of that split on the M1
c-mh-v1-no-width-split.quote: in Apple's first 64-bit cores, the integer file was in fact split about 40% 32-bit registers and 60% 64-bit registers! ... Apple no longer does that (at least I can find no evidence for it)
c-mh-v1-no-width-split.hedge: at least I can find no evidence for it

c-mh-v1-prf-banks.text: The physical register file is split into four banks that can be powered on or off individually, with allocation steered to keep as few banks active as possible
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.quote: we split our register file into multiple banks (the patent suggests 4, and I suspect that's still the case; it matches the results I have seen)
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.hedge: I suspect that's still the case
c-mh-v1-prf-banks.notes: US10372500B1 (2016); Handley ties the delay glitch near 380 ADDs to it (c-mh-v1-bank-powerup)

c-mh-v1-free-list-scanners.text: Per Apple's register-allocation patents, free registers are tracked in bitvectors searched by scanners (eight in the 2016 version), recently returned registers are reused first, and the bitvectors map onto banks so allocation stays in one powered bank
c-mh-v1-free-list-scanners.quote: rearranges the mapping of these bitvectors into the register banks so that all the (now eight rather than six) scanners are likely to find free registers in the same single bank

c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.text: The small bump near 380 ADDs with a 46-cycle (not a 45-cycle) delay is allocation exhausting the one powered bank and waiting two or three cycles for another bank to power up
c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.quote: Presumably the system copes by powering up one of the powered down banks, and that takes two or three cycles, generating the glitch we see.
c-mh-v1-bank-powerup.notes: Range two to three cycles. The model assumes 3/4 of ~380 registers (285) sit in the ROB during the delay. Handley is "open to alternative explanations".

c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.text: Hardware register caching on thread switches (thread-tagged mappings, on-demand save and restore to the L2, per Apple's 2015 patent) is probably not implemented; a patent author told Handley he believes it was not built
c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.quote: His belief ... is that while the idea is valid and will work, it has not yet been implemented in an Apple core.
c-mh-v1-no-hw-context-switch.notes: US9817664B2. Same page: the register security tag (c-mh-v1-register-security-tag) "does appear to be implemented"

c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.text: Icestorm has about 80 integer physical registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.quote: consider that Icestorm has ~80 physical integer registers and ~88 physical SIMD registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-int-prf.notes: Given in passing in the Chinook discussion; source of the numbers not stated

c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.text: Icestorm has about 88 SIMD physical registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.quote: consider that Icestorm has ~80 physical integer registers and ~88 physical SIMD registers
c-mh-v1-icestorm-fp-prf.notes: Given in passing in the Chinook discussion; source of the numbers not stated

c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.text: The M1 does not use virtual registers (late physical-register allocation) or early register de-allocation
c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.quote: But they haven't taken the next step in doing so, namely using virtual registers or something similar (for late allocation) and allowing for early register de-allocation.
c-mh-v1-no-virtual-registers.notes: Handley also says Apple does not early-release registers, and "doesn't do this yet, but probably will soon"

c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.text: ADD pairs whose first result is immediately overwritten still exhaust registers at ~380, so neither bypass-only results nor early release of overwritten registers (Apple's US10691457B1) is used on the M1
c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.quote: However a test on the M1 suggests that, in spite of the patent, neither appears to be implemented, at least not as of the M1. ... Even so, we see the jump at the usual ~380
c-mh-v1-no-bypass-early-release.notes: Filler ADD x0, x5, x5; ADD x0, x0, x0 and three more such pairs; also tried REV/CLZ/ADD from the patent. Handley guesses early release waits on the last-reference scheme and may be behind chicken bits.

c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.text: After a blocking FSQRT delay, the restart delay grows by 8 cycles per 450 NOPs queued behind it, so Retire clears about 56 NOPs per cycle
c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.quote: So the time it takes the ROB to clear 450 NOPs is 8 cycles, ie the machine clears 450/8=56 NOPs/cycle!
c-mh-v1-retire-nops-56.notes: Baseline restart delay 20 cycles; 33-FSQRT delay, 0-1800 NOPs, then 370 ADDs to use up registers.

c-mh-v1-rob-rows.text: The ROB is best modelled as about 330 rows of instruction slots
c-mh-v1-rob-rows.quote: the ROB is best thought of as consisting of ~330 "rows" where each row can hold 7 instructions.
c-mh-v1-rob-rows.notes: The NOP window gives ~324 rows (324*7=2268, c-mh-v1-nop-window); Handley says the load/store and branch probes supply the evidence

c-mh-v1-rob-row-slots.text: Each ROB row holds up to 7 instructions, only the last (failable) slot doing real recovery work
c-mh-v1-rob-row-slots.quote: only the failable slot of a 7-entry row of the ROB actually matters; the other 6 slots just hold

c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.text: Failable instructions (branches, loads and stores) must take the last slot of a ROB row; other instructions may take any slot
c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.quote: Most instructions can go in any slot, but "failable" instructions must go in the last slot (which provides extra storage).
c-mh-v1-rob-failable-slot.notes: Even an unconditional B .+4 takes the failable slot. Differs from Johnson (c-dj-retire-groups, and the retire_groups description), who has memory uops starting a group and only branches ending one.

c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.text: Retire clears 8 ROB rows per cycle, so between 8 and 56 instructions
c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.quote: So a better way to think of Retire is that Retire can clear 8 ROB rows per cycle.
c-mh-v1-retire-rows-per-cycle.notes: From the 56 NOPs/cycle drain and 7-slot rows

c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.text: The six non-failable slots of a row may not be stored at all: each of ~330 entries could hold the failable instruction and a 3-bit count of the others; not visible to tests
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.quote: We can treat the ROB as ~330 entries which hold a pair (failable instruction, 3-bit counter)
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.hedge: seems a reasonable way to save a few transistors
c-mh-v1-rob-row-counter.notes: Suggested to Handley by Arthur V.

c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.text: Retire frees FP physical registers and their History File slots at about 16 per cycle: each extra 70 FABS behind the delay adds about 4 cycles
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.quote: I think it's legitimate to see clearing 70 FABS from the ROB as taking 4 cycles, so 17.5 clearances/cycle. Probably best to read that as 16 per cycle.
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.hedge: Probably best to read that as 16 per cycle.
c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate.notes: 50 extra CMPs add about 3 cycles (50/16), which Handley takes as confirmation; consistent with c-mh-v1-reg-free-16

c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.text: FMOV filler, whose History File entries free no register, gives the same delay as FABS, so History File slots are freed at 16 per cycle whether or not a register is released
c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.quote: It appears that HF slots and registers are both freed at 16/cycle, there's no faster path for HF slots that are not freeing a physical register.
c-mh-v1-hf-free-rate.notes: Filler FMOV d31, d30 in place of FABS

c-mh-v1-kip-930.text: An ADD + FABS + STR mix reaches about 310 iterations, ~930 instructions, in flight before it stalls
c-mh-v1-kip-930.quote: we can in fact reach about 310 iterations of this before he see a jump! So ~930 realistic'ish instructions!
c-mh-v1-kip-930.hedge: It might be possible to go slightly beyond this
c-mh-v1-kip-930.notes: A lower bound for realistic code (History File slots for ADD and FABS, failable ROB slots for STR); Handley did not push further. Compare retire.issuing_window (~1000, Johnson).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.text: MOV x0, #1 filler maxes out at around 418 registers, about 38 more than ADDs
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.quote: The unexpected case is MOV x0, #1, which maxes out at around 418 physical registers.
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movimm.notes: Not the register file size: Handley reads the 418 as ~380 integer registers plus ~36 immediate registers (c-mh-v1-iregs-36).

c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.text: About 380 MOV xn, xzr instructions fit before the knee, so a move from xzr allocates an integer physical register
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.quote: So we see that about 380 xzr allocations can be performed.
c-mh-v1-int-prf-movxzr.notes: knee between N=380 and N=381 in the listed data

c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.text: MOV from xzr is not eliminated; counters show it issues, and it runs at about 6 per cycle in the integer units
c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.quote: Looking at the performance counters tells us that MOV from xzr is, in fact, not eliminated.
c-mh-v1-mov-xzr-not-elim.notes: agrees with Johnson (c-dj-mov-elim, mov x0,xzr not eliminated); the 6 per cycle slope is on the same page

c-mh-v1-mov-elim-rename.text: A MOV between two different registers issues nothing; all eight MOVs per cycle complete at rename, and the knee is the history file (~620), not the ~380 physical registers
c-mh-v1-mov-elim-rename.quote: So we're seeing not a limit at the number of physical register (380, as in the previous graph) but at the number of HF slots. ... all eight MOV's (different register case) execute purely at Rename.

c-mh-v1-rename-8wide.text: Eliminated MOVs run at about 8 per cycle, the mapper/rename throughput, against 6 per cycle for instructions that go through the integer units
c-mh-v1-rename-8wide.quote: the throughput of the MOV's is ~8/cycle, which is Mapper/Rename throughput, not the 6 we'd expect if the instruction had to go through the integer pipes

c-mh-v1-mov-self-nop.text: MOV xn, xn is treated as a NOP; it uses only ROB slots and the curve jumps at about 2300 when they run out
c-mh-v1-mov-self-nop.quote: behave just like NOPs, using no execution resources except ROB slots, and the curve jumping at around ~2300 when the ROB slots are exhausted

c-mh-v1-mov-fp-elim.text: FP/SIMD register moves (MOV.16B v0, v1) are eliminated the same way, at zero cycles and 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-mov-fp-elim.quote: The same zero-cycle (and 8-wide!) behavior holds for FP/SIMD registers (eg MOV.16B v0, v1).

c-mh-v1-hf-shared-int-fp.text: Integer MOV and FP MOV.16B draw on one shared pool of history-file slots; interleaving them puts the knee at about 310 pairs, half of 620
c-mh-v1-hf-shared-int-fp.quote: when we pair the MOV with a MOV.16B, the jump will be at ~620/2=~310, and that's exactly what we see

c-mh-v1-hf-630.text: Repeatedly duplicating fifteen different registers gives a sharp knee at 630 when the history file is full, with throughput held at 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-hf-630.quote: The result shows the expected jump (extremely sharp!) when the HF is maxed out at 630.
c-mh-v1-hf-630.notes: knee between N=629 and N=630 in the listed data

c-mh-v1-no-rda.text: Move elimination shows no limit on how many distinct registers are duplicated (15 integer plus 15 FP sources change nothing), so Handley sees no sign of a register duplicate array
c-mh-v1-no-rda.quote: We can also add 15 floating point duplications, for a total pool of 30 duplicated source registers, no difference. So, yeah, seems like no RDA is being used.
c-mh-v1-no-rda.notes: the register duplicate array is from a 2012 Apple patent; any limit is above fifteen per register file

c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.text: Sub-register moves (MOV wn, wm; MOV.8B vn, vm; MOV dn, dm) are not eliminated
c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.quote: What if we try subregisters, eg MOV wn, wm, or MOV.8B vn, vm, or MOV dn, dm? On the M1 we don't get any of these fancy tricks when copying subregisters
c-mh-v1-subreg-mov-not-elim.notes: agrees with Johnson (c-dj-mov-elim, mov w0,w1 not eliminated)

c-mh-v1-dispatch-unordered.text: What Johnson calls dispatch queues are better seen as buffers that make no ordering promise, and Handley suspects they can lose age order when the scheduler queues are full
c-mh-v1-dispatch-unordered.quote: I suspect the Apple Dispatch Buffers can lose ordering (in cases where it doesn't matter much, namely when the Scheduler Queues are so filled up that the Dispatch Buffers are more than just pass-through).

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.text: Load/store scheduling holds 48 entries as four separate 12-entry queues, not the single 48-entry queue of Johnson's diagram
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.quote: the monolithic 48 entry Load/Store Scheduling Queue is in fact 4 separate 12 entry queues, just like the other cases
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-48.notes: 4 x 12 = 48 in total. The split is argued with the load/store probes (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-4x12, "I suggest that the Scheduling Queue is split into 4 queue of 12 entries").

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-queues.text: Load/store scheduling is split into four queues of 12 entries each
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-split-queues.quote: the monolithic 48 entry Load/Store Scheduling Queue is in fact 4 separate 12 entry queues, just like the other cases

c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.text: Handley holds that the non-load/store queue sizes in Johnson's scheduler diagram are about twice too large (MUL queues ~13 each, FP queues 18 each), because a pair of queues looks like one queue to most probes
c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.quote: the other entries apart from load/store are probably about 2x too large (that is, the size of say the two MUL queues is probably ~13 each), likewise the FP queues probably 18 each
c-mh-v1-sched-johnson-2x.notes: Disagrees with Johnson's diagram. On Handley's reading, an integer total summed from the diagram's queue sizes (134, c-cc-oryon-m1-int-sched-134) counts each paired queue about twice; he gives no total of his own.

c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.text: Each scheduler queue feeds one execution unit, but queues are paired; a queue with no ready instruction can issue its partner's second-choice ready instruction, so a probe sees the sum of the pair
c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.quote: while each queue feeds a primary execution unit, the queues are paired, and if one queue does not have a runnable instruction, it can accept the "second choice" runnable instruction from the companion queue
c-mh-v1-sched-pairing.notes: Handley has seen the pairing only for load/store (c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing); the integer and FP pairings are his guesses

c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.text: On the load/store side the store queue is paired with the store+load (ambidextrous) queue; this is the one pairing Handley has observed
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.quote: beyond having seen it in action in the case of load store ... On the load/store side, the store queue is paired with the ambidextrous (store+load) queue.
c-mh-v1-sched-ls-pairing.notes: he found it because stores can go only to the store unit or the ambidextrous unit

c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.text: The two integer MUL queues are paired and hold about 13 entries each
c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.quote: Given the numbers, an obvious guess is that on the integer side ... the two MUL queues are paired (each 13 in size)
c-mh-v1-sched-int-13.notes: Half the MUL queue size in Johnson's diagram ("probably ~13 each"); Handley's 18 is the FP queue size (c-mh-v1-sched-18). No size is given for the unpaired ALU/flags and ALU queues.

c-mh-v1-sched-br-13.text: The two integer branch queues are paired, at about 13 entries each (perhaps one of 12 and one of 14)
c-mh-v1-sched-br-13.quote: two two BR queues are paired (maybe one of size 12, one of size 14, or both of size 13)

c-mh-v1-sched-int-unpaired.text: The ALU/flags queue and the plain ALU queue are not paired
c-mh-v1-sched-int-unpaired.quote: the ALU/FLAGS queue and the ALU queue stand alone and are not paired.

c-mh-v1-sched-fp-pairing.text: Handley guesses, without testing, that the two FCSEL-capable FP queues are paired
c-mh-v1-sched-fp-pairing.quote: I would guess that the two FPCSEL queues are paired, but have not tested that.

c-mh-v1-int-rate-6.text: ADDs run at 6 per cycle, the rate of the six integer units, while eliminated MOVs run at 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-int-rate-6.quote: The first segment of the graph corresponds to the 370 ADDs, processed at a slope of 6/cycle; these are followed by the MOVs, processed at 8/cycle
c-mh-v1-int-rate-6.notes: Handley names "the six integer pipelines" and six integer queues

c-mh-v1-dispatch-int.text: The integer dispatch buffer holds about 24 instructions, as two buffers of 12; after a long run of ADDs, about four cycles of rename-only MOVs run free while the buffered ADDs drain at 6 per cycle
c-mh-v1-dispatch-int.quote: The integer Dispatch Buffer has a capacity of ~24 instructions, so it soon fills up.
c-mh-v1-dispatch-int.notes: Flat region from N=370 to about 397; with FABS instead of MOVs the flat run is 23 instructions. Johnson probed 24 (12+12) directly (c-mh-v1-dispatch-int-dj).

c-mh-v1-dispatch-mul.text: The dispatch buffer feeding the two MUL units holds 12; after a run of MULs, about 50 rename-only instructions run free while it drains in 6 cycles
c-mh-v1-dispatch-mul.quote: The Dispatch Buffer that feeds the two MUL units has a capacity of 12, so will drain in 6 cycles.
c-mh-v1-dispatch-mul.notes: Flat region from N=370 to 420. Handley takes this to be one of the two 12-entry integer buffers ("a buffer of ~12 in size").

c-mh-v1-dispatch-int-two.text: Two dispatch buffers feed the six integer scheduler queues, as in Johnson's diagram
c-mh-v1-dispatch-int-two.quote: So we validate both our understanding and that there are two Dispatch Buffers feeding the six integer Scheduling Queues, as in the diagram.

c-mh-v1-mul-two-units.text: MUL runs at 2 per cycle because only two integer units multiply, and both are fully pipelined
c-mh-v1-mul-two-units.quote: We get an initial slope of two instructions per cycle (only two execution units support multiply, but they are fully pipelined).
c-mh-v1-mul-two-units.notes: a role fact for eu_int.roles (multiply on two units); the roles value is c-mh-v1-int-roles

c-mh-v1-sched-int-queues.text: Apple puts a scheduler queue in front of each execution unit, giving six integer queues
c-mh-v1-sched-int-queues.quote: Apple takes this idea to an extreme by adopting a queue in front of each execution unit ... ADD can go to any of the six integer execution unit queues

c-mh-v1-int-roles.text: Only two integer units take branches and only one divides, while ADD can go to any of the six integer queues
c-mh-v1-int-roles.quote: there are only two branch execution units, only one integer divide unit), while other integer instructions like ADD can go to any of the six integer execution unit queues
c-mh-v1-int-roles.value: branch on 2, divide on 1, ADD on all 6
c-mh-v1-int-roles.notes: Stated without a method; Handley works from Johnson's diagram. Corroborates Johnson's table (c-dj-int-roles); multiply on two units is measured in c-mh-v1-mul-two-units.

c-mh-v1-dispatch-load-balance.text: The dispatch buffer balances the queues; unit-restricted instructions go to their queues and the rest go to whichever queues are least full
c-mh-v1-dispatch-load-balance.quote: after instructions with strict requirements are sent to the appropriate queues, the remaining instructions are sent out according to which queues are least full
c-mh-v1-dispatch-load-balance.notes: Handley's reading of Apple patent US9336003B2 (multi-level dispatch, 2013)

c-mh-v1-queue-inflow-1.text: Each scheduler queue accepts one instruction per cycle, so the integer dispatch buffers drain at 6 per cycle and the FP and load/store buffers at 4
c-mh-v1-queue-inflow-1.quote: Each of the six integer queues can only accept one instruction per cycle
c-mh-v1-queue-inflow-1.notes: Proposed to explain the 8-in, 6-out filling of the integer buffer ("maybe instructions can only leave that buffer at 6/cycle, so one per scheduling queue?"); Handley gives 4 per cycle for runs of FP or load/store instructions.

c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-patent.text: Handley reads Apple's multi-level dispatch patent as buffers that accept up to eight instructions per cycle feeding queues that take one per cycle
c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-patent.quote: the buffers are capable of accepting up to eight instructions (whereas queues only need to accept one instruction per cycle)
c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-patent.notes: US9336003B2 (2013), Multi-level dispatch for a superscalar processor

c-mh-v1-age-matrix.text: Scheduler queues do not shift entries; an age matrix holds the relative age of every pair of entries, and a pairwise tournament picks the oldest ready instruction
c-mh-v1-age-matrix.quote: The age matrix tracks the temporal ordering of the instructions while not requiring them to continually be moved from one slot to another.
c-mh-v1-age-matrix.notes: Handley's reading of US20170024205A1 (non-shifting reservation station, 2015) and US10120690B1 (early age indicator, 2016)

c-mh-v1-pairing-patent.text: Handley reads Apple's 2017 issue-selection patent as offering each queue's second-choice candidate to its paired queue at the last round of the age tournament
c-mh-v1-pairing-patent.quote: So suppose that at the very last round, we also offer the second choice candidate from queue A to queue B (and vice versa).
c-mh-v1-pairing-patent.notes: US10983799B1, Selection of instructions to issue in a processor

c-mh-v1-sched-18.text: Each FP/SIMD scheduler queue holds 18 entries, sized for the long dependency chains and latencies of FP code
c-mh-v1-sched-18.quote: for FP/SIMD both long dependency chains and long instruction latencies are common, hence we see each Scheduler Queue as a hefty 18 entries in size
c-mh-v1-sched-18.notes: The 18 is the FP/SIMD queue size, not that of every scheduler queue (also "likewise the FP queues probably 18 each", half of Johnson's diagram). No method or hedge given. Integer queues ~13 (c-mh-v1-sched-int-13).

c-mh-v1-sched-pending-400.text: At most about 400 instructions wait in all the scheduler queues and dispatch buffers together, and Handley guesses the scheduler IDs come from a pool of that size
c-mh-v1-sched-pending-400.quote: which is a maximum of ~400 (worst case total occupancy of all the scheduling queues and dispatch buffers)

c-mh-v1-lsdp-mapper.text: A load-store dependency predictor sits with the mapper rather than the load/store unit, and adds a predicted store as one more dependency of the load
c-mh-v1-lsdp-mapper.quote: this table is associated not with the Load/Store unit but with the Mapper unit ... because the LSDP implementation is handled as just one more dependency of the load!
c-mh-v1-lsdp-mapper.value: LSDP at the mapper; predicted store becomes a dependency of the load
c-mh-v1-lsdp-mapper.notes: from Apple patent US20130298127A1 (load-store dependency predictor content management, 2012), which Handley presents as current

c-mh-v1-matrix-scheduler.text: Handley reads Apple's index-based wakeup patent as matrix scheduling, with a dependency bit matrix indexed by scheduler ID, an age matrix and an operand table per queue, woken by issuing units setting bits on a wide bus
c-mh-v1-matrix-scheduler.quote: a scheduling matrix that tells us which instructions are able to execute (all dependencies fulfilled) ... This idea is called matrix scheduling.
c-mh-v1-matrix-scheduler.hedge: I think you will agree that it's the only reasonable interpretation
c-mh-v1-matrix-scheduler.notes: US11036514B1 (scheduler entries storing dependency indexes for index-based wakeup, 2016); Handley puts the wakeup bus at about 400 bits

c-mh-v1-microcode-dispatch.text: Microcoded instructions are probably expanded at dispatch, after rename, rather than at decode, and the microcode ops seem not to take ROB slots
c-mh-v1-microcode-dispatch.quote: When the complex instructions are detected, they are replaced with some number of microcode instructions which are fed into the Dispatch process until they're done.
c-mh-v1-microcode-dispatch.hedge: If we take the patent literally
c-mh-v1-microcode-dispatch.notes: US9280352B2 (2011, A6 era), which Handley says "may well be (to some extent) the way the issue is still handled"

c-mh-v1-rob-1000.text: The M1's ROB holds effectively about 1000 instructions of speculative state
c-mh-v1-rob-1000.quote: So the ROB is (as of M1) effectively around 1000 instruction or so of speculative state
c-mh-v1-rob-1000.notes: a summary remark with no method; close to retire.issuing_window (1000)

c-mh-v1-issue-window-280.text: The issue queues taken together give the M1 a look-ahead window of about 280 instructions
c-mh-v1-issue-window-280.quote: the Issue Queue(s taken together) as of the M1 provide a look-ahead window of about 280 instructions
c-mh-v1-issue-window-280.notes: Handley gives no breakdown of the 280

c-mh-v1-dispatch-int-dj.text: Johnson's direct probe put the first-level integer dispatch buffer at 24 entries, split 12 + 12
c-mh-v1-dispatch-int-dj.quote: In fact Dougall's experiments (probing for exactly this size, not detecting it as a side effect like we are doing) has the 1st level int Dispatch Buffer as 24 elements (split into 12+12).

c-mh-v1-dispatch-smoothing.text: The integer dispatch buffer absorbs bursts; runs of 6k ADDs followed by 2k NOPs keep the full rate up to k=13 and slow from k=15
c-mh-v1-dispatch-smoothing.quote: Essentially the case 6*1 through 6*13 always take the fast path (102 cycles per loop iteration), anything above 6*15 takes 108 cycles
c-mh-v1-dispatch-smoothing.notes: k=14 is noisy, in between; Handley reads the transition as the buffer filling at about 2 excess ADDs per cycle over 11 cycles

c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-12.text: The FP dispatch buffer accepts 8 instructions per cycle and holds about 12
c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-12.quote: We see that we can't quite achieve that with 6*(4x FABS+4x NOP) but we can with 5*(4x FABS+4x NOP). Suggesting that the Dispatch Buffer is ~12 in size.
c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-12.notes: sensitive to how the FP instructions fall in the 8-instruction rename groups

c-mh-v1-dispatch-cmp-12.text: A CMP probe (CMP issues to three of the six integer units) fills a 12-entry buffer rather than a 24-entry one, so each integer dispatch buffer feeds three units
c-mh-v1-dispatch-cmp-12.quote: we can transfer all those CMPs into a (12-sized) buffer ... the numbers kinda work out – certainly better than assuming a 24-sized buffer
c-mh-v1-dispatch-cmp-12.notes: the counterpart of the MUL buffer (dispatch.mul_entries); together they make dispatch.int_entries

c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-8.text: Both integer dispatch buffers accept 8 instructions per cycle
c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-8.quote: It also seems that these two integer Dispatch Buffers can accept 8 instructions per cycle.
c-mh-v1-dispatch-accept-8.notes: the FP buffer also takes 8 per cycle

c-mh-v1-fp-roles.text: FCMP can execute on only one of the four FP/SIMD units
c-mh-v1-fp-roles.quote: We can try the same technique with FCMP (which can only execute down one of the four fp pipelines).
c-mh-v1-fp-roles.notes: Stated without a method; Handley also names two FCSEL-capable FP queues (c-mh-v1-sched-fp-pairing). Corroborates Johnson's table (c-dj-fp-roles).

c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-14.text: An FCMP probe sustains 14 FCMPs at full rate, suggesting the FP dispatch buffer may hold 14 rather than 12
c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-14.quote: This is so perfectly matched it suggests that perhaps the size of the FP Dispatch Buffer is slightly larger, perhaps 14 rather than 12?
c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-14.notes: The jump comes at 15 x (1 FCMP + 7 NOP); Handley finds it hard to square with Johnson's diagram. Disagrees with his own FABS probe (c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-12, 12).

c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-single.text: There is a single FP dispatch buffer, not a split one as for integer
c-mh-v1-dispatch-fp-single.quote: we have a single FP Dispatch Buffer, rather than a split buffer like integer.

c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls-probe.text: A load probe overflows the load/store dispatch buffer slightly sooner than the 12-entry CMP case, in line with Johnson's size of 10
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls-probe.quote: we overflow the LD/ST Dispatch Buffer slightly sooner than for CMP, which agrees with Dougall's result of a size of 10 for the LD/ST Dispatch Buffer.
c-mh-v1-dispatch-ls-probe.notes: the 10 is Johnson's; Handley's own probe shows only a buffer a little smaller than 12. CMP and LD are both 3-wide.

c-mh-v1-zero-other-6wide.text: Zeroing with AND x0, xzr, #1 or MOV x0, xzr is not special-cased and runs 6 per cycle in the integer units
c-mh-v1-zero-other-6wide.quote: we will try AND x0, xzr, #1) runs 6 wide ... MOV x0, xzr runs 6 wide
c-mh-v1-zero-other-6wide.notes: only MOV #0 (MOVZ) zeroes at 8 per cycle (c-mh-v1-mov-zero-rename)

c-mh-v1-eor-zero-not-idiom.text: EOR x0, x0, x0 is not a zeroing idiom; it runs one per cycle as a dependent chain
c-mh-v1-eor-zero-not-idiom.quote: EOR x0, x0, x0 runs 1 wide! Not only not an idiom, but forces the chain dependency!

c-mh-v1-mov-imm-8wide.text: Every non-zero MOV-immediate form tried runs 8 per cycle, as 2 per cycle completed at rename plus 6 in the integer units
c-mh-v1-mov-imm-8wide.quote: ALL of these (!) are recognized and run 8-wide. ... Apart from an immediate of zero, these are implemented as 2-wide in rename plus 6-wide in execution
c-mh-v1-mov-imm-8wide.notes: Forms tried include #1, #-1, #0x1234, shifted MOVZ and a logical immediate. Rename handles 8 per cycle, so 2 per cycle is 2 per 8 instructions; Handley later repeats "two free MOV# Rename's per cycle".

c-mh-v1-mov-imm-dependent.text: Chains of eliminated operations resolve within rename; MOV x0, #0 followed by MOV x1, x0 still runs 8 per cycle
c-mh-v1-mov-imm-dependent.quote: MOV x0, #0; MOV x1, x0 seems to run fine (800 ops in 100 cycles), though I'm not doing true latency tests.
c-mh-v1-mov-imm-dependent.hedge: though I'm not doing true latency tests
c-mh-v1-mov-imm-dependent.notes: chains such as MOV x2, x1; MOV x3, x2; ... are also handled at rename

c-mh-v1-movk-not-fused.text: MOV #imm plus MOVK pairs run at 4 pairs per cycle, so MOV+MOVK is not fused
c-mh-v1-movk-not-fused.quote: This runs at 4 (of these pairs) per cycle ... MOV+MOVK is not fused.
c-mh-v1-movk-not-fused.notes: agrees with Johnson's fusion list (c-dj-fusion, not mov+movk) and his MOVK throughput

c-mh-v1-fp-imm-not-special.text: FP immediates, and zeroing an FP register with FMOV dn, xzr, get no special handling at rename
c-mh-v1-fp-imm-not-special.quote: ARM supports a few floating point immediates, but the M1 does not handle these in any special way at Rename.

c-mh-v1-imm-pool-reason.text: Handley thinks Apple writes immediates into a separate immediates-only register file filled only from the decode/rename path, sparing the write ports of the main integer file
c-mh-v1-imm-pool-reason.quote: Another path (which appears to be what Apple is doing right now) is using a separate register pool. ... another alternative is to create a separate "immediates-only" register file which can only be written to by this Decode path
c-mh-v1-imm-pool-reason.hedge: which appears to be what Apple is doing right now
c-mh-v1-imm-pool-reason.notes: The evidence is the ~38 extra registers seen with MOV #1. Handley says the 2012 patent scheme (US9430243B2, constants encoded in spare register IDs) has been superseded.

c-mh-v1-mov-zero-rename.text: MOV xn, #0 is completed at rename like a register MOV or a NOP, while other immediates are only partly special-cased
c-mh-v1-mov-zero-rename.quote: MOV xn, #0 is special-cased and is handled like MOV or NOP, fully resolved at Rename.
c-mh-v1-mov-zero-rename.notes: slope 8 per cycle with a small stutter near N=620; Handley adds that it takes no physical register

c-mh-v1-hf-movreg-620.text: MOV x0, x5 uses no physical registers and maxes out at around 620 history-file entries
c-mh-v1-hf-movreg-620.quote: the MOV x0, x5 does not use physical registers at all, and maxes out at around 620 History File entries.
c-mh-v1-hf-movreg-620.notes: MOV x0, x2 shows the same (c-mh-v1-mov-elim-rename, "This case reaches 620 with no glitches")

c-mh-v1-iregs-separate.text: Thirty-two MOV x0, #1 padded with NOPs and placed before ADDs leave the ADD knee unchanged, so immediates are held outside the main integer register file, with room for more than 32
c-mh-v1-iregs-separate.quote: Look at how the green curve jumps at close to the same place as the gold curve; ie the MOV# register usage has not removed registers from those available to the ADD.
c-mh-v1-iregs-separate.notes: with 40 MOV #1 the result "suggests that there are more than 32 I registers available, perhaps as many as 40"

c-mh-v1-iregs-36.text: About 36 immediate registers exist, each able to hold a different value; 10 or 20 distinct MOV #i add 10 or 20 to the ADD knee, and 40 add about 36
c-mh-v1-iregs-36.quote: For 40 we don't get quite all the way to 420, so the number of additional iRegs appears to be around 36.
c-mh-v1-iregs-36.notes: range 32-40 ("no more than about 36..40 iRegs"; see c-mh-v1-iregs-separate)

c-mh-v1-iregs-exhausted.text: Only immediate registers can be written from rename; when none is free, MOV #imm runs 6 per cycle through the integer units
c-mh-v1-iregs-exhausted.quote: In other words, it appears that only iRegs can be written to from Rename, and when an iReg is not available, MOV# has to run 6-wide.
c-mh-v1-iregs-exhausted.notes: seen as a stretch of 6-wide execution at longer delays (e.g. 39 cycles); with short delays the iRegs free up fast enough to stay 8-wide

c-mh-v1-reg-free-16.text: When the ROB head is not blocked, registers are freed at 16 per cycle
c-mh-v1-reg-free-16.quote: Later we will see that freeing registers (when it is possible, ie if there's not a delay instruction blocking the head of the ROB) occurs at 16 registers/cycle
c-mh-v1-reg-free-16.notes: a forward reference to the measurement (c-mh-v1-reg-free-rate); the same rate as retire.rate_renames (16)

c-mh-v1-zpr.text: Handley's model has a hardwired zero physical register, distinct from xzr, and MOV #0 is a rename-time duplicate of it
c-mh-v1-zpr.quote: there is a special hardwired zero physical register (ZPR) (which, strangely, appears not to be xzr!) and a MOV #0 is treated as a Rename duplication to that ZPR

c-mh-v1-imm-model.text: In Handley's model rename can write only to the immediate registers, up to two per cycle, when the value is known and a register is free; otherwise MOV #imm goes on to scheduling and execution
c-mh-v1-imm-model.quote: there is a special write path from Rename to the iRegs, but not generic pRegs, to allow up to two writes from Rename per cycle
c-mh-v1-imm-model.notes: Handley calls MOV # "primarily a latency reduction tool" that also adds a few registers

c-mh-v2-l1-bw-internet.text: Handley puts the M1's L1 load bandwidth at 150 GB/s and attributes internet reports of ~100 GB/s to reduction code that limits the loop before the cache does
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-internet.quote: I think insufficient attention to this fact is why some internet reports for the M1 show its L1 load bandwidth as ~100GB/s rather than the 150GB/s it’s really capable of.
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-internet.notes: The measurement behind the 150 GB/s is the LDPQ loop.

c-mh-v2-zero-data.text: Runs over all-zero data were neither faster nor slower than runs over non-zero data, so no performance special case for zeroed lines was found
c-mh-v2-zero-data.quote: I did not discover any interesting cases where zero’d data is faster (or slower) than no-zero’d data.
c-mh-v2-zero-data.notes: Tested against Apple's sparse-data patent US10691610B2; Handley suggests it may be unimplemented or save power only.

c-mh-v2-clock-variation.text: During the bandwidth runs the clock mostly stays between 3 and 3.2 GHz, but after long memory-bound stretches with little CPU activity it drops as low as 2.11 GHz or even 1.74 GHz
c-mh-v2-clock-variation.quote: for the most part the frequency stays between 3 and 3.2 GHz ... the frequency drops to as low as 2.11GHz or even 1.74GHz
c-mh-v2-clock-variation.notes: The harness records both cycles and real time, giving the frequency per run.

c-mh-v2-l1-bw-150-ceiling.text: Under ideal conditions the core reaches the 150 GB/s case from L1, about six 8 B loads per cycle, but no higher
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-150-ceiling.quote: We see that the CPU can clearly (under ideal conditions) hit the 150GB/s case (~6 8B loads/cycle) but no higher.
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-150-ceiling.notes: The theoretical cases on the same page are 24 B/cycle (~75 GB/s) for three 8 B loads, 48 B/cycle (150 GB/s) for three load pairs and 96 B/cycle (300 GB/s) for three vector pairs; the measured ceiling is the middle one.

c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths.text: Two load units and the load/store unit give three loads per cycle, over three 16 B load paths from the L1D to the LSU; a load vector pair is cracked in the LSU into two 16 B cache transactions
c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths.quote: two dedicated load units, and one ambidextrous unit, so we can perform 3 ... three load paths from the L1D to the LSU, each 16B wide
c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths.notes: Offered as the explanation for the 150 GB/s ceiling (48 B/cycle = three 16 B paths).

c-mh-v2-naive-reduction-100.text: The naive sum loop and the STL accumulate() version compile to the same vectorized LDPQ code and run at about 100 GB/s (32 B/cycle) from L1
c-mh-v2-naive-reduction-100.quote: (we'd hope so given identical assembly) and run at essentially 100GB/s (ie 32B/cycle
c-mh-v2-naive-reduction-100.notes: Code-limited, not a cache limit: Handley's realistic-code figure. Kernel per iteration: two LDPQ, four two-lane vector adds, SUBS, B.NE.

c-mh-v2-scalar-reduction-width.text: The hand-split 8-way scalar reduction cannot vectorize; three scalar load pairs need six adds plus loop overhead per cycle, so it is limited by machine width, not by the LSU or cache
c-mh-v2-scalar-reduction-width.quote: M1 is wide, but it is not (3+6+2 wide!) So we’re no longer throttled by LSU or cache issues ... simply by the width of the machine compared to the width of our inner loop.
c-mh-v2-scalar-reduction-width.notes: The Reduction 8Wide table rows run at about 74-76 GB/s.

c-mh-v2-ldp-32.text: Assembly loops of LDP or LDNP (scalar pairs, 16 B per load) run at about 110 GB/s from L1, about 32 B per cycle plus 10%
c-mh-v2-ldp-32.quote: The first two loops (running at about 110GB/s) are loops of either ... They give us basically 32B(+ about 10%) per cycle.

c-mh-v2-ldnp-l1-ignored.text: The non-temporal hint makes no difference to loads that hit in L1 (LDNP matches LDP, LDNPQ matches LDPQ)
c-mh-v2-ldnp-l1-ignored.quote: You’d think the N would be irrelevant for loads that hit in L1, and that’s what we see.
c-mh-v2-ldnp-l1-ignored.notes: Handley adds the guess that the L1 ignores the hint when the data is already in cache.

c-mh-v2-ldpq-48.text: Assembly loops of LDPQ or LDNPQ (vector pairs, 32 B per load) run at almost 150 GB/s from L1, almost 48 B per cycle
c-mh-v2-ldpq-48.quote: And these two little monsters manages to run at almost 150GB/s, almost 48B/cycle!
c-mh-v2-ldpq-48.notes: A later table shows LDPQ at 47.59 B/cycle (152 GB/s) at an 87 KB footprint.

c-mh-v2-ldpq-cracked-lsu.text: Counters show an LDPQ retires as one instruction (one ROB slot) but sends two uops through the load unit, so the vector load pair is cracked inside the LSU into two single-vector loads; an LDP is one instruction and one load-unit uop
c-mh-v2-ldpq-cracked-lsu.quote: this means the vector load pair is cracked inside the LSU (so one LDP Qx, Qy is a single ROB instruction but is split in the LSU into two uOps that each load a single vector
c-mh-v2-ldpq-cracked-lsu.notes: Retired loads 1/4 and load-unit uops (LD_UNIT_UOP) 1/2 per int64 for LDPQ; 1/2 and 1/2 for LDP. Handley does not know whether the split comes after the TLB lookup.

c-mh-v2-reduction-simd-latency.text: Every SIMD operation on the M1, even ADD or ABS, has two-cycle latency, and this dependency chain, not the cache, holds the compiler's vectorized reductions to about 100 GB/s
c-mh-v2-reduction-simd-latency.quote: On the M1 every SIMD operation, even the most simple (like ADD or ABS), has a latency of two cycles.
c-mh-v2-reduction-simd-latency.notes: Latency figure stated without a method on this page. The naive and STL loops start faster at very small depths because queued work carries over.

c-mh-v2-antinaive-150.text: AntiNaive (two independent vectorizable sums) and the 2-, 3- and 4-array reductions approach the 150 GB/s L1 limit because their loops are unrolled enough to hide the SIMD add latency
c-mh-v2-antinaive-150.quote: they all do adequately well in approaching the 150GB/s limit ... the loop is unrolled enough that it’s not limited by the latency of the SIMD adds.

c-mh-v2-multiarray-falloff.text: The 2- to 4-array reductions fall off inside the L1 range with no L1 misses while the load-unit uop count rises well above its usual 0.5; Handley's best guess is aggressive L1D sub-array power-down whose wake-up tracking is confused by several sequential streams, so loads are rejected for a cycle
c-mh-v2-multiarray-falloff.quote: for these three reduction cases the value jumps much higher ... My best guess is that it represents our usual fallback when we can’t understand something, namely energy savings.
c-mh-v2-multiarray-falloff.notes: Array placement was chosen to rule out bank or set alignment. Elsewhere Handley reads a high opLd as bank collisions, which he says makes no sense here. The effect goes away once data comes from L2.

c-mh-v2-l2-transitions.text: Bandwidth curves change value together at about 3 MiB, 7.5 MiB and ~16 MiB of footprint, as one core moves from inner L2 to outer L2 to SLC to DRAM
c-mh-v2-l2-transitions.quote: the graphs stay in sync (and change value) at the expected sorts of places (3MiB, 7.5MiB, ~16MiB) as we switch from inner L2 to outer L2 to SLC to DRAM
c-mh-v2-l2-transitions.notes: Multi-array reduction curves, footprints to 128 MiB. 3 MiB is the inner L2, ~16 MiB the end of the SLC.

c-mh-v2-l2-load-range.text: Past 128 KiB, out to about 8 MB, loads come from L2 and run at about 77 to 87 GB/s depending on the code path; code details matter much less than in L1
c-mh-v2-l2-load-range.quote: Within the L2 region, precise code details no longer matter as much ... about 77 to 87GB/s depending on the exact code path
c-mh-v2-l2-load-range.notes: Range 77-87 GB/s over the reduction kernels; the non-temporal loads are the low outliers.

c-mh-v2-temporal-prefetch-l1.text: Throughout the L2 range ordinary sequential loads are prefetched into L1 in time: the L1 miss count stays near zero
c-mh-v2-temporal-prefetch-l1.quote: Throughout the L2 range, the standard code appears to be prefetched exactly as one would hope; data is (mostly) in L1 by the time one wants it
c-mh-v2-temporal-prefetch-l1.notes: L1D_CACHE_MISS_LD about 0.01-0.03 per int64 for LDPQ between 170 KB and 7 MB.

c-mh-v2-nt-load-no-l1-prefetch.text: In the L2 range the non-temporal loads (LDNP, LDNPQ) are clearly slower and miss in L1 far more often than ordinary loads, so their lines seem not to be prefetched into L1 (either fetched only to L2 or not prefetched at all)
c-mh-v2-nt-load-no-l1-prefetch.quote: the poorly performing non-temporal cases miss in L1 substantially more often than the equivalent “temporal load” cases ... whereas for the non-temporal loads, Apple seems to not even prefetch the data.
c-mh-v2-nt-load-no-l1-prefetch.notes: LDNPQ vs LDPQ tables: same 150 GB/s in L1, LDNPQ falling to about 65-68 GB/s by 1-5 MB with a rising L1 miss count. No L2-miss counter is known, so the two readings cannot be separated.

c-mh-v2-l2-load-85.text: Load bandwidth in the L2 region (about 128 KiB to 7 MiB) is about 85 GB/s, roughly 6/7 of the L1 bandwidth
c-mh-v2-l2-load-85.quote: We see that the bandwidth in the L2 region (say 128K to maybe 7M or so) is about 85GB/s. This is about 6/7 of the L1 bandwidth.

c-mh-v2-l2-l1-read-32b.text: Handley assumes a 32 B wide read path from L2 to L1, which would give 100 GB/s and move a 64 B L1 line in two cycles
c-mh-v2-l2-l1-read-32b.quote: Assume that the read path from L2 to L1 is 32B in width. ... Transferring a single L1 line (64B) should take two cycles.
c-mh-v2-l2-l1-read-32b.notes: One extra cycle of overhead per line would give about 2/3 of 100 GB/s; the measured ~85 GB/s needs less.

c-mh-v2-l2-overhead-l1-side.text: Handley places the L2 load shortfall (about 100 to 85 GB/s) on the L1 side: writing prefetched lines from the specialty buffers into the L1 blocks LSU access to those banks and causes bank collisions
c-mh-v2-l2-overhead-l1-side.quote: My guess is that the reduction from 100GB/s to 85 GB/s perhaps lies in imperfect co-ordination between the LSU (which is continually sending loads to the cache as fast as possible) and the pool of specialty buffers
c-mh-v2-l2-overhead-l1-side.notes: This one-lost-cycle-in-seven overhead is absent for L2 stores (c-mh-v2-l2-store-no-overhead).

c-mh-v2-l1-bw.text: As a rule of thumb, perfect L1 load bandwidth is about 48 B/cycle (~150 GB/s); realistic code gets about 32 B/cycle (~100 GB/s), limited by SIMD latency or non-load work
c-mh-v2-l1-bw.quote: perfect L1 load bandwidth at ~150GB/s (48B/cycle) ... realistic L1 load bandwidth at ~100GB/s (32B/cycle limited by SIMD latency
c-mh-v2-l1-bw.notes: Rule-of-thumb summary of the LDPQ runs (c-mh-v2-ldpq-48). Same list puts L2 load bandwidth at ~80% of the realistic L1 figure.

c-mh-v2-l2-inner-bw.text: Load bandwidth curves start to droop at about 3 MiB on the way to 8 MiB, so each core sees an inner L2 of 3 MiB and a slightly slower outer L2
c-mh-v2-l2-inner-bw.quote: they start to droop at around 3MiB on their way to 8MiB ... the general pattern is that there’s an “inner L2” of 3MiB, and an “outer L2”, that’s slightly slower.
c-mh-v2-l2-inner-bw.notes: The latency section only mentions the 3 MiB "near-L2" in passing. The one-quarter-of-12-MiB reading is the cachelet model (c-mh-v2-l2-cachelets).

c-mh-v2-l2-cachelets.text: Handley models the 12 MiB L2 as four 3 MiB cachelets, one per core, each split in half: one half for its own core, the other spare L2 for the other three; a lone core then sees 3 MiB inner plus 4.5 MiB outer, 7.5 MiB
c-mh-v2-l2-cachelets.quote: Half of the 3MiB cachelet is devoted to a particular core; the other half is allowed to act as excess L2 for the remaining three cores ... a total L2 (per core) of 7.5MiB
c-mh-v2-l2-cachelets.notes: Handley does not know how lines are placed in inner vs outer L2 or how cores compete; he compares it to IBM Telum. The win he sees: inner-L2 latency stays low and the outer L2 is hidden by the prefetcher.

c-mh-v2-a14-l2-effective.text: The same partitioning fits the A14: its 8 MiB L2 for two P-cores is considered 6 MiB effective, 4 MiB inner and 2 MiB outer from half of the other cachelet
c-mh-v2-a14-l2-effective.quote: the A14 (8MiB total L2, two P-cores, is considered to have 6MiB of “effective” L2. This would again consist of 4 MiB of inner cache, and 2MiB of “outer cache”
c-mh-v2-a14-l2-effective.notes: Where the 6 MiB effective figure comes from is not said.

c-mh-v2-inner-l2-latency.text: Inner-L2 latency is lower, apparently 18 cycles, and outer-L2 latency is not much higher and is hidden while the prefetcher is active
c-mh-v2-inner-l2-latency.quote: the latency for the inner L2 is smaller (apparently 18 cycles), while the latency for the outer L2 isn’t that much larger, and is hidden as long as the prefetcher is active
c-mh-v2-inner-l2-latency.notes: No method or source on this page; agrees with 7-cpu's 18 cycles. The latency section has Handley's own probes.

c-mh-v2-slc-size.text: The most reliable SLC size Handley has seen for the M1 is 8 MiB, so cached behaviour should extend to ~16 MiB
c-mh-v2-slc-size.quote: The most reliable number I’ve seen for the size of the SLC in M1 is 8MiB.

c-mh-v2-slc-dram-load-64.text: Load bandwidth drops from about 85 GB/s in L2 to about 64 GB/s once the footprint is in the SLC or DRAM
c-mh-v2-slc-dram-load-64.quote: that seems enough to explain the reduction in throughput, from about 85GB/s in L2 to ~64GB/s in SLC/DRAM.
c-mh-v2-slc-dram-load-64.notes: Single core, reduction kernels, footprints to 512 MB.

c-mh-v2-slc-matched-dram.text: SLC bandwidth is not notably different from DRAM bandwidth; Apple appears to match the SLC's bandwidth to DRAM's
c-mh-v2-slc-matched-dram.quote: the SLC does not have a notably different bandwidth from DRAM (in fact it looks like Apple essentially matches the SLC bandwidth to the DRAM bandwidth).
c-mh-v2-slc-matched-dram.notes: Handley guesses that on the M1 the NoC and SLC run no faster than needed to match DRAM, hence ~65-70 GB/s rather than the L2's ~100.

c-mh-v2-slc-link-64b.text: Handley guesses the SLC connects to the L2 over a 64 B bus at about half the CPU clock rather than 32 B at full clock; asynchronous clocking and NoC overhead then explain the drop to ~64 GB/s
c-mh-v2-slc-link-64b.quote: My guess is that the SLC is actually connected to the L2 via a bus that’s 64B wide rather than 32B. This would allow it to run at half the frequency of the CPU
c-mh-v2-slc-link-64b.notes: He allows a 32 B link at core frequency as the alternative but thinks wider and slower more likely. He sketches the Pro/Max NoC as 64 B at ~1.6 GHz.

c-mh-v2-m1max-flat-bw.text: M1 Pro and Max show no drop past L2: DRAM delivers ~100 GB/s, like L2, so bandwidth is flat from L2 to DRAM; each SLC+memory unit appears able to deliver 100 GB/s
c-mh-v2-m1max-flat-bw.quote: On M1 Pro and Max we do not see this dropoff. SLC bandwidth is still matched to DRAM, but DRAM is now at ~100 GB/s, as is L2, and bandwidth is essentially flat from L2 to DRAM!
c-mh-v2-m1max-flat-bw.notes: Also M1 Pro. The page does not say whose measurement; Handley later reads AnandTech's M1 Max graphs (c-mh-v2-m1max-core-100). A single P cluster cannot take more than ~100 GB/s.

c-mh-v2-nt-load-dram-10pct.text: In DRAM the non-temporal loads go from worst to best, perhaps 10% more bandwidth than ordinary loads
c-mh-v2-nt-load-dram-10pct.quote: Note that once we hit DRAM the previously sub-optimal non-temporal loads become optimal delivering perhaps 10% better bandwidth.
c-mh-v2-nt-load-dram-10pct.notes: His guess is that NT lines are installed in no cache on the way, so no bandwidth goes to moving victims.

c-mh-v2-lpddr4x-peak.text: The M1 appears to use standard LPDDR4x at 4266 MT/s on a 16 B interface, a peak of 4266 x 16 B = 68.256 GB/s
c-mh-v2-lpddr4x-peak.quote: Apple appears to be using more or less standard LPDDR4x at 4266MT/s, which converts to a maximum possible bandwidth of 4266*16B=68.256GB/s.

c-mh-v2-dram-efficiency.text: Measured DRAM bandwidth is about 94% of the LPDDR4x-4266 peak
c-mh-v2-dram-efficiency.quote: So they're getting about 94% bandwidth efficiency out of their DRAM, which is astonishingly high!

c-mh-v2-m1max-lpddr5.text: M1 Pro and Max move to LPDDR5 at 6400 MT/s, a peak of 102.4 GB/s per memory controller, with two or four controllers
c-mh-v2-m1max-lpddr5.quote: with the Max and Pro this switches to LPDDR5 at 6400MT/s, giving a maximum possible bandwidth of 6400*16B=102.4GB/s (times two or four memory controllers).
c-mh-v2-m1max-lpddr5.notes: Two controllers on M1 Pro, four on M1 Max.

c-mh-v2-l2-scalar.text: The M1's ~85 GB/s L2 load bandwidth is available even to code using scalar registers
c-mh-v2-l2-scalar.quote: compare with Apple’s 85GB/s or so ... whereas the Apple result is available even for code using scalar registers
c-mh-v2-l2-scalar.notes: From the Tiger Lake comparison (Intel ~140 GB/s from L2, but only with AVX256 code). Restates c-mh-v2-l2-load-85.

c-mh-v2-two-stores-per-cycle.text: With one store unit and one load/store unit, the core can process at most two stores per cycle
c-mh-v2-two-stores-per-cycle.quote: the core has one store unit, and one ambidextrous unit, so we’d expect the maximum rate at which stores can be processed is two per cycle.

c-mh-v2-l1-store-32.text: The best fill loops reach the ideal L1 store limit of 32 B per cycle, 100 GB/s
c-mh-v2-l1-store-32.quote: there are clearly cases that are able to reach the ideal limit (store 32B of data/cycle=100GB/s), and cases that don’t do so well.
c-mh-v2-l1-store-32.notes: Naive Fill2 (eight stp q0, q0 per iteration) gets essentially there.

c-mh-v2-naive-fill-90.text: The compiler's fill loop (two stp q0, q0 per iteration) reaches about 90 GB/s, not the optimum; Handley puts it down to only two stores entering the queues per cycle, since one taken branch is processed per cycle, so nothing is queued to ride out glitches
c-mh-v2-naive-fill-90.quote: this performs well, at about 90GB/s (the blue curve) but not optimally. ... the first case results in, per cycle, only two stores placed in the various queues
c-mh-v2-naive-fill-90.notes: The idiomatic C++ fill compiles to the same loop and behaves the same.

c-mh-v2-store-path-16b.text: A fill writing only 48 B of each 64 B line (three stp x0, x0) runs as fast as full-line vector fills, so there is no wider line-at-a-time path from the store queue to the L1D; stores use the 16 B store path
c-mh-v2-store-path-16b.quote: this implies that there is no special path from the STQ to the L1D that can transfer entire cache lines at a higher rate ... rather than using the baseline store 16B wide transfer path

c-mh-v2-nt-stores-slc.text: STNP and STNPQ loops run at about SLC/DRAM bandwidth even in the L1 range, suggesting lines filled in the store queue go straight to the SLC without being allocated in L1 or L2
c-mh-v2-nt-stores-slc.quote: The two non-temporal cases run at about SLC or DRAM bandwidth ... they are probably transferred all the way to SLC without ever being allocated in L1 or L2?

c-mh-v2-full-line-to-dram.text: When successive stores in the store queue fill a whole line, the line is written straight out to DRAM/SLC, not to L2, and is not counted as an L1 writeback; a copy already in L1 appears to be invalidated
c-mh-v2-full-line-to-dram.quote: as far as I can tell, the line is not written to L2, it is written all the way out to DRAM (or SLC, which amounts to the same thing) ... As far as I can tell M1 chooses invalidation
c-mh-v2-full-line-to-dram.hedge: as far as I can tell
c-mh-v2-full-line-to-dram.notes: Counters used: L1 store misses (l1MsSt), L1 writebacks (l1WbSt), non-temporal stores (stNT). A partially written line instead goes through L1 and is later written back.

c-mh-v2-store-stream-detect.text: The core detects streams of stores that are not jumbled and converts them to non-temporal stores on its own
c-mh-v2-store-stream-detect.quote: the CPU transparently detects streams of stores (as long as they aren’t “jumbled”) and converts them to non-temporal stores
c-mh-v2-store-stream-detect.notes: Naive Fill and Fill STPQ (two and four STPQ per iteration) show stNT near 0.5 per int64 and no writebacks.

c-mh-v2-nt-store-bypass.text: Non-temporal stores bypass L1, and Handley thinks also L2
c-mh-v2-nt-store-bypass.quote: So what’s definitely established is ... nontemporal stores bypass L1 (and I think also L2)
c-mh-v2-nt-store-bypass.notes: The L2 part is the hedged one.

c-mh-v2-store-stream-warmup.text: Detecting a store stream takes a few cycles, so the first stores of a fill are partly done in cache, giving noise at small depths
c-mh-v2-store-stream-warmup.quote: it takes a few cycles to confidently detect a stream of stores, hence the “noise” (not all stores ... to non-temporal, some stores being performed in cache) for the first few entries
