c-mh-v2-fill2-jumbled.text: A fill unrolled to eight STPQ per iteration is never converted to non-temporal stores and its lines go through L1 with writebacks, which Handley puts down to full scheduling queues jumbling the store order; unrolling by four instead restores streaming
c-mh-v2-fill2-jumbled.quote: To test this theory I made a very slight tweak to Naive Fill 2 so that it unrolled to an inner loop of 4 rather than 8 STPQ, and the prediction was born out
c-mh-v2-fill2-jumbled.notes: Naive Fill2 has stNT 0 and l1WbSt ~0.13 beyond L1, about 60 GB/s in L2 and ~28 GB/s in DRAM, against ~98 GB/s in L1. The hedge is on the cause.

c-mh-v2-stnpq-dram-speed.text: Explicit non-temporal STNPQ stores lose the startup noise but also the L1 performance: they run at DRAM speed at every depth
c-mh-v2-stnpq-dram-speed.quote: Suppose we tell the system from the start that we have a non-temporal stream? Then we lose that “startup” noise. But we also lose L1 performance! Basically we always run at DRAM speeds.
c-mh-v2-stnpq-dram-speed.notes: About 64-65 GB/s from 8 KB upward. Handley finds no case where STNPQ is worthwhile and has not seen it in library or compiler output.

c-mh-v2-large-store-policy.text: Handley's reading of the store policy: small stores gather and stay in cache; a stream of large (STPQ) stores is first captured in L1, but once it looks set to exceed L1 it is pushed all the way to DRAM, apparently not to L2
c-mh-v2-large-store-policy.quote: if it looks like the store stream will exceed the capacity of L1, then we stop trying to store in L1 and push the stores out all the way to DRAM
c-mh-v2-large-store-policy.notes: Not to L2, since he thinks that would keep ~100 GB/s.

c-mh-v2-partial-fill.text: A fill that writes three of the four quadrants of each line cannot be aggregated or streamed: counters show no non-temporal stores, constant writebacks, and stores mostly to lines already in L1
c-mh-v2-partial-fill.quote: And we see this in the numbers – no non-temporal stores, constant stream of writebacks, and many of the stores are to addresses that are already in L1
c-mh-v2-partial-fill.notes: ~96-98 GB/s in L1, ~52 GB/s in L2, ~21-23 GB/s in DRAM.

c-mh-v2-l2-store-100.text: In the best case the ~100 GB/s (32 B/cycle) L1 store bandwidth roughly persists into L2, at least to the 3 MiB inner L2
c-mh-v2-l2-store-100.quote: for the optimal case the L1 store bandwidth (~100GB/s = 32B/cycle) kinda persists all the way to L2 (at least out to the inner L2 of 3MB or so).
c-mh-v2-l2-store-100.notes: Store data is noisy; Handley has seen almost 100 GB/s persist to ~3 MiB in other runs.

c-mh-v2-l2-store-no-overhead.text: The one-lost-cycle-in-seven overhead of sustained L2 loads does not appear for L2 stores
c-mh-v2-l2-store-no-overhead.quote: The occasional overhead (one lost cycle every seven cycles or so) that we saw for sustained L2 loads is not present here in L2 stores.

c-mh-v2-outer-l2-store.text: In the outer L2, store bandwidth drops to maybe 80 GB/s
c-mh-v2-outer-l2-store.quote: For the outer L2 this drops to maybe 80 GB/s

c-mh-v2-slc-dram-store.text: Store bandwidth falls to about 65 GB/s in the SLC and DRAM
c-mh-v2-slc-dram-store.quote: falling to about 65GB/s for SLC and DRAM

c-mh-v2-slc-store-vs-load.text: In the SLC and DRAM range the best store curve matches loads but a few percent higher, and holds out to DRAM
c-mh-v2-slc-store-vs-load.quote: For the SLC and DRAM region, for the best case curve, we see performance essentially like for loads, but a few percent higher.
c-mh-v2-slc-store-vs-load.notes: Handley imagines the L2 packing two lines per NoC packet for stores, cutting NoC and clock-crossing overhead.

c-mh-v2-dczva-rate.text: A stream of DC ZVA sustains about two instructions (two 64 B lines) per three cycles, about 134 GB/s, better than ordinary stores but short of one per cycle (200 GB/s)
c-mh-v2-dczva-rate.quote: It looks like we can sustain about 2/3 of a DC ZVA per cycle, or to put it differently, we can execute two such instructions in three cycles (that would give about 128B/3~=42B/s~=134GB/s)
c-mh-v2-dczva-rate.notes: Ordinary stores zero a line in two cycles at 32 B/cycle; DC ZVA takes 1.5.

c-mh-v2-dczva-l2-alloc.text: DC ZVA appears to allocate zeroed lines directly in L2, probably through a cache-protocol state change rather than a data transfer; counters show no writebacks
c-mh-v2-dczva-l2-alloc.quote: DC ZVA allocates zeroed lines directly in L2 (probably by extensions to the cache protocol rather than by transferring data). Looking at the performance monitor data confirms no writebacks.
c-mh-v2-dczva-l2-alloc.notes: 1.5 cycles per line, below the 2 cycles a 32 B transfer needs, is his evidence for a protocol shortcut. The fast path reaches only L2, not the SLC. Compared to Arm's streaming mode.

c-mh-v2-dczva-with-load.text: When the lines to be zeroed were just read, DC ZVA is slow at every depth: beyond L1 each line is loaded and written back, losing the zero-allocate path
c-mh-v2-dczva-with-load.quote: As soon as we leave L1, each line has to be loaded, and the write back to L2 or SLC/DRAM is recorded in the performance monitor data as a writeback

c-mh-v2-dczva-with-store.text: Interleaving DC ZVA with ordinary STPQ stores runs at normal store speed, not at DC ZVA speed
c-mh-v2-dczva-with-store.quote: As we can see, the results are not terrible, but they run at standard store speed, not at the higher speed of a stream of DC ZVA.
c-mh-v2-dczva-with-store.notes: Four DC ZVA then four STPQ per iteration; it falls apart beyond the SLC, which Handley cannot explain.

c-mh-v2-l1d-line-dczva.text: L1 cache line length is 64 B, not the 128 B widely reported; DC ZVA clears 64 B
c-mh-v2-l1d-line-dczva.quote: DC ZVA wipes 64B of data, not 128B. Another concrete piece of evidence that Apple’s L1 cache line width (at least for the M1 P core) is actually 64B, contra to what is reported in some places on the internet.
c-mh-v2-l1d-line-dczva.notes: Earlier vol 2 pages assume 64 B lines and point forward to experiments; this DC ZVA test is one.

c-mh-v2-l2-line-128-bw.text: The L2 line is 128 B, and probably so for the rest of the SoC including the SLC, against 64 B for the L1
c-mh-v2-l2-line-128-bw.quote: In fact the final resolution to this issue is that the L1 cache line length is 64B, the cache line length for the L2 (and probably the rest of the SoC, including eg the SLC) is 128B.
c-mh-v2-l2-line-128-bw.notes: No test for the L2 figure on this page; the prefetcher-patent section dates the 128 B L2 line to around the A10. The hedge applies to the SLC.

c-mh-v2-flip-bw.text: Line-flip kernels (each line read and written back reversed) run at about 150 GB/s in L1, 110 GB/s in L2, 100 GB/s in the SLC and 60 GB/s in DRAM
c-mh-v2-flip-bw.quote: Immediately obvious points are that the L1 performance is about 150GB/s, the L2 performance is about 110GB/s, the SLC performance is about 100GB/s, falling to about 60GB/s in DRAM.
c-mh-v2-flip-bw.notes: Value is the L1 figure. Flip CL (permute and no permute) and Flip Address range; two LDP + two STP of q registers per iteration.

c-mh-v2-l1-copy-chokepoint.text: Copying in L1 reaches ~150 GB/s, not the 200 GB/s of 100 GB/s loads plus 100 GB/s stores: two lines take five cycles instead of four, a chokepoint Handley did not expect given separate load and store paths
c-mh-v2-l1-copy-chokepoint.quote: There appears to be a chokepoint in L1. I would expect have expected we could sustain 200GB/s in L1 ... Two lines should take four cycles but we get the number we see if we assume two lines takes five cycles.

c-mh-v2-flip-partial.text: A flip that leaves part of each line unwritten, so no full line goes to L2, is still pegged just over 150 GB/s, so L1-to-L2 line writes are not the L1 copy limit
c-mh-v2-flip-partial.quote: I tested this by modifying Flip CL to only write back some of the cache line not completely overwrite the cache line ... we’re still pegged at just slightly over 150GB/s.

c-mh-v2-copy-store-stream-bypass.text: Copies fall off at 128 KiB, not at the 64 KiB a cache holding source and destination lines would give (nor at half the L2 or SLC), so full-line store streams bypass the caches to DRAM even within a copy, and the stream detector tracks store addresses only
c-mh-v2-copy-store-stream-bypass.quote: Look at the way the performance falls off at 128kiB. ... the overwritten line is bypassed all the way to DRAM ... track only stores addresses (not all addresses)

c-mh-v2-coherence-hypothesis.text: Handley's best, weak hypothesis for the copy limits is coherence processing in L1 or L2, perhaps running every other cycle because a line crosses the 32 B L1-L2 paths only every two cycles
c-mh-v2-coherence-hypothesis.quote: My current best (not great) hypothesis is that the constraint is processing coherence in either L1 or L2.
c-mh-v2-coherence-hypothesis.notes: He calls the story "pretty flimsy". He offers the same explanation for the ~100 GB/s L2 limit on mixed traffic (c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l2-100).

c-mh-v2-naive-copy-2ops.text: The compiler turns the naive copy loop into LDR q0; STR q0; SUBS; B.NE, and with one taken branch per cycle that issues only two memory ops per cycle
c-mh-v2-naive-copy-2ops.quote: Recall that the CPU can only handle one taken branch per cycle, so the net result is that we only issue two (rather than four) memory ops per cycle!

c-mh-v2-copy-l1-170.text: Unrolled copies (LDP/STP of q-register pairs), memcpy() and STL copy approach 170 GB/s at about 64 KiB, short of 200 GB/s
c-mh-v2-copy-l1-170.quote: We don’t reach the 200GB/s that one might hope for, but at around 64kiB we get close at about 170GB/s.
c-mh-v2-copy-l1-170.notes: Peak of the best copy code, very noisy; Handley's rule-of-thumb L1 copy figure is 150 GB/s.

c-mh-v2-l2-copy-100.text: Within L2, copies settle just over 100 GB/s, more than a single 32 B/cycle L1-L2 link could carry
c-mh-v2-l2-copy-100.quote: the long term (within L2) pattern is just over 100GB/s; which is better than what’s possible if we assume a link between L1 and L2 of 32B/s!
c-mh-v2-l2-copy-100.notes: Naive Copy, Naive Copy2, memcpy() and STL copy, linear-axis plot.

c-mh-v2-l1-l2-split-paths.text: The L1 and L2 must be joined by separate read and write paths, each 32 B wide
c-mh-v2-l1-l2-split-paths.quote: I think we have to assume separate read and write paths from L1 to L2, each 32B in width.
c-mh-v2-l1-l2-split-paths.hedge: I think we have to assume
c-mh-v2-l1-l2-split-paths.notes: Handley's summary: about one line read and one line written every four cycles, slightly more than even a perfect shared 32 B/cycle link could give.

c-mh-v2-ldnt-copy-l2.text: memcpy() and STL copy use non-temporal loads (LDNT) where the naive loops use plain loads, and this clearly helps from 128 KiB out to about 1500 KiB
c-mh-v2-ldnt-copy-l2.quote: The Naive Code (both versions) use LD and ST; the memcpy() and STL differ in that they use LDNT and ST, ie they use a non-temporal load. This clearly helps in the range from 128kIB out to about 1500kiB.

c-mh-v2-nt-load-buffer-model.text: Handley's model for the LDNT gain: the L1 keeps its 128 KiB of load data and later non-temporal loads are fed to the LSU from the prefetch buffers without replacing L1 lines, so part of the footprint still runs at L1 speed
c-mh-v2-nt-load-buffer-model.quote: In the second model the cache holds onto 128 kiB of data and all loads after that point are routed from the prefetch specialty buffers to the LSU, without replacing L1 lines.
c-mh-v2-nt-load-buffer-model.notes: Both of his models assume stores are silently made non-temporal, so the L1 holds only load data. The plain-load copies fit the other model, a strictly LRU L1 with no reuse.

c-mh-v2-copy-beyond-l2.text: Beyond L2, copy bandwidth drops to about 60 GB/s over the SLC and DRAM, and here non-temporal loads are clearly worse than ordinary loads
c-mh-v2-copy-beyond-l2.quote: Beyond L2 performance drops to about 60GB/s over the SLC and DRAM range. One thing we see is that in this range non-temporal loads are unequivocally worse than temporal loads.

c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl.text: Handley thinks the L2 uses random rather than LRU replacement: ordinary loads keep partly hitting in L2 between 8 and 16 MiB, while non-temporal loads, never installed in L2, drop straight to SLC bandwidth
c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl.quote: the L2 replacement is random rather than LRU, giving the reverse of the effect we saw earlier moving from L1 to L2.

c-mh-v2-copy-no-turnaround.text: Copy costs nothing over pure load or store traffic at the NoC/SLC or in DRAM, so the memory controller hides DRAM read-write switching well
c-mh-v2-copy-no-turnaround.quote: Finally we see no real cost to copy as opposed to pure load/store traffic, either at the NoC (and so SLC performance) or in DRAM. ... we seem to see a good memory controller here.

c-mh-v2-memmove-160.text: memmove() shifting data down by 16 to 256 B copies at about 160 GB/s in L1; the 8 B shift, which splits some 16 B loads across lines, still gets 150 GB/s
c-mh-v2-memmove-160.quote: they essentially cluster together giving perfect copy performance of 160GB/s or so. Even the misaligned 8B case ... you still get 150GB/s!

c-mh-v2-memmove-nt-dropped.text: memmove() runs the same bcopy code as memcpy(), with loads marked non-temporal, but counters show no non-temporal loads for memmove; Handley infers the hardware drops the hint when it sees the lines reused
c-mh-v2-memmove-nt-dropped.quote: we see that this number is as expected (essentially all loads non-temporal) for the C Copy and STL code, but is zero for the memmove code, even though they all route to the same inner loop
c-mh-v2-memmove-nt-dropped.notes: memmove drops sharply to ~100 GB/s at the L1 boundary and tracks the Flip curves, unlike memcpy's drawn-out LDNT transition. He credits the prefetcher.

c-mh-v2-m1max-core-100.text: From AnandTech's M1 Max data, a single M1 Max core sustains 100 GB/s out to the SLC and DRAM
c-mh-v2-m1max-core-100.quote: A single M1M core can now sustain 100GB/s out to DRAM and the SLC. So the NoC can sustain that.
c-mh-v2-m1max-core-100.notes: AnandTech M1 Max review. The same copy test shows 150 GB/s in L1.

c-mh-v2-one-thread-saturates.text: The M1 saturates its SLC and DRAM bandwidth at 65 GB/s with one thread; more threads add nothing
c-mh-v2-one-thread-saturates.quote: The M1 saturates its SLC and DRAM bandwidth at 65GB/s with just one thread, further threads see no improvement.
c-mh-v2-one-thread-saturates.notes: Stated next to AnandTech's M1 Max thread-scaling graph, where a second thread nearly doubles bandwidth; the page does not say whether the M1 thread-scaling result is Handley's own.

c-mh-v2-m1max-slc-split.text: On M1 Pro and Max the SLC and its memory controller are split into two (Pro) or four (Max) independent, address-striped units, which the die shots confirm
c-mh-v2-m1max-slc-split.quote: The natural assumption is that “the” SLC (and associated memory controller) are now split into (two for the Pro, four for the Max) independent entities striped by address
c-mh-v2-m1max-slc-split.notes: Two on M1 Pro. Stripe granularity unknown (?64 B to ?512 B).

c-mh-v2-slc-even-odd.text: The SLC and memory controller are split into even and odd halves by cache line, Apple's common pattern
c-mh-v2-slc-even-odd.quote: the SLC and memory controller are split into Apple’s common pattern of even and odd halves by cache line
c-mh-v2-slc-even-odd.notes: Handley refers to his own discussion elsewhere; not argued on this page.

c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l1-170.text: Unbalanced kernels (three loads and one store per cycle) approach almost 170 GB/s in L1, against about 150 GB/s for balanced copies
c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l1-170.quote: we can approach almost 170 GB/s in L1 for unbalanced operations (specifically three loads plus one store).
c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l1-170.notes: Add Op (C=A+B) and FMAC Op (D=A+B|C, no real multiply); depth axis rescaled by hand.

c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l2-100.text: The unbalanced kernels run at about 100 GB/s in L2, the same ~100 GB/s seen for other mixes, which Handley attributes to passing coherence information between L1 and L2 rather than to data bandwidth
c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l2-100.quote: We also see that these unbalanced ops run at around 100GB/s in L2, the same sort of ~100GB/s we seem to always see
c-mh-v2-unbalanced-l2-100.notes: The coherence explanation is hedged ("I think ... ? (Anyone else have a better theory?)").

c-mh-v2-shared-load-store-path.text: DRAM, and probably the NoC and SLC, use one shared path for loads and stores, so running loads alongside stores does not add bandwidth there
c-mh-v2-shared-load-store-path.quote: NoC (and thus SLC) is probably like DRAM – a common path uses for loads and stores, not separate load and store paths, so same effect there.
c-mh-v2-shared-load-store-path.notes: The L1-L2 link he guesses to have separate load and store paths, while saying he does not know how it is built.

c-mh-v2-add-overwrite-200.text: With A=A+B, each store lands on the line loaded a cycle earlier, the stores overlap loads at no visible cost, and L1 throughput reaches almost 200 GB/s
c-mh-v2-add-overwrite-200.quote: In this case Apple’s magic L1 cache should be able to kick in, so that the cost of the stores is essentially invisible, being overlapped with loads from the same line. And indeed it does. Damn! Almost 200 GB/s!
c-mh-v2-add-overwrite-200.notes: Same for FMAC Overwrite; L2 is also slightly better for both.

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-dram.text: DRAM and SLC give about 60-68 GB/s whatever the access pattern
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-dram.quote: DRAM and SLC give you about 60..68GB/s regardless of what you do
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-dram.notes: Range 60-68 GB/s; value is the midpoint.

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l2-load.text: L2 gives about 85 GB/s for loads

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l2-store.text: L2 gives about 100 GB/s for stores

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l2-copy.text: L2 gives about 135 GB/s for copies, and 90-110 GB/s for more unbalanced load/store mixes
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l2-copy.quote: L2 can give you 85 GB/s (load), 100GB/s (store), 135 GB/s (copy), with worse results (90..110) GB/s as we moved to a more unbalanced mix of loads and stores
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l2-copy.notes: 135 is above the copy figures earlier in the section (~110 GB/s for flips, c-mh-v2-flip-bw; just over 100 GB/s for copies, c-mh-v2-l2-copy-100); the text does not reconcile them.

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l1-copy.text: L1 gives about 150 GB/s for copies

c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l1-load.text: The summary gives L1 load bandwidth as about 110 GB/s, with 100 GB/s for stores and 200 GB/s for the best mix of two loads and one store to a loaded line
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l1-load.quote: L1 can give you 110GB/s (load), 100GB/s (store), 150 GB/s (copy), 200GB/s (optimal mix of two loads, one store to the same as a load address)
c-mh-v2-bw-summary-l1-load.notes: 110 GB/s matches the LDP and realistic-code results; the perfect LDPQ figure is ~150 GB/s, 48 B/cycle (c-mh-v2-l1-bw).

c-mh-v2-l1-bw-basics.text: Three LDP (X-register pair) loads per cycle with autoincrement addressing load 48 B/cycle from the L1, a peak of 153.6 GB/s at 3.2 GHz
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-basics.quote: within L1 we can load 48B/cycle ... the maximum load throughput from L1D is 48B*3.2GHz=153.6GB/s
c-mh-v2-l1-bw-basics.notes: LDP x0, [x2, #16] or the post-index form run at essentially three per cycle; manual base increments add a dependency chain. For the perfect-48 vs realistic-32 B/cycle rule of thumb see c-mh-v2-l1-bw

c-mh-v2-l1-lsu-128b.text: Each load moves at most 128 bits from the L1D to the LSU, so a vector LDP needs two cycles of data transfer
c-mh-v2-l1-lsu-128b.quote: the width from L1D to the LSU for each load appears to be 128b, so something like a vector LDP takes two cycles for the data transfer
c-mh-v2-l1-lsu-128b.notes: See c-mh-v2-ldpq-throughput (LDP Q at 1.5 per cycle, two cache traversals each)

c-mh-v2-dram-random-64.text: For random loads that mostly miss to DRAM, the M1 delivers around 64 GB/s
c-mh-v2-dram-random-64.quote: mostly misses to DRAM for every load ... M1 appears to provide a bandwidth of around 64GB/s
c-mh-v2-dram-random-64.notes: Given right after he points readers to AnandTech's A13 and M1 articles for bandwidth and latency numbers; he does not say whose figure it is. He adds that the M1 has twice the A13's DRAM bandwidth

c-mh-v2-slc-memory-side.text: The M1's system level cache is a memory-side cache, associated with the DRAM controller rather than with the CPUs or any other block
c-mh-v2-slc-memory-side.quote: it's a memory-side cache. In other words you can think of it as being a cache that is tightly associated with the DRAM (and more specifically with the DRAM controller)
c-mh-v2-slc-memory-side.notes: He lists benefits this allows: streaming traffic bypassing the SLC, and the SLC acting as a virtual write queue (ISCA 2010; known in IBM POWER8). He does not show the M1 doing either

c-mh-v2-ls-pipes.text: The load/store pipes are best summarized as two load-only, one store-only and one ambidextrous pipeline, four in all
c-mh-v2-ls-pipes.quote: the best way to summarize is something like there are ... 2 load-only pipelines ... 1 store-only pipeline ... 1 ambidextrous pipeline
c-mh-v2-ls-pipes.notes: Starts from the instruction tables' 3 loads or 2 stores per cycle

c-mh-v2-ls-mix.text: The core runs 3 loads + 1 store or 2 loads + 2 stores in one cycle, but not 3 loads + 2 stores
c-mh-v2-ls-mix.quote: we should be able to run 3 loads+1 store, or 2 loads+2stores in one cycle, and we can; but we can't, for example, run 3 loads and 2 stores in a cycle
c-mh-v2-ls-mix.notes: Interleaved store/load streams reach 3.99-4.0 ops/cycle and one store plus three loads 3.97-4.0. Ice Lake does 2+2 but cannot switch to 3+1

c-mh-v2-tlb-two-pages.text: Probes of three loads, two on one page and one on a page 16 KiB away, take 2.8 cycles per two probes, against one cycle per probe when all three share a page and cache line
c-mh-v2-tlb-two-pages.quote: LDR [x1]; LDR [x1+8]; LDR [x1+16K] 2 probes per 2.8 cycles (so about 1.4 cycles per
c-mh-v2-tlb-two-pages.notes: No address update, so no L1 or TLB misses; about 2.14 loads serviced per cycle

c-mh-v2-tlb-three-pages.text: Probes of three loads on three pages 16 KiB apart take 5 cycles per two probes
c-mh-v2-tlb-three-pages.quote: LDR [x1]; LDR [x1+16K]; LDR [x1+32K] 2 probes per 5 cycles (so about 2.5 cycles per
c-mh-v2-tlb-three-pages.notes: Handley reads this as about 1 + 1/6 requests serviced per TLB lookup

c-mh-v2-dtlb-single-port.text: The L1 dTLB does one lookup per cycle, and the result is shared over piggyback ports with every waiting load or store to the same page, so the TLB is single-ported
c-mh-v2-dtlb-single-port.quote: one TLB lookup per cycle, but that TLB lookup result can service multiple requestors that all have the same page number
c-mh-v2-dtlb-single-port.notes: Up to four loads/stores on the same page share one translation. Handley guesses each piggyback port also receives the page permissions.

c-mh-v2-tlb-queues.text: Requests wait for the TLB in 4 queues of up to 4 entries, binned by low page-number bits; each cycle the oldest request is translated together with the others in its queue on the same page
c-mh-v2-tlb-queues.quote: The results of these simulations do not prove, but strongly suggest, that the system is using 4 queues, each queue holds up to four entries
c-mh-v2-tlb-queues.hedge: do not prove, but strongly suggest
c-mh-v2-tlb-queues.notes: Stochastic simulations; the system favours latency (oldest first) over waiting for queues to fill, and a request may wait up to three cycles. The four-ops-per-cycle case needs at least four queues of at least four entries

c-mh-v2-l1-entry-queues.text: Requests entering the L1 are queued the same way, four queues of up to four requestors, the scarce resource being access to a bank: requests to different lines in the same bank must wait
c-mh-v2-l1-entry-queues.quote: Very much the same structure (servicing multiple requests when possible, four queues, holding up to four requestors) is used at entry into the L1
c-mh-v2-l1-entry-queues.notes: Handley mentions 16 banks "to simplify tremendously"; see c-mh-v2-l1d-banks

c-mh-v2-tlb-autoinc.text: When each base register auto-increments by #200, the 16K- and 32K-offset probes run at close to three loads per cycle, which Handley explains as the loads spreading evenly over the four TLB queues
c-mh-v2-tlb-autoinc.quote: But this substantially improves things! Giving a throughput of very close one one cycle per three loads

c-mh-v2-tlb-4ops.text: Two loads and two stores to four pages at offsets of k x (16 KiB + 80 B) sustain four operations per cycle
c-mh-v2-tlb-4ops.quote: if you use the four offsets (0, 1, 2, 3)*(16*1024+64+16) you will sustain four operations per cycle
c-mh-v2-tlb-4ops.notes: Two loads + two stores on one page also run at full rate; one access on another page gives about one cycle per quad (2.6-2.7 requests per lookup). Three loads + one store, or auto-updates, break the symmetry.

c-mh-v2-tlb-no-sharing.text: A load stream that touches a new page on every access, over about 16 pages, can share no TLB lookups and drops to about one load per cycle (0.97 cycles per load)
c-mh-v2-tlb-no-sharing.quote: no TLB lookup can be shared, and the number of accesses processed per cycle drops from the ideal of three or four down to to just very slightly below 1.
c-mh-v2-tlb-no-sharing.notes: Loads only, offsets (0, 1, 2) x (16 KiB + 80 B), wrapped every 256 KiB; wrapping at 128 KiB (8-12 pages live) doubles throughput to 2 loads/cycle

c-mh-v2-tlb-queue-overflow.text: Spreading the same stream over 32 or 64 pages makes each load take two cycles; Handley guesses a load that cannot be enqueued for the TLB (4 x 4 slots) is replayed
c-mh-v2-tlb-queue-overflow.quote: If we go in the other direction, making the BIC happen at either 512K or 1024K, each load now takes two cycles.
c-mh-v2-tlb-queue-overflow.notes: He does not think TLB entries, cache lines or line segments are the bottleneck; his guess is that each load is submitted twice, the first time unsuccessfully

c-mh-v2-page-cross-31.text: A load that crosses a page boundary costs 31 cycles; three such loads to the same page pair take 93 cycles, with no reuse of the translations
c-mh-v2-page-cross-31.quote: What is surprising, perhaps, is just how bad it is - 31 cycles per load!
c-mh-v2-page-cross-31.notes: He presumes microcode performs the two TLB lookups and two accesses. Two normal loads plus one page-crossing load still take 31 cycles per iteration. Compare c-ox-page-cross (about 28 extra cycles)

c-mh-v2-l1d-size.text: The L1D is 128 KiB and holds 2048 lines
c-mh-v2-l1d-size.quote: And we know that the L1D is 128kiB, so it holds 2048 lines.
c-mh-v2-l1d-size.notes: Handley calls size and line length the only definite facts, but gives no method on this page

c-mh-v2-l1d-line.text: The L1D line is 64 B, not the 128 B line Handley had taken from internet claims until his own tests showed otherwise
c-mh-v2-l1d-line.quote: We know that cache lines are 64B (eventually we'll see experiments to this effect).
c-mh-v2-l1d-line.notes: The 128 B line and a 100 GB/s in-L1 load bandwidth were problematic internet claims he (in)validated with his own tests. The DC ZVA test (64 B L1 lines, 128 B L2 lines) is c-mh-v2-l1d-line-dczva

c-mh-v2-l1d-8way.text: Handley's working model of the L1D is 8-way set associative with 256 sets indexed by address bits 6-13 (the bits untranslated with 16 KiB pages), which he labels conjecture
c-mh-v2-l1d-8way.quote: the cache is 8-way set associative ... And we know that the L1D is 128kiB, so it holds 2048 lines. Those two are definite. The rest is conjecture.
c-mh-v2-l1d-8way.notes: 2048 lines in 256 sets of 8; addresses 16 KiB apart compete for 8 lines. Untested here (see c-mh-v2-l1d-8way-tlb). Handley thinks the real lookup is closer to c-mh-v2-l1d-hashed-lookup.

c-mh-v2-dtlb-160-aside.text: In passing, the M1's L1 TLB holds 160 pages
c-mh-v2-dtlb-160-aside.quote: But that's not quite as bad as you might think. The M1 TLB holds 160 pages
c-mh-v2-dtlb-160-aside.notes: Aside in his estimate of the storage cost of a D2D-style TLB; his measurement (at least 160 entries, 128+32) is c-mh-v2-dtlb

c-mh-v2-no-large-pages.text: Apple appears uninterested in large pages, possibly because range registers cover much the same need
c-mh-v2-no-large-pages.quote: Apple so far has appeared uninterested in these (possibly because they use range registers, which solve much the same problem

c-mh-v2-l1d-hashed-lookup.text: Handley thinks the L1D is in effect a direct-mapped cache with a two-stage lookup (8 untranslated set bits, then a 3-bit hash of the physical address from a fast TLB-side table), because no way misprediction is seen; the L2 TLB shows similar signs
c-mh-v2-l1d-hashed-lookup.quote: Ultimately, I think something like this last, most complicated setup, is in fact what we are seeing. ... there never seems to be way misprediction [the L1 case]
c-mh-v2-l1d-hashed-lookup.notes: Handley cites US8472267B2 (its micro-TLB supplies one physical address bit early) as a stripped-down version. In the L2 TLB, overflowing one set's ways misbehaves; he guesses the L2 does something similar.

c-mh-v2-way-pred-test.text: Byte loads to six sets, each at a randomly chosen one of eight 16 KiB-apart pages, take 2.53 cycles per three loads against 2.39 without randomness, and the gap closes once the bases avoid shared banks, so no way misprediction is visible
c-mh-v2-way-pred-test.quote: we see no evidence of way misprediction. When I use random numbers in the array, time per (three loads) is 2.53 cycles; when I use all zeros that time is 2.39 cycles.
c-mh-v2-way-pred-test.hedge: Assuming I got the details correct (hah!)
c-mh-v2-way-pred-test.notes: The residual gap tracked LD_UNIT_UOP (bank-collision resubmissions), not L2 traffic; moving x9 and x10 to offset 16 in their lines removed it.

c-mh-v2-way-pred-hashed.text: The L1D does not use a standard set-indexed way predictor; Handley suggests one indexed by a hash of the virtual address (perhaps with the ASID), covering at least 2048 and more likely 4096 entries
c-mh-v2-way-pred-hashed.quote: This all suggests to me we're absolutely not using a standard way predictor (table indexed by setID); but we may well be using a way predictor of the form I described
c-mh-v2-way-pred-hashed.notes: A 12-bit hash into a 4096-entry table of predicted ways is the only scheme he knows that matches the accuracy of the M1 way predictor; he knows of no paper or Apple patent describing it

c-mh-v2-ld-unit-uop.text: The LD_UNIT_UOP counter mostly counts bank collisions: it counts how often the LSU submits a load request to the L1, and most resubmissions come from bank collisions
c-mh-v2-ld-unit-uop.quote: looks like, under most conditions, this counter counts bank collisions. More precisely, it counts how often a load request is submitted by the LSU to the L1
c-mh-v2-ld-unit-uop.notes: About 1.2 per load in the zero case, 1.3 in the random case of the way-prediction probe. The later tables' "traversals" column is his reading of an M1 performance counter

c-mh-v2-l1d-byte-subarrays.text: Handley reads his timings as showing the L1D is built from byte-wide (perhaps two-byte) sub-arrays, so a cycle powers only the bytes it uses and can write some bytes of a line while reading others
c-mh-v2-l1d-byte-subarrays.quote: My timings suggest that we do in fact have these very narrow cache sub-arrays.
c-mh-v2-l1d-byte-subarrays.notes: The lowest-level access is the byte, or perhaps the two-byte word; "Apple apparently sub-array their cache by bytes". Apple's patents call these sub-arrays banks

c-mh-v2-concurrent-store-load.text: Per Apple's patent, a store writes the byte sub-arrays a load is not using in the same cycle, even partially when the two overlap, and line IDs found by loads' tag lookups are attached to pending stores
c-mh-v2-concurrent-store-load.quote: As long as the bytes differ, I can perform the loads and stores in the same cycle because they live in different sub-arrays.
c-mh-v2-concurrent-store-load.notes: US9448936B2 (2014), Concurrent store and load operations

c-mh-v2-store-write-buffers.text: A store that is no longer speculative moves with its data into a write buffer between the store queue and the L1, freeing its store-queue entry; patents suggest at least four such buffers, with some store coalescing
c-mh-v2-store-write-buffers.quote: patents suggest there are at least four of these buffers, and that there is probably some sort of store coalescing happening
c-mh-v2-store-write-buffers.notes: In Handley's store flow a store first borrows the translation and line ID from a load to the same page or line, and later writes the L1 on a load's line access or a dedicated store access. Patents not named.

c-mh-v2-stores-free.text: Tests show that stores very rarely cost load bandwidth
c-mh-v2-stores-free.quote: A variety of tests seem to validate the above model, bottom line being that you very rarely lose load bandwidth to stores.
c-mh-v2-stores-free.notes: His summary: "for the most part stores never consume load bandwidth"

c-mh-v2-unaligned-free.text: Aligned halfword loads behave like byte loads, and non-aligned halfword loads pay essentially no penalty
c-mh-v2-unaligned-free.quote: non-aligned halfwords pay essentially no penalty, given the mechanisms we have described (and again what we see)

c-mh-v2-misaligned-single-request.text: Per Apple's patent, a load that straddles two cache lines stays one unit that sends two line requests to the cache; only a page-crossing load falls back to microcode
c-mh-v2-misaligned-single-request.quote: a misaligned load is still handled as a single unit, with two line requests sent to the cache

c-mh-v2-l1d-bank-width.text: Each L1D bank is 16 B wide, so a 256 B row spans the 16 banks and addresses 256 B apart share a bank
c-mh-v2-l1d-bank-width.quote: So, at a physical level, the cache consists of 16 banks, each bank is 16B wide.
c-mh-v2-l1d-bank-width.notes: Model stated up front and fitted to the stride tables (c-mh-v2-l1d-banks)

c-mh-v2-l1d-banks.text: The L1D has 16 banks, each 16 B wide
c-mh-v2-l1d-banks.quote: seems reasonable to me to conclude that the EO3 and ABCD3 models describe the byte loads ... which in turn implies 16 banks, each 16B wide.
c-mh-v2-l1d-banks.hedge: it seems reasonable to me to conclude
c-mh-v2-l1d-banks.notes: The Intel designs Handley knows used 8 banks

c-mh-v2-loads-per-cycle.text: Byte loads stepping by 0 to 32 B run at three per cycle
c-mh-v2-loads-per-cycle.quote: Note that nothing interesting happens till 64B; within margin of noise we achieve three loads per cycle.
c-mh-v2-loads-per-cycle.notes: 2.97-3.0 loads/cycle; halfword, word, doubleword and 128-bit loads give the same

c-mh-v2-bank-stride-sweep.text: Byte loads stepping by 64 B run at 2.35 per cycle, by 128 B at 1.71 and by 256 B at 1.0, as they crowd onto four, two and one bank, with 1.28, 1.75 and 3 traversals per load
c-mh-v2-bank-stride-sweep.notes: Stochastic models with three-request lookahead (EO3 for two banks: 1.66; ABCD3 for four banks: 2.27) come close to the 1.71 and 2.35 measured

c-mh-v2-piggyback.text: Several loads to the same 16 B bank element are served by one bank access, the bytes for each load extracted and routed to its register, so they still run at three per cycle
c-mh-v2-piggyback.quote: When we are loading from the same 16B element (the case for loads separated by 0, 1, 2, 4) the piggybacking scheme works!
c-mh-v2-piggyback.notes: Three overlapping 16 B loads at A, A+1, A+2 are served from 18 B across two banks without serialising

c-mh-v2-l1-lookahead-3.text: Each cycle the LSU offers three load requests to the L1, which serves the first and any later ones bound for other banks; the traversal counter (1.75) fits this three-request model (1.8) better than a four-request one (2.28)
c-mh-v2-l1-lookahead-3.quote: I can give various pleading excuses for why the Apple value means something different from what it seems to mean, but EO3 looks like the way to bet.
c-mh-v2-l1-lookahead-3.hedge: looks like the way to bet
c-mh-v2-l1-lookahead-3.notes: Requests reach the cache in roughly random order (c-mh-v2-load-order). He suggests holding the rejected request in a buffer at the L1 would gain about 5 %

c-mh-v2-width-independent.text: Byte, halfword, word, doubleword and 128-bit loads give the same throughput at every step, so only the bank pattern of the addresses matters
c-mh-v2-width-independent.quote: The loaded width does not matter, only the pattern of addresses (ie which banks are accessed).
c-mh-v2-width-independent.notes: Steps of 0-256 B, and 512 and 1024 B for 128-bit loads

c-mh-v2-ldp-x-single.text: An LDP of two X registers takes two register remaps but one ROB entry and one cache submission, and performs like a single 128-bit load
c-mh-v2-ldp-x-single.quote: Also note that a load pair X is not cracked either as regards retirement (second to last column; one entry in the ROB for each load pair X instruction) or cracked for submission to the cache

c-mh-v2-ldpq-throughput.text: LDP of two Q registers runs at 1.5 per cycle with two cache traversals each, against three per cycle for the equivalent pair of LDR Q, so both move 48 B per cycle
c-mh-v2-ldpq-throughput.quote: The LDPQ case performs 1.5 loads per cycle; in both cases 3*16B gets transferred to the LSU.
c-mh-v2-ldpq-throughput.notes: LoadPQ table: 1.5 up to a 64 B step, 1.17 at 128 B and 0.86 at 256 B, half the LDR Q pair rates of 2.35 and 1.71

c-mh-v2-ldpq-late-crack.text: LDP Q is split into two 16 B requests only at submission to the cache, after address generation, TLB and way lookup; rename and the ROB see one instruction
c-mh-v2-ldpq-late-crack.quote: This all suggests to me that a LDPQ is cracked, but very late in the LSU (probably after TLB and way lookup) into two LDQ instructions.
c-mh-v2-ldpq-late-crack.notes: Not cracked at decode: "256b=32B via a single instruction that splits into two at the point of cache access"

c-mh-v2-line-cross-loads.text: Doubleword and 128-bit loads that each straddle two cache lines run at the same rates as aligned loads, three per cycle at small steps, with the same bank-collision pattern
c-mh-v2-line-cross-loads.quote: These probes correspond to loads from a base address that is a cacheline aligned address minus one. So every load straddles two cache lines. ... Whether we load from two lines or not, we see the same pattern of collisions.
c-mh-v2-line-cross-loads.notes: LoadX1 and LoadQ1 tables. Line-straddling LDP Q pairs fall further, to 0.53 pairs/cycle at a 256 B step, because both halves need the same bank

c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths-6.text: The L1 has six 16 B data paths to the LSU, since three line-straddling loads per cycle each read two banks
c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths-6.quote: But what these results do suggest is that in fact we have not three 16B wide paths from the L1 to the LSU, but 6 such paths.
c-mh-v2-l1-load-paths-6.notes: From LoadX1 at a 64 B step approaching three loads per cycle; Handley had earlier left it at "three (four? six?)"

c-mh-v2-subarray-guess.text: Each bank, logically 512 rows of 16 B, may be built from four sub-arrays of 128 rows that work in parallel, which would explain line-straddling LDP Q pairs at a 256 B step running slightly above 0.5 per cycle
c-mh-v2-subarray-guess.quote: the basic SRAM subarray may be 128b wide (16B*8) and 128 rows high, so that there are four such sub-arrays in a bank
c-mh-v2-subarray-guess.notes: Sits uneasily with his byte-wide sub-array reading (c-mh-v2-l1d-byte-subarrays)

c-mh-v2-no-parallel-sources.text: Apple does not yet seem to serve some loads from the store queue or the L1's specialty buffers in parallel with the L1D to raise load bandwidth
c-mh-v2-no-parallel-sources.quote: Apple doesn't yet seem to be exploiting aggressively the performance amplification available in having some loads serviced by either the Store Queue or the Specialty Buffers, in parallel with the L1D

c-mh-v2-4-lines-per-cycle.text: Three loads and one store per cycle to four different lines (320 B step) show that four cache lines can be addressed per cycle, so way determination handles four addresses per cycle
c-mh-v2-4-lines-per-cycle.quote: shows us that we can access 4 different cache lines per cycle, ie however we perform address to way translation, we can perform four of those, and submit 4 addresses, to the cache, per cycle
c-mh-v2-4-lines-per-cycle.notes: The text says the 320 B case gives a throughput of 4; the printed Store1Load3B table row reads 3.37 ops/cycle. He also says more than two (three, presumably four) indices can be submitted per cycle

c-mh-v2-stores-per-cycle.text: Byte stores stepping by 0 to 128 B run at two per cycle, falling to 1.02 at a 256 B step
c-mh-v2-stores-per-cycle.quote: This works perfectly all the way out to 128 -- we can submit two stores to the cache per cycle
c-mh-v2-stores-per-cycle.notes: StoreB table; a store that overwrites the previous one still runs at full speed

c-mh-v2-store-fire-forget.text: Stores cross from the LSU to the L1 once, even under bank conflicts, so they are latched in buffers at the L1 that write them into the banks whenever loads leave room
c-mh-v2-store-fire-forget.quote: What I think is happening is that stores are submitted to the cache as ... latched to some buffer(s), and the buffer(s) opportunistically feed bytes to the L1D whenever loads aren't using resources
c-mh-v2-store-fire-forget.notes: Store traversals stay at 1 except for three loads + one store at 64-256 B steps (1.04-1.08), read as occasional buffer overflow, loads presumably having priority. One or two stores can wait at the L1 on a bank collision.

c-mh-v2-load-order.text: Loads reach the L1 in jumbled order, mainly because one scheduler queue pair drains through a load unit and the ambidextrous unit while the other drains through one load unit; stores stay much closer to program order
c-mh-v2-load-order.quote: My guess is that the primary reason loads are reordered is the ambidextrous load/store queue.
c-mh-v2-load-order.notes: Handley also suspects the instruction pool between rename and the scheduling queues does not preserve order; the bank-collision models assume randomly ordered requests

c-mh-v2-store-bw-32.text: 128-bit stores also run at two per cycle, so the LSU can move at least 32 B of store data per cycle to the cache
c-mh-v2-store-bw-32.quote: Storing vectors shows the same pattern, so there's at least 32B of bandwidth (two 16B stores per cycle) from LSU to the cache.
c-mh-v2-store-bw-32.notes: StoreQ: 2.0 per cycle out to a 128 B step, 1.02 at 256 B; STP Q pairs run at 1.0 pair (2 x 16 B) per cycle at every step tried, 0-256 B

c-mh-v2-misaligned-store-16.text: 16-byte stores that each straddle a line boundary run at two per cycle up to an 8 B step but only 1.23 at a 16 B step and 1.0 beyond
c-mh-v2-misaligned-store-16.quote: Now we see trouble start at at offset of 16 ... it should be able to run at 2*16B per cycle, not the 1.25 (20B/cycle) we see.
c-mh-v2-misaligned-store-16.notes: StoreQ1 table; his text rounds to 1.25. Line-straddling STP Q pairs fall to 0.53-0.61 pairs/cycle from a 32 B step

c-mh-v2-store-paths-2.text: There are only two 16 B store data paths from the LSU to the L1D
c-mh-v2-store-paths-2.quote: there are only two 16B store paths from the LSU to the L1D (and perhaps also a wider path to the pool of specialty buffers than can transfer an entire cache line?)
c-mh-v2-store-paths-2.notes: From the misaligned 16 B store results (c-mh-v2-misaligned-store-16), unlike misaligned loads, which keep three per cycle; one of the conclusions he calls solid

c-mh-v2-sq-slot-32b.text: Store-queue slots seem to be 32 B wide: stores aggregate within a slot and a store torn across a line takes two slots, which predicts about 1.33 misaligned 16 B stores per cycle
c-mh-v2-sq-slot-32b.quote: the numbers we see here seem to suggest that + the width of a slot in the store queue is 32B (rather than 64B)
c-mh-v2-sq-slot-32b.notes: He adds that he does not especially trust any aspect of this explanation

c-mh-v2-same-address-storeload.text: A store, load, store, load stream to one address runs at 3.66 operations per cycle, the loads served from the store queue
c-mh-v2-same-address-storeload.quote: both the loads (they will go to different physical registers, even though, of course, the first load is meaningless) will be serviced out of the store queue, not the L1D
c-mh-v2-same-address-storeload.notes: He sees a glitch costing about one op in twelve. Slightly over one register remap per load, which he puts down to initial flushes before the load/store alias detector was trained

c-mh-v2-storeload-same-bank.text: Interleaved byte stores and loads to alternate bytes of one 16 B element (steps of 1-4 B) run at 3.99 operations per cycle, so a bank serves a load and a store to different bytes in the same cycle
c-mh-v2-storeload-same-bank.quote: Apple's patents claim these can happen in the same cycle; we activate one bank, send the appropriate read and write byte enables ... and this certainly seems to be possible
c-mh-v2-storeload-same-bank.notes: StoreLoadB table: about 3.2 ops/cycle at 8-32 B steps with no cache bank collisions counted (c-mh-v2-sq-banks-guess), 3.2 at 64 B with 1.44 load traversals, 2.0 at 128 B, 1.03 at 256 B

c-mh-v2-partial-forwarding.text: Interleaved 16 B stores and loads offset by 1-4 B, each load overlapping the previous store, still run at four operations per cycle, merging store-queue bytes with L1 bytes
c-mh-v2-partial-forwarding.quote: the first load has to pull in 15 bytes from the store queue and one byte from the L1 cache, then glue them together. And this is done without a glitch!
c-mh-v2-partial-forwarding.notes: StoreLoadQ table: 3.99-4.0 for steps of 0-4 B, 2.97 at 8 B

c-mh-v2-sq-banks-guess.text: Mixed store/load streams at 8-32 B steps stall at about 3.2 operations per cycle with no cache bank collisions counted, which Handley guesses comes from collisions between sub-queues of a banked store queue
c-mh-v2-sq-banks-guess.quote: My best guess is that perhaps the store queue is split into multiple sub-queues
c-mh-v2-sq-banks-guess.hedge: My best guess is that perhaps
c-mh-v2-sq-banks-guess.notes: Also invoked for 16 B stores/loads at 8-16 B steps, and for four stores then four loads, which worsens the 64 and 128 B steps without more load resubmissions

c-mh-v2-l1d-latency.text: Strided pointer chases take 3 cycles per load within the L1 (up to 128 KiB) and, to first approximation, 4 cycles per load beyond it, the stride prefetcher hiding L2, SLC and DRAM latency
c-mh-v2-l1d-latency.quote: For the first part of the graph (within L1, so depth up to 128K) every load takes 3 cycles. Once we're past L1 (so loading from L2, then SLC, then DRAM) to first approximation latency is 4 cycles.
c-mh-v2-l1d-latency.notes: The 4 cycles beyond L1 is a prefetched strided chain (63-65 B strides), not a cache latency. An 8 B linear chain gives the same 3 cycles (c-mh-v2-stride-to-dram)

c-mh-v2-ptr-chase-fastpath.text: The 3-cycle pointer-chase latency is a fast path: the loaded value is reused inside the LSU as the next address, saving the cycle needed to move it to the integer unit
c-mh-v2-ptr-chase-fastpath.quote: a special load case that can be accelerated because the result of the load will be re-used in the LSU (so we avoid one cycle of overhead moving the load result to the integer unit)

c-mh-v2-load-alu-4.text: Adding zero to each loaded pointer raises the chase to 5 cycles per load: the load takes 4 cycles once its value must go to the integer unit, plus 1 for the add
c-mh-v2-load-alu-4.quote: The cycles per load jumps to five (blue line). This is expected. The load now takes 4 rather than 3 cycles because we cannot use the fast path
c-mh-v2-load-alu-4.notes: Handley also says standard loads take 4 cycles, more for vector/FP loads

c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction.text: No load address prediction is seen: dividing each loaded pointer by one (12 cycles per load) gives no speed-up, and a random order within the L1 is no slower than a linear one
c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction.quote: we see no difference until we move beyond the L1 ... load addresses that can be predicted) remains as before - apparently not present in M1
c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction.notes: The same sentence calls all zero-cycle loads (register reuse, values stored to the stack) absent, a conclusion carried over and not tested here; vol 1 measures register-matched zero-cycle loads (c-mh-v1-zcl-*)

c-mh-v2-ldp-ptr-first.text: Pointer chasing through LDP keeps the 3-cycle fast path only when the next pointer is the first register of the pair; with the payload first, each step is slower
c-mh-v2-ldp-ptr-first.quote: And only the first register of a load pair can be internally forwarded in the LSU for pointer-chasing acceleration.
c-mh-v2-ldp-ptr-first.notes: A table gives 3.0 cycles per load with the pointer first and 4.0 with the payload first

c-mh-v2-stride-to-dram.text: A linear chain of 8 B nodes keeps its 3-cycle L1 latency at every depth tested, out to about 1000 MB: the prefetcher covers L2, SLC and DRAM
c-mh-v2-stride-to-dram.quote: Note also that the prefetching is correctly orchestrated not just out to L2 but all the way out to deep DRAM (the largest depth we test is ~1000MB).

c-mh-v2-near-l2-3mib.text: The linear-chain latency curve steps slightly past the near L2 of 3 MiB, where the first access to each line takes 4 rather than 3 cycles
c-mh-v2-near-l2-3mib.quote: The prefetcher seems to get the calculation slightly incorrect once we go past the near-L2 (3MiB) so that accessing the line the first time takes 4 rather than 3 cycles

c-mh-v2-stride-max.text: Stride prefetching works for every stride Handley tried up to just under two pages, though with odd variation by stride (e.g. 2 KiB worse than 8 KiB, 272 B much worse than 256 B in DRAM)
c-mh-v2-stride-max.quote: there are stride prefetchers, which all appear to work, right up to a stride of just under two pages.
c-mh-v2-stride-max.hedge: I don't feel confident saying anything beyond
c-mh-v2-stride-max.notes: Handley adds that the TLB tests suggest stride prefetching ends between 16K and 32K strides, and later guesses strides are tracked in about 16 bits (a 32 KiB stride is tracked but prefetches poorly)

c-mh-v2-stride-streams-16.text: The core sustains at least 16 simultaneous stride prefetch streams; four run cleanly out to deep DRAM
c-mh-v2-stride-streams-16.quote: the system can sustain at least 16 simultaneous stride prefetchers. - it can sustain four stride prefetchers with barely a sweat (even out to deep DRAM!)
c-mh-v2-stride-streams-16.notes: Lower bound. With eight streams, occasional glitches near 16 MB and 64 MB, and stream tracking seems to stop beyond about 256 MB

c-mh-v2-backward-stride.text: A backward linear stride is prefetched as well as a forward one
c-mh-v2-backward-stride.quote: Below we see a backward linear stride being prefetched just as well as a forward linear sequence

c-mh-v2-mixed-strides.text: With interleaved chains of different strides and signs that use one element per line, prefetching keeps up for four chains, is acceptable for eight, and falls behind beyond eight
c-mh-v2-mixed-strides.quote: you're still going to do fine for four such arrays, and you can't really complain even with eight such arrays. But beyond eight you are going to be unhappy

c-mh-v2-spatial-prefetch.text: Chains shuffled randomly within 16 KiB boxes are still prefetched out to DRAM, so some spatial prefetcher exists
c-mh-v2-spatial-prefetch.quote: these "randomized" patterns are still being prefetched. ... Beyond the brute fact of some sort of spatial prefetcher, it's difficult to say more
c-mh-v2-spatial-prefetch.notes: Handley warns the 8 B-node version mostly shows 8 nodes sharing each line, not the prefetcher

c-mh-v2-dram-350.text: A random access out to DRAM costs about 350 cycles
c-mh-v2-dram-350.quote: A random access out to DRAM costs about 350 cycles.
c-mh-v2-dram-350.notes: In cycles, not ns. Handley later says purely random DRAM access is ~300 cycles. The fully random curve itself is not shown

c-mh-v2-stride-lockon.text: The stride prefetcher seems to need about 4 accesses to lock onto a pattern, plus a few more before its prefetches arrive in time
c-mh-v2-stride-lockon.quote: the stride prefetcher probably requires something like seeing 4 accesses to lock onto the pattern
c-mh-v2-stride-lockon.notes: 64 B nodes in a 1 MiB space; little gain until boxes of 512 B (8 nodes)

c-mh-v2-region-prefetch.text: Random nodes in randomly ordered boxes still gain a little latency, so a region prefetcher exists, but it is never very aggressive
c-mh-v2-region-prefetch.quote: this situation is somewhat amenable to a region prefetcher. And it seems that we have something like that. ... (which is apparently never very aggressive; we get some latency reduction but not much)
c-mh-v2-region-prefetch.notes: Handley guesses it needs ~4 spatially correlated loads, within perhaps less than a page, to activate

c-mh-v2-hybrid-prefetch.text: The box tests show a hybrid region+stride prefetcher; less certainly, a spatial prefetcher as well, not tuned well against the others
c-mh-v2-hybrid-prefetch.quote: I think the definite take-away is the existence of a hybrid region+stride predictor; the less definite takeaway is that perhaps there's also a spatial predictor

c-mh-v2-next-line.text: A next-line prefetcher probably exists, and the 64 B vs 128 B node results hint at a meta-scheme choosing among prefetchers
c-mh-v2-next-line.quote: is the likely existence of a next-line prefetcher.

c-mh-v2-three-prefetchers.text: With 16 KiB boxes out to DRAM, three kinds of prefetcher are seen working: stride (forward and backward), hybrid region+stride, and pure region
c-mh-v2-three-prefetchers.quote: We can see three very different prefetchers seem to be present (and functional, all the way out to DRAM)
c-mh-v2-three-prefetchers.notes: Measured counterpart of the patent-based list in c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds

c-mh-v2-ghb-box.text: Shrinking the box from 16 KiB to 15000 B changes the random-in-box results sharply, which Handley explains by a GHB-like prefetcher history of a little under 256 entries
c-mh-v2-ghb-box.quote: My assumption is that the prefetcher is something like a GHB prefetcher ... Suppose that the GHB holds a little under 256 entries.
c-mh-v2-ghb-box.notes: Upper bound; Handley later floats "let's say three times as many entries (240)" for Apple against ~80 for x86 and Arm cores

c-mh-v2-region-to-l2.text: Low-confidence (spatial/region) prefetches go into the L2 but not the L1; stride prefetches go into the L1
c-mh-v2-region-to-l2.quote: the prefetcher is smart enough that for uncertain cases (so spatial/region prefetching, as opposed to stride prefetching) prefetching is done into L2, but not into L1.

c-mh-v2-slc-spatial.text: Random placements in randomly ordered boxes still run at ~50 cycles per load out to DRAM depths, which Handley reads as data coming from the SLC, perhaps filled by a spatial prefetcher at the memory controller
c-mh-v2-slc-spatial.quote: still runs at ~50 cycles/load. This suggests to me that the data is being loaded from the SLC. ... One could imagine the memory controller, after every DRAM page is opened, consulting the spatial prefetcher
c-mh-v2-slc-spatial.notes: Handley says the opposite for the patents (prefetching stays within the cluster, not the SLC)

c-mh-v2-temporal.text: Apple does have a temporal prefetcher or equivalent; AnandTech's tests miss it because they use 16 KiB regions, just beyond its reach, while 15 KiB regions show it
c-mh-v2-temporal.quote: I think the correct analysis is that Apple does have a Temporal Prefetcher (or equivalent); it just doesn't show up when the tests probe a region size of 16K
c-mh-v2-temporal.notes: Disagrees with AnandTech's reading that Apple has no temporal prefetcher

c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds.text: Apple's current data prefetch scheme: an access-map (AMPM) prefetcher over regions that detects strides and dense patterns, plus auxiliary large-stride, spatial memory streaming (SMS) and pointer (content-directed) matchers, coordinated ad hoc
c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds.quote: Apple's current scheme appears to be ... AMPM matcher detects strides ... and "dense" patterns ... auxiliary matcher detects large stride streams ... detects SMS (Spatial Memory Streaming) patterns ... detects what look like pointers in newly loaded L1 cache lines
c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds.value: AMPM region (strides, dense), large stride, SMS, pointer (content-directed)
c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds.notes: Synthesis of the prefetcher patents with the box tests

c-mh-v2-ampm-2k.text: Apple's primary prefetcher is an access-map (AMPM) prefetcher keyed on load addresses grouped in 2 KiB regions
c-mh-v2-ampm-2k.quote: Apple's primary prefetcher is an AMPM prefetcher, based on load addresses clustered in regions of 2kiB.
c-mh-v2-ampm-2k.notes: US9015422B2 (2013); the 2015 patent may track a moving 2 KiB within 4 KiB

c-mh-v2-prefetch-at-lsu.text: The prefetcher sits at the LSU and sees every virtual load/store address, up to four per cycle, not just cache misses, so streams cross page boundaries
c-mh-v2-prefetch-at-lsu.quote: Apple differs in that their prefetcher sits at the LSU and sees every (virtual) address that streams through. This is up to four addresses a cycle.
c-mh-v2-prefetch-at-lsu.notes: First seen in US20070294482A1 (2006), which places the prefetch unit in the LSU

c-mh-v2-prefetch-filter.text: Incoming addresses are filtered and queued, and the rest of the prefetch unit processes one address per cycle
c-mh-v2-prefetch-filter.quote: The first thing done to all these addresses is that they are "filtered", most are thrown away, the interesting ones are queued, and ultimately the rest of the Prefetch Unit only processes one address per cycle

c-mh-v2-ampm-map.text: Each access map covers a 2 KiB region as 32 two-bit slots, one per 64 B line (demand fetched, prefetched and used, prefetched, or not accessed), matched against predefined patterns
c-mh-v2-ampm-map.quote: the regions used by the Prefetch Unit are apparently 2kiB in size. So a single entry for an Access Mapped region has 32 slots (2kiB/64). Each slot is two bits in size
c-mh-v2-ampm-map.notes: US9015422B2 (2013). The patent gives no count of tracked regions; the AMPM paper suggests 50-60

c-mh-v2-ampm-throttle.text: A credit scheme throttles the prefetcher to about 4 outstanding prefetches per region
c-mh-v2-ampm-throttle.quote: throttles the prefetcher so that (essentially) a maximum of about 4 outstanding prefetches are allowed per region.

c-mh-v2-unified-prefetch.text: The L1 prefetcher drives both levels: high-confidence prefetches go through the L1 and on to a per-CPU prefetch queue at the L2 if they miss; low-confidence ones go straight to the L2 queue, which pulls from SLC/DRAM into the L2
c-mh-v2-unified-prefetch.quote: The L1 Prefetcher is now fully in charge, generating two different streams of requests, one designed to pull data from L2 into L1, the second designed to pull data from SLC/DRAM into L2.
c-mh-v2-unified-prefetch.notes: US10180905B1 (2016). Per-region state now holds virtual and physical addresses. Earlier (US9971694B1, 2015) a separate L2 prefetcher per core was steered by the L1 unit

c-mh-v2-l2-line-128.text: The M1 has 64 B lines in the L1 and 128 B lines in the L2 and SLC
c-mh-v2-l2-line-128.quote: So we have the system we still have as of M1, with an L1 that has 64B lines, and and L2 (+SLC) that has 128B lines.
c-mh-v2-l2-line-128.notes: Handley's guess from the access-map granularity bit in US10180905B1 (2016), placing the change at about the A10

c-mh-v2-density-pattern.text: One predefined pattern is a density pattern: when many lines of a region have been accessed, the rest are prefetched at low confidence, acting as a region prefetcher
c-mh-v2-density-pattern.quote: pattern, which effectively behaves like a region prefetcher; ie if we're accessed many lines within a region ... lines of that region are prefetched as low confidence lines

c-mh-v2-prefetch-throttle.text: Every 32 cycles the L2 judges how busy the per-CPU prefetch queues are; over a history of busy periods it sets a throttle level, and L1 prefetchers then drop requests from regions below a quality threshold (50 %, 75 %, 90 %)
c-mh-v2-prefetch-throttle.quote: Every 32 cycle we loop over each CPU Prefetch Request Queue in the L2, and decide whether or not it should be throttled.
c-mh-v2-prefetch-throttle.notes: US9904624B1 (2016); example thresholds 16 requests and 4 low-confidence requests per queue, history of ~20 periods

c-mh-v2-content-directed.text: A content-directed prefetcher scans lines entering the L1 for pointer-like 8-byte-aligned values, filters them and prefetches by a quality table; Handley saw no evidence of it in his tests
c-mh-v2-content-directed.quote: as data lines enter the L1 cache, they are scanned to see if they contain any values that look "like" pointers (the patent suggests doing this only on 8-byte aligned boundaries ... we saw no evidence for anything like this
c-mh-v2-content-directed.notes: US9886385B1 (2016); Handley guesses it arrived with the A11. Requests go straight to the L2

c-mh-v2-augury-dmp.text: Security researchers (Augury, 2022) found evidence of a data memory-dependent prefetcher on the M1, matching the patent
c-mh-v2-augury-dmp.quote: A team investigating security have found evidence of a Content-Dependent Prefetcher on the M1

c-mh-v2-mini-access-maps.text: The filter holds one- or two-entry mini access maps, so a region gets a full access map only after a second or third access
c-mh-v2-mini-access-maps.quote: We create some very small (one or two entry) "mini Access Maps" living in the filter.

c-mh-v2-ampm-granularity.text: For some long patterns the access-map field granularity grows from 64 B to 128 B and then 256 B
c-mh-v2-ampm-granularity.quote: we bump the granularity of each field in the Access Map from 64B to 128B then even to 256B.

c-mh-v2-large-stride.text: A secondary large-stride prefetcher, a conventional stride table, catches strides the AMPM cannot: longer than half a region, about 1000 bytes
c-mh-v2-large-stride.quote: the AMPM scheme, flexible as it is, cannot detect strides that are longer than half the size of a region (so, let's say, strides long than about 1000 bytes).

c-mh-v2-sms.text: A secondary spatial memory streaming prefetcher stores access patterns by PC and, once confident, hands a pattern back to the AMPM prefetcher to replay at the new base address
c-mh-v2-sms.quote: This essentially tries to track access patterns associated with a given PC. ... the SMSP returns the full pattern up to the AMPM Prefetcher, which will replay it

c-mh-v2-secondary-coverage.text: The large-stride prefetcher reports its coverage of an access map to the AMPM prefetcher and takes over the stream once that coverage is large enough
c-mh-v2-secondary-coverage.quote: once the coverage of the Stride Prefetcher is a large enough fraction of the coverage of the AMPM Prefetcher, we switch to Stride assuming primary control for this stream.
c-mh-v2-secondary-coverage.notes: US11176045B2 (2020); Handley does not say which chip implements it

c-mh-v2-prefetch-not-slc.text: Prefetching seems to stay within the cluster, using the L2 but not extending to the SLC
c-mh-v2-prefetch-not-slc.quote: It's unclear that, even today, Apple extends prefetching up to the SLC; it looks like prefetching is considered ... to be done within a cluster, exploiting the L2 but not involving the SLC
c-mh-v2-prefetch-not-slc.notes: From US9098418B2 and US9047198B2 (2012), which coordinate L1 and L2 prefetch and translate L2 prefetches across pages

c-mh-v2-no-i-stream-prefetch.text: The M1 has no stream prefetcher for instructions
c-mh-v2-no-i-stream-prefetch.quote: Is there the equivalent of a stream prefetcher for Instructions? Well, maybe there is on other CPUs, but on M1 there is not
c-mh-v2-no-i-stream-prefetch.notes: Handley's explanation for the low L2 code-fetch bandwidth in Chips and Cheese's data; argued in vol 4

c-mh-v2-dtlb.text: L1 TLB holds at least 160 entries (128 + 32), not the 128 suggested on the internet
c-mh-v2-dtlb.quote: This seems to suggest that the L1 TLB holds at least 160 entries or so (128+32).
c-mh-v2-dtlb.notes: Nodes spaced 16 KiB+64 B stay at best-case latency to 161 nodes (2676 KiB).

c-mh-v2-dtlb-5way.text: The L1 data TLB is five-way set associative, indexed by virtual-address bits 14-18, as shown by where latency jumps for node spacings from 32 KiB+64 B to 512 KiB+64 B
c-mh-v2-dtlb-5way.quote: I think it's pretty clear that we are using 5 bits of the virtual address (so bits 14..18) to index into a five-way associative set.
c-mh-v2-dtlb-5way.value: 5-way set associative, indexed by VA bits 14-18
c-mh-v2-dtlb-5way.notes: Handley spells out 160 entries as 32 sets of five and rules out 128 set-associative + 32 fully associative, and says the internet's 128-entry L1D TLB is not what he sees

c-mh-v2-dtlb-random-repl.text: Past the L1 TLB capacity latency climbs linearly from 3 to 9 cycles rather than stepping, so the L1 TLB probably uses random replacement
c-mh-v2-dtlb-random-repl.quote: Note also how latency climbs linearly from the initial 3 cycles to 9 cycles. This is the signature of ... replacement in a cache, rather than LRU ... My guess is the L1 TLB is random replacement

c-mh-v2-page-16k.text: 8 KiB node spacing jumps at the same ~2.5 MiB depth and then pays about half the TLB cost per node, which confirms 16 KiB pages
c-mh-v2-page-16k.quote: this confirms one more point, that the page size really is 16kiB

c-mh-v2-no-large-pages-tlb.text: Apple shows no interest in large pages on the M1: only 16 KiB pages, with range registers presumably covering the I/O and OS cases
c-mh-v2-no-large-pages-tlb.quote: Apple appears to have no interest in large pages. This seems to make sense given that the easy large page cases (IO and OS situations) they can cover with Range Registers
c-mh-v2-no-large-pages-tlb.notes: Handley elsewhere calls range registers "likely (though not proved)"

c-mh-v2-tlb2-drowsy.text: Noisy timing on the first L2 TLB accesses suggests the L2 TLB is split into banks that sleep quickly and take a few cycles to wake
c-mh-v2-tlb2-drowsy.quote: My guess is that the L2 TLB is aggressively drowsy (ie it's divided into physically distinct banks, those banks are designed to go to sleep rapidly, and take a few cycles to wake up out of sleep)
c-mh-v2-tlb2-drowsy.notes: Handley later suggests the L2 TLB, like the L2, may be three segments that sleep or power down independently

c-mh-v2-tlb2-hit-9.text: A load that misses the L1 TLB, hits the L2 TLB and hits the L1D takes 9 cycles, flat from ~2.5 MB out to ~50 MB for most node spacings
c-mh-v2-tlb2-hit-9.quote: corresponding to a TLB lookup that hits in L2 TLB but not L1 TLB, along with a subsequent data lookup that hits in L1, together forming a latency of 9 cycles.
c-mh-v2-tlb2-hit-9.notes: Total load latency, not a miss penalty (7-cpu gives a 6-cycle L1 dTLB miss penalty). 16 KiB+64 B spacing shows 12-15 cycles instead. AnandTech sees ~9 cycles rising, Handley flat

c-mh-v2-tlb1-prefetch.text: Some TLB prefetching fills the L1 TLB, since loads past its capacity cost only 9 cycles
c-mh-v2-tlb1-prefetch.quote: The quick summary seems to be that we do have TLB prefetching (one way or another) into the TLB1

c-mh-v2-dtlb-l2-3072.text: Latency jumps for many node spacings at ~48 MB, which is 3072 16 KiB pages, giving a 3072-entry L2 TLB
c-mh-v2-dtlb-l2-3072.quote: corresponds to 3072 16kB pages, suggesting an L2 TLB size of 3072, which is in accord with what I've seen elsewhere on the internet.

c-mh-v2-tlb2-miss-25.text: Missing the L2 TLB adds about 25 cycles (to ~55 per load), the mapping being rebuilt from the MMU cache
c-mh-v2-tlb2-miss-25.quote: a jump to ~55 cycles (additional 25 cycles) when page lookups miss in TLB2 and we have to use the MMU cache to reconstruct the mapping.
c-mh-v2-tlb2-miss-25.notes: 16 KiB+64 B node spacing; elsewhere Handley gives 45-55 cycles after the jump, and "~25 cycles" from the MMU cache

c-mh-v2-l2-increment-15.text: In the 16 KiB+64 B probe, an L1 TLB miss raises latency to ~15 cycles, and also missing the L1D (L2 hit) to ~30, read as ~15 cycles each for the L2 TLB and the L2
c-mh-v2-l2-increment-15.quote: a jump to around 30 cycles when loads miss in L1 and have to come out of L2. So apparently ~15 cycles to hit in TLB2, then another ~15 cycles to hit in L2.
c-mh-v2-l2-increment-15.notes: Increments over an L1 hit in a TLB probe, not a load-to-use L2 latency; see c-mh-v2-l2-latency-17. Handley calls a ~16-cycle jump "about the L2 latency"

c-mh-v2-tlb2-org.text: All 3072 L2 TLB entries are usable with power-of-two node spacings, so the L2 TLB is probably 1024 hashed sets of three ways rather than plainly set associative
c-mh-v2-tlb2-org.quote: the TLB2 is probably not set associative. Or, to be more precise, it's organized as 1024 entries that are each three ways. So you perform a hash of the virtual address down to a number in the range 0..1023
c-mh-v2-tlb2-org.notes: The hash might XOR the ten lowest page bits with the next ten. Handley later gives 256 sets of 12 ways instead (c-mh-v2-tlb2-256x12)

c-mh-v2-tlb2-256x12.text: The M1's 3072-entry L2 TLB is probably 256 sets of 12 ways
c-mh-v2-tlb2-256x12.quote: This compares with the M1's design which is 3072 entries, probably 256 sets of 12 ways.
c-mh-v2-tlb2-256x12.notes: Aside while comparing with the 256x16 TLB of US20220066947A1; disagrees with Handley's own 1024x3 (c-mh-v2-tlb2-org)

c-mh-v2-page-table-3.text: With 16 KiB pages a superpage covers 256 MiB and a root page 4 TiB, so only three page-table levels are needed
c-mh-v2-page-table-3.quote: a superpage will cover 28 bits of address space (256MiB) and a root page will cover 42 bits (4TiB). So (at least for now!) only three levels of page table are
c-mh-v2-page-table-3.notes: Handley expects the page-walk cache to hold the root and recent superpages and the leaf tables to be in the L2

c-mh-v2-mmu-cache.text: The cost of L2 TLB misses suggests Apple uses an MMU (page-walk) cache of some form
c-mh-v2-mmu-cache.quote: The performance of TLB lookups that miss in the TLB2 suggests that Apple is using an MMU cache of some form, but I did not examine this closely.

c-mh-v2-no-tlb2-prefetcher.text: There is no dedicated L2 TLB prefetcher; the virtual-address data prefetchers touch, and so prefetch, the translations they need
c-mh-v2-no-tlb2-prefetcher.quote: Overall what we see suggests that Apple has no dedicated TLB2 prefetcher, and relies on the standard prefetchers (which operate in virtual address space, so will automatically touch required mappings, ie will prefetch in TLB entries)
c-mh-v2-no-tlb2-prefetcher.notes: 16 KiB-strided chains beat the expected TLB2+MMU-cache+L2 cost by 10-12 cycles between 48 and ~250 MB

c-mh-v2-no-pte-prefetch.text: No serious TLB prefetching is seen: Apple may keep the extra PTEs from each fetched line (US8397049B2) but does no stride PTE prefetching
c-mh-v2-no-pte-prefetch.quote: I found no evidence of serious TLB prefetching. ... does not appear to engage in even basic stride PTE prefetching.

c-mh-v2-tlb2-shared-guess.text: Handley's preferred design has the L2 TLB, MMU cache and page walkers shared at cluster level, for which he has no direct evidence
c-mh-v2-tlb2-shared-guess.quote: So in my fantasy of how the M1 should be designed, all three of TLB2, the MMU cache, and the Page Walkers (state plus implementation logic) form a shared cluster-level entity!
c-mh-v2-tlb2-shared-guess.notes: Handley says "I want to be true ... but have no direct evidence for"; the striping patent's diagrams also suggest a shared L2 TLB

c-mh-v2-tlb2-per-cluster.text: A 2013 cluster maintenance patent adds to evidence, without proof, that the L2 TLB and page walkers are per cluster, not per core
c-mh-v2-tlb2-per-cluster.quote: one more data point in the collection of evidence (many substantial pieces, but no smoking gun) that the L2 TLB and associated page-walkers are per-cluster, not per-core.

c-mh-v2-tlbi-range.text: For a TLB range invalidation, hardware estimates the cycles for walking every entry versus looking up every page in the range and uses the faster
c-mh-v2-tlbi-range.quote: And so the patent calculates the cycle count for each option, and chooses whichever way will be faster!
c-mh-v2-tlbi-range.notes: US20200218663A1 (2019); Handley does not say whether the M1 implements it

c-mh-v2-asid-16.quote: My guess is that Apple uses a 16b ASID

c-mh-v2-vmid-8.text: Apple probably uses 8-bit VMIDs for now
c-mh-v2-vmid-8.quote: ARM VMIDs are likewise either 8 or 16 bits; my guess is that (for now) Apple uses 8 bits.

c-mh-v2-tlb-striping.text: Striping ASID/VMID fields across the L2 TLB's SRAMs lets invalidation by ASID or VMID compare four entries at once, 4x as fast
c-mh-v2-tlb-striping.quote: the patent describes a non-obvious way of storing data in the L2 TLB such that we can perform the operation 4x as fast
c-mh-v2-tlb-striping.notes: US20220066947A1 (2020); Handley says these patents appear not to be implemented on the M1, perhaps on the A15/M2

c-mh-v2-tlb-patent-256x16.text: The striping patent's L2 TLB is 256 sets of 16 ways, built from 8 physical blocks of two ways each
c-mh-v2-tlb-patent-256x16.quote: the L2 TLB describes is apparently 256 sets of 16 ways. ... The physical TLB (the 16 ways) consists of 8 identical physical blocks each handling two ways.

c-mh-v2-splinter-page-sizes.text: A common TLB holds mixed page sizes with a size bit per entry, and the design allows five sizes: 16K, 64K, 2M, 32M and 512M
c-mh-v2-splinter-page-sizes.quote: has a size bit indicating whether the entry corresponds to a small vs large page. ... In fact the design envisages 5 different page sizes: 16K, 64K, 2M, 32M, and 512M.
c-mh-v2-splinter-page-sizes.notes: US20220075734A1 (2020), for hypervisors using large pages that the guest splinters

c-mh-v2-page-size-presence.text: Per translation context the TLB keeps a five-bit page-size-presence vector, refreshed by full scans, and a priority order so lookups try only the page sizes present
c-mh-v2-page-size-presence.quote: This creates a "Page Size Presence" bitvector five bits long, with 1 set for each present page size.

c-mh-v2-mmu-cache-patent.text: For two-stage translation Apple names three walk caches, S1TC, S2TC and HTLB, and ties their replacement to tracking which entries a completed walk has made redundant
c-mh-v2-mmu-cache-patent.quote: Apple calls these S1TC ... S2TC ... and HTLB (Hypervisor TLB), which give a full lookup of a VA, through GPA to PA. All of these caches are present in the SoC.
c-mh-v2-mmu-cache-patent.notes: US11429535B1 (2021). Handley guesses this lives in a per-cluster L2 TLB/walker/MMU and at the SLC for IOMMUs

c-mh-v2-accel-tlbi.text: Invalidations sent over the NoC to accelerator TLBs are bundled, up to about 8 per request, and dropped when the accelerator was powered down
c-mh-v2-accel-tlbi.quote: the patent suggests bundling perhaps up to 8 TLB invalidation in one request.
c-mh-v2-accel-tlbi.notes: US20200379920A1 (2019); not tied to a chip

c-mh-v2-l2-latency-17.text: A chain of randomly placed 64 B nodes in a 1 MiB block (in the L2) takes about 17 cycles per load
c-mh-v2-l2-latency-17.quote: On the far left side we have one 64B node in a 64B box, each box randomly placed. So pure randomness, and about 17 cycle latency.
c-mh-v2-l2-latency-17.notes: Handley also expects "around 16cycles or so" for a random L2 chain, and gives the inner L2 latency as "apparently 18 cycles" (c-mh-v2-inner-l2-latency)

c-mh-v2-l2-inner.text: Bandwidth curves droop at about 3 MiB; Handley reads this as each core having an inner L2 of 3 MiB (a quarter of the 12 MiB L2) plus a slightly slower outer L2
c-mh-v2-l2-inner.quote: there's an "inner L2" of 3MiB, and an "outer L2", that's slightly slower ... So each core has an "inner L2" of 3MiB (one quarter of the 12MiB L2).
c-mh-v2-l2-inner.notes: The knee is measured; the four 3 MiB cachelets, each half private and half shared (outer L2 of 4.5 MiB, 7.5 MiB per core), are Handley's guess, restated in c-mh-v2-near-l2-3mib and c-mh-v2-l2-outer

c-mh-v2-l2-outer.text: Beyond its 3 MiB inner L2, a core still has 4.5 MiB of outer L2
c-mh-v2-l2-outer.quote: 3MiB L2 only reflects the inner L2, we still have 4.5MiB of outer L2.
c-mh-v2-l2-outer.notes: The arithmetic (three times 1.5 MiB, 7.5 MiB per core) is in c-mh-v2-l2-inner

c-mh-v2-l2-segments.text: From several Apple patents, the (inner) L2 is three physical segments of 1 MiB with independent power control, any of which may be asleep (an extra cycle to wake) or off
c-mh-v2-l2-segments.quote: based on multiple Apple patents is that the L2 is split into three "physical segments" with independent voltage/power control, each 1MiB in size.

c-mh-v2-l2-not-24way.text: Handley doubts the usual description of the 3 MiB inner L2 as 24-way set associative, since 24 tag compares per access would cost too much power
c-mh-v2-l2-not-24way.quote: is that it is a 24-way set associative cache. But does this really make sense? ... This is what the internet seems to imagine, but to me it makes no sense.

c-mh-v2-l2-assoc-hash.text: The L2 behaves as three-way associative (one way per segment) with a hashed index, which pathological node spacings collapse onto an eighth of the cache
c-mh-v2-l2-assoc-hash.quote: the overall cache is always three-way associative (three segments) but pathological address patterns will hash all addresses to only an eighth of the cache
c-mh-v2-l2-assoc-hash.notes: Read from 16K64 chains that run ~20 cycles slower than expected out to ~96 MB

c-mh-v2-l2-cpu-hash.text: The inner and outer L2 may be logical, defined by hash functions that include the CPU ID with a per-CPU line budget, rather than physical structures
c-mh-v2-l2-cpu-hash.quote: I suspect hash functions are perhaps also used to define the inner and outer L2 caches, so that these are not physical structures.

c-mh-v2-l2-p2p.text: Chips and Cheese's multi-core read bandwidth (four cores get four times one core's L2 bandwidth) suggests a point-to-point L2 connection to each P core
c-mh-v2-l2-p2p.quote: the P L2 has what looks like point-to-point (rather than a shared) connection to each of the four cores it services

c-mh-v2-l2-ifetch-quarter.text: Per Chips and Cheese, sustained L1I bandwidth is 8 instructions (32 B) per cycle, and code fetch from the L2 about a quarter of that
c-mh-v2-l2-ifetch-quarter.quote: while the (sustained) L1I bandwidth is 8 instructions (ie 32B) per cycle, the sustained bandwidth from L2 is apparently about a quarter of that.

c-mh-v2-l1d-8way-tlb.text: The L1D is indexed by address bits 6-13 (256 sets of 64 B lines) with eight ways, so 16 KiB-spaced nodes all share one set and spill to the L2 after eight
c-mh-v2-l1d-8way-tlb.quote: The eight address bits 6..13 give the set into which to place the line. Each set can hold up to eight lines. That's what 8-way set-associative means!
c-mh-v2-l1d-8way-tlb.notes: Explains why 16 KiB-spaced chains cost 16+ cycles per load from ~36 nodes. Handley later qualifies how ways are chosen (c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash).

c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash.text: The L1D seems to place each line in a way chosen deterministically from low physical page-address bits (hashed with index bits) rather than by ordinary tag-matched ways, with no way prediction
