c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash.quote: we appear to have learned one more fact about the M1's L1D ... like a deterministic algorithm to place lines in sets, rather than the usual ways.
c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash.notes: Spacings of 32K-128K+64 B use all eight ways, 256K/512K+64 B only one, 16K+64 B about four; Handley never sees a way misprediction and cannot name the hash

c-mh-v3-barrier-colors.text: Per a 2012 Apple patent, barriers tag memory requests with a color that changes at each barrier, and no request of a later color completes until every request of the earlier color has
c-mh-v3-barrier-colors.quote: mark requests as they come in via some tag that changes when a barrier is encountered ... not allow any request with a tag later than N to complete until all requests tagged as N are complete
c-mh-v3-barrier-colors.notes: US9582276B2 (2012), speculative and architectural color values.

c-mh-v3-barrier-l1-l2.text: Apple appears to enforce barrier ordering between the L1 and the L2, so the L2 and beyond see the correct order while accesses between the LSU and the L1 stay free to reorder
c-mh-v3-barrier-l1-l2.quote: what Apple appear to do is implement the barrier between the L1 and L2, ensuring that the outside world (ie L2 and beyond) see correct ordering
c-mh-v3-barrier-l1-l2.notes: Handley assumes this orders the cache's MESI state changes and snoop responses.

c-mh-v3-pio-strands.text: Per a 2009 patent, a PIO controller labels buffered PIO writes so writes to one peripheral stay in order while writes to different peripherals interleave
c-mh-v3-pio-strands.quote: a PIO controller, and a labelling of PIO transactions, that allows for reordering between strands but not within strands
c-mh-v3-pio-strands.notes: US8032673B2 (2009). Handley reads the patent's source ID as a destination ID.

c-mh-v3-dsb-excluded-region.text: Per a 2020 patent, system registers can mark an address region as IO-like, and a DSB flag selects a strong form that orders all loads and stores or a mild form that need not wait for IO accesses
c-mh-v3-dsb-excluded-region.quote: one or more system registers that allow defining a region of space as IO-like ... to distinguish between a “strong” DSB
c-mh-v3-dsb-excluded-region.notes: US20220083338A1 (2020). With the mild form a core can acknowledge a remote DSB before its slow IO accesses complete.

c-mh-v3-remote-dsb.text: A DSB that involves other cores reaches them as an interrupt; each appears to discard its front end, drain its back end and all cache transactions, then acknowledge and resume fetch
c-mh-v3-remote-dsb.quote: the current solution appears to be essentially to throw away everything in the front-end, wait for all instructions in the back end to complete
c-mh-v3-remote-dsb.notes: Local barriers can use the color scheme; DSBs sent to other cores have no such shortcut. Flushing the front end also covers fetched instructions from a page that just became non-executable.

c-mh-v3-fused-stxr-barrier.text: Per a 2010 patent, a store-exclusive and the barrier after it are fused into one operation that needs only one trip out to the point of coherency
c-mh-v3-fused-stxr-barrier.quote: The solution is to fuse them together to create a single op (understood by the caches and the fabric) that only requires one such expensive outward trip.
c-mh-v3-fused-stxr-barrier.notes: US20110208915A1 (2010); Handley calls the details doubtless obsolete. The fusion happens in the LSU when no load or store lies between the two.

c-mh-v3-load-poison.text: Per a 2013 patent, each load carries a poison bit that is set if its cache line is modified before the load becomes non-speculative, and the load then recovers by replay or flush
c-mh-v3-load-poison.quote: Every load has associated with it a "poison bit", and if the cache line from which the load was read is modified before the load becomes non-speculative, then the poison bit is set
c-mh-v3-load-poison.notes: US9383995B2 (2013), extended to non-cacheable loads by US10747535B1 (2016). It keeps an older load from seeing newer data than a younger load to the same address.

c-mh-v3-wfe-poison.text: Per a 2014 patent, loads after a WFE may execute before the core wakes; on waking the LSU checks for poisoned loads, so part of the LSU must stay awake to match snooped Modified lines against the load queue
c-mh-v3-wfe-poison.quote: after we wake up frome the WEV, we check the LSU to see if any loads have poison bits associated with them, and Recover appropriately
c-mh-v3-wfe-poison.notes: US9501284B2 (2014). Handley writes WEV for the wait-for-event instruction.

c-mh-v3-lsq-cam-filter.text: Per a 2019 patent, the load/store queue keeps one bit for whether any entry is poisoned, and summary values such as the oldest valid load age, so most searches of the queue can be skipped
c-mh-v3-lsq-cam-filter.quote: the LSQ tracks a single bit as to whether any entry in the queue is poisoned, and behaves differently in these two cases
c-mh-v3-lsq-cam-filter.notes: US20200264888A1 (2019), CAM filtering based on microarchitectural state.

c-mh-v3-l2-dup-tags.text: Per a 2010 patent, the L2 holds duplicate tags for the L1s of its cores behind a coherence point on the fabric, where the 2006 design routed every snoop from one core straight to the L2 and the other core
c-mh-v3-l2-dup-tags.quote: we now have a Coherence Point on the fabric ... Now the L2 holds duplicate tags for the L1’s of the various cores attached to it

c-mh-v3-l2-snoop-filter.text: With its duplicate L1 tags the L2 filters out most snoops as irrelevant to the other cores, which saves energy and may let the L1 handle its now rare snoops on a slower path
c-mh-v3-l2-snoop-filter.quote: a snoop from one core can be handled by the L2 (which can filter out most snoops as being irrelevant to any other core, and so can discard them)

c-mh-v3-l1-line-counters.text: Per the 2010 patent, the L1 counts its valid and modified lines, presumably to decide how soon the cache can be put to sleep
c-mh-v3-l1-line-counters.quote: the L1 now has various counters of things like how many valid blocks and how many modified blocks it contains

c-mh-v3-l1-flush-walk.text: Flushing the L1 in the 2006 and 2010 designs walks every way of every set, presumably one per cycle, and can stop early only once the modified-line count reaches zero
c-mh-v3-l1-flush-walk.quote: flushing the cache seemed to require cycling through every way of every set (presumably one per cycle) asking that way to flush itself if it is modified

c-mh-v3-snoop-while-l1-sleeps.text: Because the L2 filters snoops, a sleeping core's L1 can stay powered but unclocked and mostly need not be woken to answer snoops
c-mh-v3-snoop-while-l1-sleeps.quote: snoops can be handled by the L2 while the L1 sleeps, and mostly without having to wake the L1
c-mh-v3-snoop-while-l1-sleeps.notes: Handley's power ladder: clock gating for very short naps, a retained (unclocked, likely undervolted) L1 for longer sleeps, then flush and power off.

c-mh-v3-l1-flush-engine.text: Per a 2013 patent, an asynchronous flush engine copies a core's modified L1 lines to the L2 while the core is partly powered down, then the core powers off fully
c-mh-v3-l1-flush-engine.quote: Now we have a separate asynchronous engine that allows the main CPU to partially power down while the engine copies all modified lines out to L2, before fully powering down the core.
c-mh-v3-l1-flush-engine.notes: US20140195737A1 (2013). The L1 and the engine must keep handling snoops on not yet written lines until power off.

c-mh-v3-flush-engine-in-l2.text: The flush engine belongs to the L2, not to each core: it pulls modified lines out of an L1, finding them through the L2's duplicate L1 tags, so one engine serves the whole cluster
c-mh-v3-flush-engine-in-l2.quote: the flush engine is associated with the L2 core rather than the L1 cores. Thus, in a sense, it pulls modified lines from the L1

c-mh-v3-l2-flush-to-slc.text: When all the L2's clients sleep, the flush engine walks the L2 tags and pushes modified lines to the SLC until it has matched the maintained count of modified lines, and then the whole L2 can shut down
c-mh-v3-l2-flush-to-slc.quote: if all the clients of the L2 go to sleep, then after a while it makes sense to also shut down the entire L2 ... the flush engine gets repurposed for that job

c-mh-v3-dup-tag-power.text: Per a 2013 patent, once a core's L1 has lost power the L2 also powers off the duplicate tags it keeps for that L1, since there is nothing left to snoop
c-mh-v3-dup-tag-power.quote: once an L1 client has lost power, there's no point in snooping for that client any more ... Apple pulls the power on the duplicate tags
c-mh-v3-dup-tag-power.notes: US20140189411A1 (2013), power control for cache structures.

c-mh-v3-flush-without-sleep.text: Per a 2018 patent, one extra bit in the flush control register, which Handley assumes is at L2 level, lets the sleep flush machinery flush caches for software maintenance without putting the core to sleep
c-mh-v3-flush-without-sleep.quote: we add one extra bit to this control register so that the flush machinery goes through everything as before, except with that bit set, it omits the steps that before would put the CPU to sleep
c-mh-v3-flush-without-sleep.notes: US10552323B1 (2018). Handley thinks it serves I-cache and L1 maintenance, perhaps not TLB.

c-mh-v3-sleep-invalidate-queue.text: Per a 2020 patent, a unit outside the core, which Handley assumes is the L2, records I-cache and TLB invalidations for a sleeping core and feeds them to it on waking, flushing the whole I-cache or TLB if the record overflows
c-mh-v3-sleep-invalidate-queue.quote: external to the CPU (I assume the L2 since it's doing this sort of work in various other cases) records the various I-cache and TLB invalidation requests

c-mh-v3-fiu-throttle.text: Per a 2018 patent, cache and TLB maintenance requests for a core wait in a per-cluster Fabric Interface Unit, and a core that has taken enough of them refuses more until counters show it has made progress on normal code
c-mh-v3-fiu-throttle.quote: something the patent calls The FIU, Fabric Interface Unit, which is a per-processor-complex object ... successive maintenance requests are held in a queue in the FIU, not the CPU
c-mh-v3-fiu-throttle.notes: US11080188B1 (2018). Handley reads it as protection against a guest OS flooding other cores with maintenance requests.

c-mh-v3-deferred-invalidate-poison.text: Per a 2021 patent, a cache marks lines hit by invalidation requests as poisoned and synchronizes them in the background, stalling only accesses to poisoned lines and any barrier that needs full synchronization
c-mh-v3-deferred-invalidate-poison.quote: rather than the cache handling each invalidation request immediately, it marks the relevant cache line as “poisoned”
c-mh-v3-deferred-invalidate-poison.notes: US20230017473A1 (2021), filed after the M1 shipped; Handley suggests both this and the FIU scheme may end up implemented.

c-mh-v3-drowsy-l2.text: The L2 is run as a drowsy cache: banks idle for some time sleep at a voltage that retains data and need a cycle or two to wake on access
c-mh-v3-drowsy-l2.quote: banks that haven't been accessed for some time are put to sleep, with enough voltage to retain data, but requiring a cycle or two to wake up on access

c-mh-v3-l2-sleep-by-way.text: The unit put to sleep is one way of every set: with each way in its own independently powered bank, sleeping a bank leaves the other ways fully active and costs a wake-up cycle for lines in the sleeping way
c-mh-v3-l2-sleep-by-way.quote: The unit that is actually put to sleep is a way in each set.
c-mh-v3-l2-sleep-by-way.notes: Handley's 8-way L2 here is an illustration.

c-mh-v3-l2-sleep-leakage.text: Per a 2014 patent, the idle count before an L2 bank sleeps is set from the part's characterized leakage and the temperature measured just before, so a leakier or hotter L2 sleeps banks sooner
c-mh-v3-l2-sleep-leakage.quote: Based on the temperature and the leakiness of the L2, an idle count is established.

c-mh-v3-l2-12-ways-2014.text: Per a 2014 patent, Apple's L2 then had 12 ways in three separately powered groups, so a third or two thirds of the cache could be powered down
c-mh-v3-l2-12-ways-2014.quote: at that time Apple's L2 had 12 ways, and these were split into three separately powered collections, so that either one third or two thirds of the cache could be powered down
c-mh-v3-l2-12-ways-2014.hedge: Details have surely changed since then
c-mh-v3-l2-12-ways-2014.notes: US20150309939A1 (2014), selective cache way-group power down.

c-mh-v3-l2-thirds.text: Apple still seems to run the L2 and the L2 TLB in thirds (full, two thirds or one third active), which Handley gives as the reason both sizes are multiples of 3
c-mh-v3-l2-thirds.quote: Apple still seems to operate L2 (and TLB2) at a 3-way granularity, that is each of these can run at full capacity, at 2/3, or at 1/3 ... Hence L2 and TLB2 sizes being multiples of 3
c-mh-v3-l2-thirds.notes: The idle third is either asleep or powered off. Consistent with the 12 MiB L2 and the 3072-entry L2 TLB.

c-mh-v3-l2-powerdown-counters.text: Per the 2014 patent, three counters of references to each way group pick the third to power down, and three more count hits to the MRU, middle and LRU four ways of all sets to decide whether to power down at all
c-mh-v3-l2-powerdown-counters.quote: There are two orthogonal sets of three counters. One set counts the number of references to each of the three physical banks. The lowest value tells us which bank will be powered down.
c-mh-v3-l2-powerdown-counters.notes: Modified lines in the chosen group are flushed first; the patent's cost also weighs lines held in L1s and how busy the group has been.

c-mh-v3-l2-powerup.text: A powered-down part of the L2 comes back when the L2 misses often, with further tests for whether the misses involve reused lines rather than compulsory or streaming misses
c-mh-v3-l2-powerup.quote: Obviously the first signal is that you are missing frequently in the L2 (suggesting your L2 is too small)

c-mh-v3-slc-dup-tags-l2.text: The SLC snoop-filters the L2s with duplicate L2 tags of its own, powered by way, so the matching way group of the duplicate tags powers down with the L2's
c-mh-v3-slc-dup-tags-l2.quote: the SLC snoop-filters the L2, using a set of duplicated tags stored with the SLC. These duplicate tags are also powered by way
c-mh-v3-slc-dup-tags-l2.notes: US9823730B2 (2015), power management of cache duplicate tags.

c-mh-v3-sparse-zero-lines.text: A 2017 patent records all-zero line writes as a bit in the line's tag without writing the data array and serves reads of such lines without reading it; Handley thinks its diagrams look like the L2
c-mh-v3-sparse-zero-lines.quote: don’t perform the write, instead note the line (eg by setting a bit in the cache line tag)
c-mh-v3-sparse-zero-lines.notes: US10691610B2 (2017). Vol 2 found no speed difference with all-zero data (c-mh-v2-zero-data).

c-mh-v3-sparse-loser-bank.text: The same patent keeps invalid and all-zero lines in one loser bank that stays powered off until real data must be stored there, and repacks data later to power it down again
c-mh-v3-sparse-loser-bank.quote: maintain one cache bank as the "loser" banks holding the invalid lines and the "all zero" lines

c-mh-v3-a10-shared-l2.text: A 2017 patent describes the A10, whose efficiency cores used the performance cores' L2 as their own, so that L2 had to stay powered whenever the efficiency cores ran
c-mh-v3-a10-shared-l2.quote: it describes the A10 (and only the A10). The idea is we have performance cores with an associated L2, and efficiency cores that use the L2 of the performance cores as their L2.
c-mh-v3-a10-shared-l2.notes: US10147464B1 (2017). Running the shared L2 at its own frequency means buffering between clock domains.

c-mh-v3-cluster-shared-frequency.text: Cores that share an L2 must either all run at one frequency or pay a much higher L2 access cost for buffering across clock domains
c-mh-v3-cluster-shared-frequency.quote: When cores share an L2 (and other hardware), either they all run at the same frequency, or the cost to access the L2 is substantially higher because of buffering across clock domains.
c-mh-v3-cluster-shared-frequency.notes: Handley asks whether four is the right number of cores per shared L2 and frequency domain.

c-mh-v3-slc-neither-incl-excl.text: Apple's cache levels are neither inclusive nor exclusive; the SLC keeps tags for the contents of every L2 but not the data, so reading such a line means asking that L2
c-mh-v3-slc-neither-incl-excl.quote: What Apple do, however, is neither exclusive nor inclusive. ... This definitely happens for the SLC, which has tags that give the contents of all the L2s, but not the lines
c-mh-v3-slc-neither-incl-excl.notes: For lookup the SLC contains the L2s, for data it does not. 7-cpu suggests an exclusive SLC (c-7cpu-slc-exclusive).

c-mh-v3-l2-covering-tags-hint.text: There are hints that the L2 likewise keeps covering tags for the L1s without holding all their data, but no patent Handley found says so unequivocally
c-mh-v3-l2-covering-tags-hint.quote: There are hints that the L2 also does this relative to the L1 (so it has covering tags, but may not include the L1 line data)
c-mh-v3-l2-covering-tags-hint.notes: He adds that this may have changed over the years.

c-mh-v3-snoop-levels.text: Core-to-core snooping mostly stays inside a cluster, handled by that cluster's L2 for its four cores, while snoops between clusters or between different IP blocks are filtered at the SLC level
c-mh-v3-snoop-levels.quote: core to core snooping will mostly occur within a core cluster, and can be handled well by having the L2 for that cluster snoop for all 4 processors of the cluster

c-mh-v3-coherence-point.text: The snooping attributed to the SLC is done by the Coherence Point, once closely tied to the SLC and increasingly a separate unit
c-mh-v3-coherence-point.quote: The snooping is performed by what’s called the Coherence Point, which in the past was closely associated with the SLC, but has become more and more a separate entity.

c-mh-v3-four-hop.text: Per a 2013 patent, a request for a line held in another CPU's cache goes to the SLC, whose duplicate tags locate it; the line moves from that cache to the SLC and then to the requester, a four-hop protocol
c-mh-v3-four-hop.quote: If you count the interactions, you can call this a “four hop” protocol.
c-mh-v3-four-hop.notes: US20150067246A1 (2013), black box duplicate tags. Passing through the SLC lets it keep a copy, which matters less as L2s have grown.

c-mh-v3-three-hop.text: A 2020 patent adds a three-hop protocol in which the SLC tells the owning CPU to send the line straight to the requester, bypassing the SLC
c-mh-v3-three-hop.quote: a 2020 patent for a new Apple three hop cache protocol ... then E sends the data directly to P bypassing the SLC
c-mh-v3-three-hop.hedge: This may or may not be in the M1
c-mh-v3-three-hop.notes: Handley says it may be only for the M2 and later. See c-mh-v3-scalable-coherence.

c-mh-v3-ctt-queues.text: In the 2013 duplicate-tag design every request enters a Current Transaction Table and is checked against the duplicate tags; a miss goes on to the memory interface, a hit is routed to the cache holding the line
c-mh-v3-ctt-queues.quote: All memory requests first hit the CTT (Current Transaction Table). The simplest sort of request will be placed in the IRQ (Incoming Request Queue), and have the request address tested against the DTs (Duplicate Tags).
c-mh-v3-ctt-queues.notes: Data returned from another cache passes through a copyback queue to the requester; a state machine keeps the steps in order.

c-mh-v3-victim-addq.text: A modified victim's address waits in a victim address queue, removed from the duplicate tags, until its data is safe in the SLC or DRAM, and requests to that address are held meanwhile
c-mh-v3-victim-addq.quote: From now until we’re done, if another request comes in matching an address in Victim AddQ, the new request is paused until the address in VictimAddQ is no longer present

c-mh-v3-parallel-coherence-pipes.text: Per a 2018 patent, an incoming snoop is checked against a cache's own tags and its duplicate tags at the same time
c-mh-v3-parallel-coherence-pipes.quote: The patent says "look at both simultaneously", with a bunch of complications that then result
c-mh-v3-parallel-coherence-pipes.notes: US20200081838A1 (2018). Complications: both tag sets hit, the line is locked by a load exclusive, or the request has passed the global ordering point.

c-mh-v3-slc-four-slices.text: The 2018 patent's figure, probably close to the current SLC, shows one pool of request queues feeding four arbiters that route requests to four slices
c-mh-v3-slc-four-slices.quote: Four arbitrators (in principle there could be more, but four seems reasonable for an M1 class SoC) route these requests to one of four "slices".
c-mh-v3-slc-four-slices.hedge: four seems reasonable for an M1 class SoC

c-mh-v3-slc-slice-hash.text: Handley's guess is that physical address bits 6 and 7 pick the slice in the simplest case, or a hash of more bits, which on Pro, Max and Ultra also spreads lines across SLCs
c-mh-v3-slc-slice-hash.quote: use bits 6 and 7 to choose one of the 4 arbitrators and slices. But of course one can use a more complicated hash that uses more address bits.
c-mh-v3-slc-slice-hash.hedge: an obvious way to think about this
c-mh-v3-slc-slice-hash.notes: His example assumes a 64 B line; nobody states the actual selection.

c-mh-v3-l2-incl-instr-2007.text: Per a 2007 patent, the L2 is inclusive for instructions
c-mh-v3-l2-incl-instr-2007.quote: what that says, among other things is that the L2 is ... inclusive for instructions
c-mh-v3-l2-incl-instr-2007.notes: US7702858B2 (2007). Handley sees no point in it, unless as a way to keep instruction lines in the L2 longer.

c-mh-v3-l2-victim-data-2007.text: Per the same 2007 patent, the L2 is a victim cache for data: lines fill the L1 directly from their source and reach the L2 only when evicted from the L1
c-mh-v3-l2-victim-data-2007.quote: victim for data. In other words a data line is loaded directly from its source (let’s say DRAM) into L1, without being stored in L2.
c-mh-v3-l2-victim-data-2007.notes: A line reloaded from the L2 then sits in both caches.

c-mh-v3-l2-pending-tag-2013.text: Per a 2013 patent, on a miss in both L1 and L2 the L2 allocates a tag marked pending without the data, and the L1 copy is marked clean-evict so it is copied to the L2 when the L1 evicts it
c-mh-v3-l2-pending-tag-2013.quote: a tag is allocated for the line, but the data is not copied into the line. The tag is marked with a “pending” bit.
c-mh-v3-l2-pending-tag-2013.notes: US20150149722A1 (2013), delaying cache data array updates.

c-mh-v3-selective-victim.text: Per a companion 2013 patent, each L1 set tracks how actively its lines are used, and clean lines from little-used sets are dropped rather than copied to the L2, as they also are when L1-L2 traffic is heavy
c-mh-v3-selective-victim.quote: under these conditions of low usage, when a clean line is to be overwritten in L1, it is not copied up to L2
c-mh-v3-selective-victim.notes: US20150149721A1, granted as US9298620B2 (2013). The pending L2 tag then turns invalid, so no useful L2 line is lost to it.

c-mh-v3-l2-dup-tags-unclear.text: Whether the L2 keeps duplicate L1 tags is unclear: the 2013 victimization patent does not use them, while the 2013 flush-engine patent states plainly that the L2 has them
c-mh-v3-l2-dup-tags-unclear.quote: The main issue that is uncertain is whether L2 has duplicate tags like the SLC ... patent very definitely states that there are L1 duplicate tags in the L2

c-mh-v3-l1-2048-lines.text: The L1 data cache holds 2048 lines
c-mh-v3-l1-2048-lines.quote: There are 2048 lines in the L1.
c-mh-v3-l1-2048-lines.notes: Equals 128 KiB in 64 B lines (l1d.size, l1d.line).

c-mh-v3-flush-dirty-only.text: The 2013 flush engine writes back only dirty L1 lines before power-off, extracting them by telling the L1 each line has been snooped, a method that cannot move clean lines
c-mh-v3-flush-dirty-only.quote: The 2013 Flush Engine patent suggests that only dirty lines are written back to L2 ... indicating that the line has been snooped, so that it needs to be written to the L2

c-mh-v3-dram-fill-l1-only.text: Handley's summary of the current flow: data fetched from DRAM is installed in the L1 only, not in the L2 or the SLC
c-mh-v3-dram-fill-l1-only.quote: when the L1 makes a request for data that has to come all the way from DRAM, that data + will NOT be installed in the SLC + will NOT be installed in the L2
c-mh-v3-dram-fill-l1-only.notes: He calls the picture somewhat unsatisfactory and likely to have changed many times.

c-mh-v3-l1-victim-to-l2.text: A line cast out of the L1 may go to the L2 as a victim if it looks useful and the L1-L2 path is not backed up, and an L2 castout may likewise go to the SLC as a victim
c-mh-v3-l1-victim-to-l2.quote: it could be sent to L2 as a victim cache, depending on whether the line appears to be useful and if transporting it to L2 is not too expensive

c-mh-v3-full-line-write-l2.text: A newly created 64 B line written quickly by a core appears to be written whole to the L2 without allocating in the L1; partial writes update the L1 copy
c-mh-v3-full-line-write-l2.quote: a completely newly created line (64B of rapidly written data) is created on the L1. This appears to be written as a complete line to L2 without allocating in L1.

c-mh-v3-l2-writeback-path.text: A modified line cast out of the L2 is written back either straight to the memory controller or to the SLC, which writes it to DRAM later
c-mh-v3-l2-writeback-path.quote: when a modified line is cast out of L2, it has to be a writeback of course. Under some conditions could go straight to the Memory Controller

c-mh-v3-prefetch-two-targets.text: The prefetch unit beside the L1 issues two streams, a high-confidence one into the L1 and a lower-confidence or later one into the L2; L2 prefetches never used carry a prefetch bit and are not saved to the SLC
c-mh-v3-prefetch-two-targets.quote: prefetches are generated in the Prefetch Unit (associated with L1) as two different streams, one targeting the L1 (high confidence, needed immediately), one targeting the L2
c-mh-v3-prefetch-two-targets.notes: Whether L1-targeted lines also allocate in the L2 Handley does not know.

c-mh-v3-prefetch-no-slc.text: The newest prefetcher targets only the L1 and L2, not the SLC, and fetches TLB entries only as a side effect of translating its virtual-address stream
c-mh-v3-prefetch-no-slc.quote: The newest prefetcher design seems to have no interest in the SLC; it targets only L1 and L2

c-mh-v3-slc-victim-allocator.text: Per a 2018 patent, each cluster's L2 has an Allocator whose counters (L2 demand misses, dirty share of evictions, prefetch accuracy, streaming prefetches) decide whether L2 victims go to the SLC or bypass it
c-mh-v3-slc-victim-allocator.quote: each cluster L2 has dedicated hardware called an Allocator containing multiple counters tracking various things
c-mh-v3-slc-victim-allocator.notes: US10963392B1 (2018). With little expected reuse, clean victims are dropped and dirty ones go straight to DRAM, bypassing the SLC.

c-mh-v3-clean-victim-modes.text: Handley expects the M1 to track line usefulness at both L1 and L2 and not to write clean victims that have not proved useful out to the next cache, toggling between keeping and dropping clean victims
c-mh-v3-clean-victim-modes.quote: One expects that in the M1 the best aspects of all these designs are used at both the L1 and L2 levels

c-mh-v3-l2-inclusive-2013.text: Around 2013 and 2014 (the A7 and A8 generation) the L2 was inclusive, so replacement avoided lines also held in an L1; whether it still is remains unclear
c-mh-v3-l2-inclusive-2013.quote: if your L2 is inclusive (as it was say around 2013..2014 so around A7, A8 generation; unclear today) then you should not replace a line that is an inclusive line

c-mh-v3-line-state-bits.text: Apple's per-line state includes bits marking a line as part of a stream, brought in by a prefetcher, or having made a trip (into the L1, evicted to the L2, back into the L1)
c-mh-v3-line-state-bits.quote: Along with the other data stored by Apple for each cache line we have bits that indicate ... the line has made a “trip”

c-mh-v3-l2-lru-placement.text: Per a 2013 patent, an incoming L2 line is placed at an LRU position chosen from its history, low for lines not expected to be reused and high (LRU7 in an 8-way example) for likely useful ones
c-mh-v3-l2-lru-placement.quote: If we place a new line at LRU0, that’s saying that we will accept the line in the L2, but we’re not very confident it will be useful
c-mh-v3-l2-lru-placement.notes: US9563575B2 (2013). Lines enter the L2 as L1 victims, so arrival alone does not show usefulness. Vol 2 timing suggested random L2 replacement on the M1 (c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl).

c-mh-v3-l2-stream-lru0.text: A streaming line evicted from the L1 enters the L2 at LRU0 and moves up one step if reused, so a long stream replaces only earlier stream lines and can displace about an eighth, or perhaps a quarter, of the L2
c-mh-v3-l2-stream-lru0.quote: the stream can only wipe out one 1/8th (or maybe 1/4) of the L2 cache, it can’t remove the other 7/8th of useful material in the cache

c-mh-v3-l2-prefetch-slots.text: Prefetched lines that have not been used get the four lowest LRU slots, on the view that they are low-confidence prefetches and should be used soon if at all
c-mh-v3-l2-prefetch-slots.quote: Prefetches we are slightly more tolerant of. They get the four lowest slots to hang around in

c-mh-v3-l2-trip-lines.text: Even lines that have made a trip can occupy only three quarters of the L2 until a hit in the L2 promotes them to LRU7
c-mh-v3-l2-trip-lines.quote: even the probably useful trip lines only get access to 3/4 of the cache

c-mh-v3-true-lru.text: The 2013 replacement patent assumes true LRU ordering but does not say how it is built
c-mh-v3-true-lru.quote: The patents talks about using a “true LRU”, but does not explain how this is done.
c-mh-v3-true-lru.notes: Handley's alternative, a random choice among lines below a desirability score, is his own proposal.

c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-quota.text: Per a 2014 follow-up, each L2 line also records which CPU last accessed it, each CPU has a line quota, and replacement takes the least recently used line among CPUs over quota
c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-quota.quote: adds to the other per-line state, an ID for which CPU most recently accessed each line. Each CPU has a cache line quota
c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-quota.notes: US20150309944A1 (2014), methods for cache line eviction.

c-mh-v3-superways.text: Handley reads a 2020 patent as grouping the ways of a highly associative cache into a few super-ways ranked by LRU, a hash fixing each line's slot within a super-way, which saves LRU bits and suits powering down the coldest way group
c-mh-v3-superways.quote: we can save a whole lot of LRU-ordering bits by use of the super-ways; and we can make the cache shutdown mechanism more efficient
c-mh-v3-superways.notes: US11144476B2 (2020), LRU ranking in a multi-port cache. His 256 sets, 128 ways and four super-ways of 32 are made-up numbers.

c-mh-v3-moesi.text: Apple has likely used MOESI since at least the A6 and A7, whose Owned state lets a modified line pass directly from one cache to another
c-mh-v3-moesi.quote: it seems likely that, from at least the A6 and A7 days, Apple was using MOESI as their cache

c-mh-v3-directory.text: Apple's coherence is in effect a directory protocol, the duplicate tags in the coherence point serving as the directory, although Apple calls it snooping
c-mh-v3-directory.quote: Apple essentially uses a directory protocol (the Duplicate Tags stored in the Coherence Point, as will be discussed in massive detail when we cover the Fabric/SLC/Memory Controller, are essentially a directory)

c-mh-v3-page-unshared-snoop.text: A 2009 patent marks never-shared pages in the page tables, carried through the TLB to the cache, so lines in them skip snoop broadcasts; Handley wonders whether the M1 has it
c-mh-v3-page-unshared-snoop.quote: Most pages are never shared, so suppose we indicate in the page tables, propagated to the TLB and then to the cache, that pages are not shared.
c-mh-v3-page-unshared-snoop.hedge: So maybe it's present in the M1?
c-mh-v3-page-unshared-snoop.notes: US20100235586A1 (2009). Handley guesses it served the dual-package Mac Pro, not phones.

c-mh-v3-sharing-tracking.text: A 2011 patent has each device learn from snoop traffic which lines others may hold and suppress snoops for lines no one else can have, refining the tracking granularity per address range from statistics
c-mh-v3-sharing-tracking.quote: if it knows that no other device can be holding a particular line, snoop broadcasts related to that line can be suppressed
c-mh-v3-sharing-tracking.notes: US8856456B2 (2011), aimed at coherence between a CPU and a GPU.

c-mh-v3-scalable-coherence.text: A 2020 patent defines a protocol built on MOESI that allows several outstanding transactions per line; each snoop carries the expected state change, so a cache can detect a snoop that arrived out of order and wait
c-mh-v3-scalable-coherence.quote: multiple transactions to a specific cache line may be outstanding ... What Apple do instead is to include, with each Snoop transaction, the state the line is supposed to be in
c-mh-v3-scalable-coherence.notes: US20220083472A1 (2020), scalable cache coherency protocol. Handley sees it suited to something the size of an M1 Ultra.

c-mh-v3-sideways-fill.text: The same protocol lets fill and copyback messages name a target device, so data moves sideways from cache to cache, merging MOESI with MESIF-style forwarding of clean lines
c-mh-v3-sideways-fill.quote: This aspect of the protocol is essentially a merging of MOESI (allow sharing of modified lines) and MERSI/MESIF (allow sideways transfer of non-modified lines).
c-mh-v3-sideways-fill.notes: Extended shared states decide which sharer forwards a clean line; some message pairs are bundled into one.

c-mh-v3-inter-cluster-snoop.text: A 2020 patent shortens some inter-cluster transfers: a NoC arbitration node between a cluster and the SLC copies certain snoop responses and returns one to the requester as if from the SLC
c-mh-v3-inter-cluster-snoop.quote: This patent uses a hack to convert some of the four-hop transactions that should route through the SLC to faster three-hop transactions.
c-mh-v3-inter-cluster-snoop.notes: US11016913B1 (2020), inter cluster snoop latency reduction.

c-mh-v3-cache-as-ram.text: A 2019 patent lets a cache map address ranges onto some of its lines through in-cache registers, so that device DMA can land directly in the cache instead of DRAM
c-mh-v3-cache-as-ram.quote: allow a cache ... to have certain address ranges mapped (via in-cache registers) to some lines of the cache
c-mh-v3-cache-as-ram.notes: US10922232B1 (2019). The patent covers L1 to L3, with L1 examples; its focus is ordering memory and IO requests to such a cache without deadlock.

c-mh-v3-dma-into-l2.text: Unlike Intel's automatic DDIO into the L3, Apple's scheme seems to need a driver to set up the mapping and puts the data in the L2, which Handley thinks the SLC's duplicate tags make possible
c-mh-v3-dma-into-l2.quote: Intel’s scheme goes to L3, whereas Apple’s scheme goes to L2. I’m guessing this is feasible ... because of the duplicate tags

c-mh-v3-slc-dynamic-ram.text: A 2021 patent maps a physical address range into a cache, probably the SLC, on demand, for example for camera frames read by the GPU or encoder; removing the range clears the lines and makes the range invalid
c-mh-v3-slc-dynamic-ram.quote: the ability to map a physical address range into a cache (probably SLC) rather than DRAM
c-mh-v3-slc-dynamic-ram.notes: US20230067307A1 (2021). It also suggests keeping alternate lines of a large buffer in the SLC to interleave hits with DRAM misses.

c-mh-v3-slc-tagless-ram.text: A 2009 patent sets part of the SLC aside as tagless memory reached through range registers, mainly for the GPU and image processor; Handley would not be surprised if the M1 has both this and the 2019 scheme
c-mh-v3-slc-tagless-ram.quote: this storage isn't used like traditional cache storage, and so doesn't require tags; rather a few range registers in the SLC can route addresses as appropriate to this storage
c-mh-v3-slc-tagless-ram.hedge: I wouldn't be surprised if both are present on the M1

c-mh-v3-display-from-slc.text: Per a 2013 patent, when the display buffer is static the system copies it into the SLC and the display controller reads from the SLC instead of DRAM
c-mh-v3-display-from-slc.quote: When the system detects that the contents of the display buffer are static, the display buffer is copied to the SLC, and the display controller runs out of SLC rather than DRAM.
c-mh-v3-display-from-slc.notes: US9261939B2 (2013). Related patents sleep the SLC arrays not being read and detect a static screen by a CRC unchanged for N frames.

c-mh-v3-replacement-policy-bit.text: Per a 2009 patent, a bit in each cache set selects LRU or a limited FIFO for streams, set per request from the page tables or from range registers in the MMU
c-mh-v3-replacement-policy-bit.quote: provide a bit specifying the replacement policy for this particular cache set
c-mh-v3-replacement-policy-bit.notes: US8392658B2 (2009). Handley suspects large caches gain more from hashed, low-associativity placement.

c-mh-v3-cache-filter.text: Per a 2019 patent, software names an address range to filter and the cache keeps only a fraction of its lines on write, passing the rest to DRAM, so a data set too big for the cache still gets some hits
c-mh-v3-cache-filter.quote: you describe the address range you want to “filter” and the cache HW should do the rest for you, deciding which lines to retain on write and which to pass through to DRAM
c-mh-v3-cache-filter.notes: US11256629B2 (2019). The SLC can skip tag checks for filtered addresses it knows it does not hold.

c-mh-v3-fill-source-telemetry.text: Per a 2019 patent, per-core counters track where L1 misses are filled from (another L1 or the cluster L2, another cluster, the SLC or DRAM) to steer DRAM, fabric and cluster frequencies and thread placement
c-mh-v3-fill-source-telemetry.quote: describing per-core counters that track these cache fill sources

c-mh-v3-cluster-clock-shared.text: A whole cluster changes frequency together, so a single core can only be slowed by gating its clock to every second or fourth edge, which saves switching power but not voltage
c-mh-v3-cluster-clock-shared.quote: the frequency of an entire cluster has to change together, so it’s hard to directly slow down a single core

c-mh-v3-telemetry-l3-design.text: The same 2019 patent shows two clusters of four cores with a per-core L2 and a per-cluster L3, unlike other Apple patents, which makes Handley wonder whether it shows a fourth-generation design
c-mh-v3-telemetry-l3-design.quote: It describes a design with - two clusters - four cores in each cluster - a per-core L2 and - a shared per-cluster L3 (which the patent calls LLC)
c-mh-v3-telemetry-l3-design.hedge: it makes one wonder if we are seeing an aspect of the 4th gen design
c-mh-v3-telemetry-l3-design.notes: Handley groups Apple patents into designs up to the A6, the A7 to A10, and the A11 to M1; this one fits none.

c-mh-v3-ecluster-uses-pl2.text: Handley reads a 2017 patent as letting the E cluster use the P cluster's L2 while the P cores sleep, the P L2's DVFS state following the P cores when any is awake and set for the E cores otherwise
c-mh-v3-ecluster-uses-pl2.quote: the P cluster’s L2 is available to (and used by) the E cluster ... if one or more P cores is awake, set the P L2 DVFS state to match the P cores
c-mh-v3-ecluster-uses-pl2.notes: US10147464B1 (2017), the patent he earlier tied to the A10; here he applies it to phones, iPads and M1 laptops and suggests benchmarks could test it.

c-mh-v3-mmu-at-slc.text: Apple appears to split the MMU: TLBs act as small L1 caches while the page walkers form one shared unit at the SLC and memory-controller level, serving every client on the chip
c-mh-v3-mmu-at-slc.quote: the TLB is something like a simple L1 cache, while the rest of the MMU (page walkers and suchlike) appears to be a unitary entity living up at the SLC/memory controller level
c-mh-v3-mmu-at-slc.hedge: I can’t be sure of the details
c-mh-v3-mmu-at-slc.notes: Based in part on US9652560B1 (2011), a non-blocking MMU beside the SLC. See c-mh-v3-atu-in-cluster.

c-mh-v3-sprr-index.text: Per a 2019 patent (APRR/SPRR), a page carries a permission index into a short 4-entry table instead of permission bits, so one core can switch a page's permissions without a TLB shootdown
c-mh-v3-sprr-index.quote: a page no longer has a set of permission bits, rather it has a "permission index" ... the first part of the index is used to index a (short, 4 entry) table
c-mh-v3-sprr-index.notes: US20210064539A1 (2019), unified address translation. Two halves of the index serve A and B conditions; B is set briefly on the core changing the page.

c-mh-v3-atu-in-cluster.text: Handley reads the 2019 patent as moving the address translation unit out of the core: a core keeps a small L1 TLB, and misses go to the cluster (L2) level, which holds a large L2 TLB shared by its cores and the page walkers
c-mh-v3-atu-in-cluster.quote: If the L1 TLB misses, the request goes up to the Processor Complex (ie L2 cache) which will have a large L2 TLB, shared across the cores that share the L2 cache, the page walkers
c-mh-v3-atu-in-cluster.notes: US20210064539A1 (2019). Agrees with vol 2 (c-mh-v2-tlb2-per-cluster). Handley suggests a shared ATU might filter TLB shootdowns as the L2 filters L1 snoops.

c-mh-v3-slc-io-coherence.text: The SLC holds the coherence point and tags of the other caches (the P and E L2s), so a peripheral reading a buffer still in a CPU's L1 gets the data through the SLC from that L2 and L1, with no software flush
c-mh-v3-slc-io-coherence.quote: the SLC will see that address A is present within an L2 tag, and so will request the data from the L2, which will request it from the L1
c-mh-v3-slc-io-coherence.notes: Only Device memory is then truly uncacheable.

c-mh-v3-uncached-load-merge.text: Per a 2019 patent, each cache controller has a pool of buffers for uncacheable loads, merging later loads to the same line until a timer expires or a full-width load is built
c-mh-v3-uncached-load-merge.quote: there is a pool of buffers in each cache controller for the use of uncachable loads ... when a load is placed in one of these buffers a timer starts
c-mh-v3-uncached-load-merge.notes: US20210056024A1 (2019), serial miss requests in a non-coherent memory system.

c-mh-v3-l2-line-patent.text: A 2015 Apple patent on L2 request ordering gives the L2 line as 128 B; vol 2 measured 64 B L1 lines and had assumed the same for L2 and SLC, and the SLC line stays unresolved
c-mh-v3-l2-line-patent.quote: The patent tells us that the L2 cache line is 128B
c-mh-v3-l2-line-patent.notes: US10127153B1 (2015), cache dependency handling. Agrees with c-mh-v2-l2-line-128 and c-mh-v3-l2-line-128.

c-mh-v3-l2-order-unit.text: Per the 2015 patent, requests queued at the L2 from its L1 clients are ordered per 128 B L2 line: in order within a line, out of order across lines
c-mh-v3-l2-order-unit.quote: requests that go to the same L2 line must be handled in order, but can be handled out of order relative to requests touching any other L2 line
c-mh-v3-l2-order-unit.notes: A write to half an L2 line changes state for the whole line, which is why the L2 line, not the L1 line, is the unit.

c-mh-v3-l2-half-line-bypass.text: When a write to one half of an L2 line and a later read of the other half come from the same core, the read may go first, since they are separate L1 lines; from different cores the read waits
c-mh-v3-l2-half-line-bypass.quote: if the read and write are to the same core, then we know that there is no conceptual problem, as far as the L1 is concerned, these are separate lines

c-mh-v3-no-buses.text: There seems no reason to think the M1 has physical buses, except perhaps for debug or very slow peripherals; its interconnect is a network on chip
c-mh-v3-no-buses.quote: There seems no reason to believe there are any physical buses on an M1 (perhaps there are for very specialized tasks like debug and for very slow peripherals like buttons?)
c-mh-v3-no-buses.hedge: There seems no reason to believe

c-mh-v3-l2-switch.text: Apple places each CPU cluster below an L2 that acts as a switch between the cluster's cores and the rest of the SoC
c-mh-v3-l2-switch.quote: Apple clusters CPU’s below an L2 that acts as a Switch between the cores of a cluster and the rest of the SoC

c-mh-v3-device-store-path.text: A store to Device memory, once non-speculative, skips the cache and goes through the L2 onto the NoC as a small write message, its physical address mapped to a destination block ID around the L2 exit or NoC entry
c-mh-v3-device-store-path.quote: the store, once it becomes non-speculative, rather than storing its data in the cache will immediately send it out to the L2 and then onto the NoC
c-mh-v3-device-store-path.hedge: the details are so low level they are never made clear
c-mh-v3-device-store-path.notes: Handley compares the address lookup with the System Address Map in Arm's CMN-600.

c-mh-v3-request-path.text: A normal memory request passes from the core through L1 and L2 into the Switch, then to Coherence, which checks every other L1/L2, then to the SLC, then to the memory controller
c-mh-v3-request-path.quote: It flows from the CPU through L1, through L2, into the Switch which sends it to Coherence.
c-mh-v3-request-path.notes: Four layers in order Switch, Coherence, SLC, memory controller; Apple has moved more of the upper three into the NoC itself

c-mh-v3-device-bypass.text: Device-memory requests from the core bypass L1 and L2 and go straight to the Switch, which routes them to the target hardware without passing Coherence, the SLC or the memory controller
c-mh-v3-device-bypass.quote: Device Memory messages bypass Coherence, the SLC and the Memory Controller because they have nothing to do with any of that stuff.

c-mh-v3-slc-mc-frontend.text: The SLC is best seen as a front end to the memory controller rather than a conventional cache: a write that lands in the SLC counts as written to DRAM
c-mh-v3-slc-mc-frontend.quote: the SLC should not be thought of as a traditional style cache, it should be thought of as a front-end to the memory controller, so writing to the SLC is as good as writing to DRAM

c-mh-v3-dma-write-slc.text: A request from an IO block that misses in Coherence is checked against the SLC; a write is stored in the SLC and a read that misses there goes on to the memory controller
c-mh-v3-dma-write-slc.quote: if the request is a write, store in SLC; if it's a read that does not match in SLC go to the memory
c-mh-v3-dma-write-slc.hedge: I think the way that works is

c-mh-v3-uncacheable-caching.text: Even requests to uncacheable ranges can be cached in full by the SLC, because it is a memory-side cache, and in part by the CPU caches through the Coherence tags
c-mh-v3-uncacheable-caching.quote: The SLC caching always works because the SLC is a memory-side cache; the CPU-side caching works because we’ve put some smarts into Coherence.
c-mh-v3-uncacheable-caching.notes: The SLC side mainly helps IO blocks and saves energy; the Coherence side mainly helps the CPU

c-mh-v3-cpu-qos-fixed.text: The priority of CPU memory requests used to be fixed and fairly low; a recent patent makes it somewhat more dynamic
c-mh-v3-cpu-qos-fixed.quote: What priority does the CPU get? I think that used to be fixed and fairly low

c-mh-v3-qos-five.text: Apple's patents mostly describe five QoS settings in three priority bands; two of the bands hold one realtime and one non-realtime setting, which can age differently
c-mh-v3-qos-five.quote: The Apple patents mostly talk about 5 QoS Settings which (more or less) represent three priority bands.

c-mh-v3-qos-bands.text: The QoS bands are: high, RT Red; mid, RT Yellow and NRT Low Latency; low, RT Green and NRT Bulk
c-mh-v3-qos-bands.quote: We have, according to the patents, 3+2 QoS classes, which we can think of as forming three bands,

c-mh-v3-qos-evolution.text: Fabric priority evolved from keeping realtime traffic glitch-free (PA Semi to early A7), to bandwidth reservation, and by about 2020 to also guaranteeing minimum progress
c-mh-v3-qos-evolution.quote: now (as of 2020) we’re preserving these previous two desiderata, while also adding minimum progress guarantees.

c-mh-v3-fabric-credits.text: In the current (about 2020) design a requester needs credits to enter the fabric and then the memory controller, which enforces bandwidth and flow control and lets fabric queues stay small
c-mh-v3-fabric-credits.quote: To enter the fabric (and then to enter the memory controller) requires credits.
c-mh-v3-fabric-credits.notes: Small fabric queues save area and power and cut latency (less bufferbloat)

c-mh-v3-fabric-arbitration.text: Inside the fabric and memory controller, arbiters at routing points use grant counters and QoS levels to keep latency low and guarantee minimum progress
c-mh-v3-fabric-arbitration.quote: Once in the fabric (or memory controller) arbitration takes over at various routing points ... counters (grants) and flow markings (QoS levels) to ensure low latency and minimum progress

c-mh-v3-six-vcs.text: The current fabric uses three virtual channels (RealTime, Low Latency, Bulk), each in a posted and a non-posted form, six in all
c-mh-v3-six-vcs.quote: the three virtual channels I listed above come as posted and non-posted versions, so there are in fact six basic Apple virtual channels.
c-mh-v3-six-vcs.notes: The virtual channels replace the older QoS-plus-flowID tagging; Handley calls the scheme PCIe-inspired

c-mh-v3-flowid-gone.text: The separate flow IDs once used to tag streams such as GPU request streams appear to be gone in the most recent designs
c-mh-v3-flowid-gone.quote: The distinct flowIDs, used apparently to tag things like different streams of GPU requests, appear to be gone in the most recent designs.

c-mh-v3-vc-ordering.text: Ordering is fixed within a virtual channel, as in PCIe
c-mh-v3-vc-ordering.quote: I believe that for both Apple and PCIe, ordering must remain fixed within a Virtual Channel.
c-mh-v3-vc-ordering.notes: Patents differ on whether each virtual channel has its own hardware queue; Handley guesses separate queues for routing but not at the memory controller

c-mh-v3-credits-dram.text: For DRAM, credits act as both flow control and bandwidth allocation: a requester's credits set how many requests it may queue at the memory controller before it is throttled
c-mh-v3-credits-dram.quote: the credits of each ... essentially control how many requests the ... can queue up at the Memory Controller before it is throttled, and so the credits act as bandwidth allocation.
c-mh-v3-credits-dram.notes: There is no dedicated pool of memory controller slots per requester

c-mh-v3-gen2-credits.text: The second-generation fabric (about 2012 to 2018) used credits only for flow control between the Coherence Point and the memory controller queues
c-mh-v3-gen2-credits.quote: The second generation Fabric (~2012 to ~2018) used credits for flow control between the Coherence Point (essentially the start of processing all memory requests) and the Memory Controller proper

c-mh-v3-gen3-credits.text: The third-generation fabric (after about 2018) uses credits end to end for bandwidth allocation and flow control
c-mh-v3-gen3-credits.quote: The third generation (post ~2018) Fabric uses credits end-to-end throughout the Fabric for bandwidth allocation and flow control.

c-mh-v3-2010-five-ports.text: The first Apple design (2010) feeds the memory controller through five independent ports, realtime, two GPU, CPU and non-realtime, with no network beyond that and no SLC
c-mh-v3-2010-five-ports.quote: We have nothing like a SoC! We have five independent paths that flow data into the memory
c-mh-v3-2010-five-ports.notes: From US20120072677A1, which Handley places at the A4 or A5. Camera and display sit on the realtime port

c-mh-v3-2010-port-roles.text: In the 2010 design the GPU ports favour bandwidth over latency and the CPU port favours latency over bandwidth
c-mh-v3-2010-port-roles.quote: the two port for the GPU are obvious. However they prioritize bandwidth over latency. - the CPU port prioritize latency over bandwidth.

c-mh-v3-2010-mc-queues.text: Inside the 2010 memory controller a switch routes five inputs to seven outputs, and requests then pass three queue levels: MCIU, presorting queues (PSQ) and the memory interface (MIF)
c-mh-v3-2010-mc-queues.quote: The MCIUs (Memory Channel Interface Units) are queues feeding the PSQs (Presorting Queues) which feed the third level of queues in the MIF (Memory Interface Unit).

c-mh-v3-2010-bw-ports.text: In the 2010 design bandwidth is shared by giving each of the five ports a proportion programmed into the memory controller
c-mh-v3-2010-bw-ports.quote: For this initial 2010 design, bandwidth is allocated to the five ports

c-mh-v3-2010-inband-upgrade.text: When a flow ID's QoS rises, the memory controller raises every queued request of that flow to the new QoS (an in-band upgrade)
c-mh-v3-2010-inband-upgrade.quote: The memory controller, when it sees a change in the QoS of a flowID, will upgrade all queued items with that flowID to the new QoS.
c-mh-v3-2010-inband-upgrade.notes: A flow ID is a few source bits plus a few grouping bits; from 2012 Apple calls it a group ID

c-mh-v3-2010-aiu-arb.text: The 2010 interface unit always serves RT Red and RT Yellow requests first; otherwise it serves the ports by weighted round robin with weights from bandwidth-sharing registers
c-mh-v3-2010-aiu-arb.quote: as long as there (RT Red and RT Yellow) requests present, they are always serviced first.

c-mh-v3-2010-aging.text: The three later queue levels of the 2010 memory controller raise a request's QoS once it has waited past a set count
c-mh-v3-2010-aging.quote: The three subsequent queue levels all use counter based arbitration, so that if a given request remains in a queue for longer than a certain count, the request will have its QoS upgraded.

c-mh-v3-mc-affinity.text: The memory controller sorts requests into affinity buckets (same DRAM page, or a different bank or rank), and its last stage picks read or write mode and which bucket to send to DRAM
c-mh-v3-mc-affinity.quote: These are sorted in different buckets of affine operations (while still tagged with their QoS)
c-mh-v3-mc-affinity.notes: From the 2010 patents (US8510521B2); Handley expects the details to change with every SoC

c-mh-v3-2011-nrt-throttle.text: A 2011 change caps the non-realtime requests held in the memory controller's internal queues while realtime traffic is present, and keeps the cap for a while after it leaves
c-mh-v3-2011-nrt-throttle.quote: use a counter to limit the number of NRT transactions enqueued in these later stages when RT traffic is present.

c-mh-v3-2011-dwrr.text: In 2011 bandwidth among high-QoS requesters is split by deficit-weighted round robin, with tokens per epoch that the memory controller counts but does not report back
c-mh-v3-2011-dwrr.quote: The primary idea here is to service the ... using deficit-weighted round robin.

c-mh-v3-credit-return.text: In the most recent designs a credit is spent when a request is made and returned when it is fulfilled, so credits also give flow control, and throttling happens at entry to the fabric
c-mh-v3-credit-return.quote: credits in the most recent designs (as opposed to the tokens of this 2011 design) are spent when an ... makes a request, and returned when the request is fulfilled

c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-qos.text: The L2 sets the QoS of each core's memory requests from its count of that core's outstanding requests: few outstanding means latency mode and high QoS, many means bandwidth mode and low QoS
c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-qos.quote: The L2 keeps track of the number of outstanding memory requests (with characterization of prefetch vs demand, read vs write, and code vs data) for each core.
c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-qos.hedge: perhaps A6? level design, but probably continuing forward
c-mh-v3-l2-cpu-qos.notes: From US8751746B2. Dirty castouts and most prefetches go out at low priority, instruction demand misses at the highest. No count of outstanding misses is given

c-mh-v3-tournament.text: Fabric queues find their highest-priority entry each cycle by a tournament of pairwise comparisons over log2(N) rounds, the same scheme as the core's scheduling queues
c-mh-v3-tournament.quote: a tournament scheme whereby each entry is compared with its neighbor, the winner of each pair being compared against the next pair

c-mh-v3-no-cwf-split.text: A 2018 patent suggests the memory system does not split multi-beat reads to send the critical word first
c-mh-v3-no-cwf-split.quote: suggest that there’s no attempt being made (yet?) to split multi-beat read transactions to allow for critical word first.
c-mh-v3-no-cwf-split.notes: From US10649922B2. Apple patented critical-word-first forwarding and splitting in 2010; Handley cannot tell whether either is used now

c-mh-v3-l1-l2-32b.text: The L1 to L2 path appears to be 32 B wide, moving 64 B L1 lines
c-mh-v3-l1-l2-32b.quote: the L1 to L2 width appears to be 32B (transferring 64B lines)

c-mh-v3-l2-line-128.text: The L2 line, and the line used across the rest of the SoC, appears to be 128 B
c-mh-v3-l2-line-128.quote: the L2 and System line width appears to be 128B

c-mh-v3-m1-dram-banks.text: The M1 has at least two DRAM banks in the sense of separately powerable DRAM devices; the Pro, Max and Ultra have more
c-mh-v3-m1-dram-banks.quote: on either the M1 (which has at least two such “banks”) to the Pro, Max, and Ultra, all providing ever more DRAM banks
c-mh-v3-m1-dram-banks.notes: He suggests Apple could power some down in a low-power mode, as a 2010 Intel Mac patent (US8799553B2) remaps memory on the fly; he does not know if it is used

c-mh-v3-dram-hash.text: Apple may combine address bits (a permutation hash) rather than extract fixed bits to pick the DRAM channel, rank and bank; a 2010 patent makes the interleave selection programmable
c-mh-v3-dram-hash.quote: Apple might employ more sophisticated addressing hashes than the basic “extract n bits from location m”
c-mh-v3-dram-hash.notes: From US20120137090A1, which lets the OS vary the permutation

c-mh-v3-slc-behind-mc.text: The SLC is owned and controlled by the memory controller and sits behind it, outside coherency; to every other block it looks like DRAM that responds faster
c-mh-v3-slc-behind-mc.quote: it's just a strange piece of DRAM that responds faster than normal DRAM.

c-mh-v3-three-generations.text: Apple's fabric has had three generations: a memory controller with almost no NoC (2010), a layered memory controller and NoC that adds the SLC (2012), and a third that moves much of the layering into the NoC
c-mh-v3-three-generations.quote: Moving functionality down into the NoC means that there are now fewer layers of queues
c-mh-v3-three-generations.notes: In the third generation each queue arbiter weighs more factors instead of one feature per layer

c-mh-v3-slc-a7.text: The SLC first appears in a 2012 patent; the A7 die shows a large SRAM block that is presumably the SLC, and the A6 has none
c-mh-v3-slc-a7.quote: The A7 die shot shows a large block of SRAM that is presumably the SLC; we do not see such a block on the A6 die.
c-mh-v3-slc-a7.notes: The patent is US20140059297A1, System cache with sticky allocation

c-mh-v3-2012-xbars.text: The 2012 NoC has at least two crossbar levels: a central switch feeding either an IO crossbar or a coherence crossbar between GPU and CPU
c-mh-v3-2012-xbars.quote: at least two cross-bar switch levels (a “central” level feeding out to either an IO crossbar or a “Coherence” crossbar that switches between GPU and CPU

c-mh-v3-duplicate-tags.text: The Coherence Point holds duplicate tags (line address and MOESI state) for every block's cache; for a two-level cache they mirror the L2
c-mh-v3-duplicate-tags.quote: So it has a set of Duplicate Tags ... If the cache has two levels, the tags describe the L2 contents
c-mh-v3-duplicate-tags.notes: A request that matches a duplicate tag is sent down to the owning cache; one that matches none goes on to the SLC

c-mh-v3-pseudo-l3.text: Where Intel's L3 holds tags and data and is inclusive, Apple's coherence point is a tag-only pseudo-L3 whose data stay in the blocks' own caches
c-mh-v3-pseudo-l3.quote: Apple constructs a pseudo-L3 as (tags+ [data is whatever’s in the various compute caches])

c-mh-v3-uncached-l2-ways.text: A read to an uncacheable IO range fetches a full line into the L2, but only a few L2 ways may hold such lines
c-mh-v3-uncached-l2-ways.quote: that full line is stored in the L2, but only a small number of ways of the L2 are allowed to hold the data.
c-mh-v3-uncached-l2-ways.notes: From US9043554B2; the lines are expected to stream with little reuse

c-mh-v3-uncached-write-gather.text: Writes to uncacheable ranges are gathered into full lines, which then go to the fabric bypassing L1 and L2
c-mh-v3-uncached-write-gather.quote: tries to gather them to a full cache line before the entire cache line is sent out.

c-mh-v3-flush-engine.text: Apple cores have a flush engine: the core can cut power at once while a lower-power block flushes modified L1 lines to the L2 before the L1 powers off
c-mh-v3-flush-engine.quote: allowing a lower power logic block to flush modified lines in the L1 to L2, before the L1 also cuts power.

c-mh-v3-remote-cache-slc.text: Unused or partly powered-down private caches, for example spare CPU L2, can extend the SLC, with the duplicate tags then acting as SLC tags
c-mh-v3-remote-cache-slc.quote: The idea is to use that private Compute Cache as an extension of the SLC, with the Duplicate tags now acting as SLC tags
c-mh-v3-remote-cache-slc.notes: From US9280471B2; Apple's example lends spare CPU L2 to the GPU

c-mh-v3-remote-cache-latency.text: Fetching a line from a remote private cache through the SLC might take about 50 ns, against about 100 ns to DRAM
c-mh-v3-remote-cache-latency.quote: maybe 50 ns or so (?) to get the data via a trip all the way to the SLC then rerouted to a private cache, rather than 100ns to DRAM
c-mh-v3-remote-cache-latency.notes: A guess, not a measurement. The 100 ns DRAM figure fits c-7cpu-dram-latency (L2 latency plus 91 ns)

c-mh-v3-slc-io-proxy.text: The SLC can act as a cache controller for small caches in IO blocks outside the coherence domain, turning one request into the simpler commands such a cache needs
c-mh-v3-slc-io-proxy.quote: creating a fake cache controller in the SLC to manage the IO cache
c-mh-v3-slc-io-proxy.hedge: what I think this 2016 patent is about

c-mh-v3-bw-controller.text: A central bandwidth management controller watches fabric statistics (latency, bandwidth use, queue depths) and tells limiter circuits in front of each IP block to slow down; it can also change fabric speed, with hysteresis
c-mh-v3-bw-controller.quote: central Bandwidth Management Controller that tracks various statistics related to the fabric

c-mh-v3-coherence-no-qos.text: In the 2012 design the Coherence Point ignores QoS and keeps short queues; most buffering sits in the QoS-ordered Switch, and credits pass among Switch, Coherence and memory controller so a request moves on only when a slot opens
c-mh-v3-coherence-no-qos.quote: So Apple drops worrying about QoS at the Coherence point. ... make the Coherence Point queues not very deep

c-mh-v3-buffer-at-source.text: The 2018 redesign moves most buffering out of the Switch into each source block, before requests enter the fabric
c-mh-v3-buffer-at-source.quote: the 2018 redesign, at which point the buffering mostly moves to the next stage, in each source ... before the data even is allowed into the Fabric.

c-mh-v3-two-pipelines.text: The 2012 design has two pipelines from Coherence through the SLC to the memory controller, split by hashed address (for example even and odd lines), each arbitrating only its own half
c-mh-v3-two-pipelines.quote: a striking pattern is the existence of two pipelines from Coherence through the SLC to the Memory Controller.
c-mh-v3-two-pipelines.notes: The split may extend to two memory channels. Barriers and the shared return path still tie the two pipelines together

c-mh-v3-eight-pipelines.text: The 2018 redesign splits the Coherence to SLC to memory controller path across 8 or more address-interleaved pipelines
c-mh-v3-eight-pipelines.quote: The 2018 redesign takes this far further, splitting across 8 or more such pipelines.
c-mh-v3-eight-pipelines.notes: A lower bound, not tied to a chip. Compare c-mh-v2-slc-even-odd, which splits the M1 SLC and memory controller into even and odd halves

c-mh-v3-display-qos.text: The display controller raises its request QoS when its local buffer runs low and lowers it once the buffer passes a safety level; a later patent moves the thresholds when the memory controller is busy
c-mh-v3-display-qos.quote: If the buffer fullness sinks too low, we increase QoS; then when the buffer fullness rises above a safety level, we reduce QoS.
c-mh-v3-display-qos.notes: From US8963938B2 and US9019291B2. Each request is kept at the lowest QoS that does the job so the memory controller can sort for bandwidth

c-mh-v3-merge-escalate.text: When the memory controller merges a new request with a queued one for the same line, it raises the queued request's priority so a high-QoS request does not wait at low priority
c-mh-v3-merge-escalate.quote: a high QoS request that comes in might be attached to a pre-existing low QoS request for that line, and then just sit in the queue at low priority!

c-mh-v3-victim-request.text: Besides reads and writes, a cache can send a victim request: the line moves from one cache to another (L2 to SLC) with ownership, and since it need not be dirty it need not reach DRAM
c-mh-v3-victim-request.quote: victim request (address, line of data, plus a flag saying “move ownership of this address+data from cache A to cache B”)

c-mh-v3-2012-cp-64.text: The 2012 Coherence Point has two queues, each a table of outstanding transactions; the patent's example holds 64, each with one address or two for a victim
c-mh-v3-2012-cp-64.quote: in the 2012 patent, the example given is 64 pending transactions

c-mh-v3-strands.text: The Coherence Point keeps same-address transactions in order by linking matching entries into lists (strands); only unlinked entries or list heads may move on to the SLC
c-mh-v3-strands.quote: If we find a match, we create a linked list of transactions, so that the earliest transaction points to the next later one
c-mh-v3-strands.notes: From US20140173218A1. Handley guesses the next item waits until the SLC confirms the one before

c-mh-v3-fabric-interrupts.text: Device interrupts become fabric messages ordered behind the device's earlier writes, so those writes are globally visible by the time the CPU takes the interrupt
c-mh-v3-fabric-interrupts.quote: the interrupt is converted into a fabric message, just like other fabric messages.

c-mh-v3-retry-queue.text: A cache such as the L2 or SLC links same-address requests and internal operations in a retry queue; scheduling by priority and age never breaks into a linked list
c-mh-v3-retry-queue.quote: a cache (think L2 or SLC) can have both external requests and internal operations (like flushing out data prior to powering down some part of the cache).

c-mh-v3-write-table.text: A requester's write buffer is split into a pending-request buffer holding data and a small write table holding hashed addresses of writes in flight, which later requests check for ordering
c-mh-v3-write-table.quote: the write buffer is now split into two buffers
c-mh-v3-write-table.notes: From US20220083369A1. A false hash match only delays an unrelated write by about a hundred cycles

c-mh-v3-victim-fill.text: Lines allocate in L1; an L1 victim moves to the L2 and an L2 victim moves to the SLC, so the L2 is a victim cache for L1 and the SLC holds L2 victims; prefetches into the L2 are the exception
c-mh-v3-victim-fill.quote: When a line in L1 is eventually replaced, it will be moved to L2 (ie L2 is a victim cache for L1), and likewise when a line in L2 is replaced, that line will be moved to SLC.
c-mh-v3-victim-fill.hedge: As far as I can tell
c-mh-v3-victim-fill.notes: Fits c-7cpu-slc-exclusive and the cached region past L2 out to ~16 MiB in c-mh-v2-slc-size

c-mh-v3-slc-pending.text: On a miss the SLC allocates the line at once in a pending state; later requests to it wait in a replay buffer until the data arrive, so no miss queue has to be searched
c-mh-v3-slc-pending.quote: the line is marked as “pending”. Then any subsequent request for this line will also see it as pending. All requests to pending lines go into a replay buffer

c-mh-v3-slc-device-alloc.text: By default, reads from blocks other than the CPU allocate their lines in the SLC, probably modulated for blocks with their own caches and for streaming flows
c-mh-v3-slc-device-alloc.quote: by default non-CPU requests are allocated in the SLC on read of a line

c-mh-v3-groupid-16.text: Requests carry a group (flow) ID; the 2012 sticky-allocation patent suggests 16 of them, 4 bits, perhaps more on newer chips
c-mh-v3-groupid-16.quote: this next patent suggests there are 16 of these, 4 bits, though of course this may have risen in more modern SoCs
c-mh-v3-groupid-16.hedge: this may have risen in more modern SoCs

c-mh-v3-slc-sticky.text: SLC lines record the requester's group ID and a sticky bit; a sticky line stays until it is marked non-sticky
c-mh-v3-slc-sticky.quote: lines marked as sticky will persist until they are marked non-sticky.

c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.text: SLC replacement takes an invalid line first, then an LRU dirty line, and otherwise a random line, drawing again if that line is sticky
c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.quote: first priority is to use invalid lines. Next in (negative) priority is LRU lines that are dirty. ... If it’s sticky, we generate a new random number and try again.
c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.value: invalid, then LRU dirty, then random non-sticky
c-mh-v3-slc-replacement.notes: Dirty LRU lines go first because a recently written line is less likely to be touched again than a recently read one

c-mh-v3-slc-frame-relabel.text: All SLC data of one GPU frame share a flow ID; for the next frame the GPU can relabel those lines to a new ID, or a hit by the new ID takes them over
c-mh-v3-slc-frame-relabel.quote: the GPU can tell the SLC to relabel all flowID X lines as now belonging to flowID Y
c-mh-v3-slc-frame-relabel.notes: Video capture, video decode and the display pipe use flow IDs the same way

c-mh-v3-slc-quotas.text: A group ID may have an SLC quota capping its lines, giving three levels of persistence: sticky lines, then the group's quota, then general replacement
c-mh-v3-slc-quotas.quote: groupIDs may have SLC quotas associated with them, so that given groupID cannot use more than a certain number of lines.
c-mh-v3-slc-quotas.notes: From US20140075118A1; quotas may oversubscribe the cache

c-mh-v3-slc-hints.text: Requests can carry SLC hints: do-not-allocate, de-allocate (a hit line becomes LRU dirty and goes first), and a per-group sticky-replace hint
c-mh-v3-slc-hints.quote: a do-not-allocate hint, which means what it says. ... a de-allocate hint. ... a (per flowID) sticky-replace hint.

c-mh-v3-cpu-no-slc-alloc.text: CPU and GPU misses never allocate lines in the SLC; the do-not-allocate hint is for other hardware blocks
c-mh-v3-cpu-no-slc-alloc.quote: I think this is for HW devices, and that CPU/GPU misses would never allocate in the SLC anyway.

c-mh-v3-quota-drop.text: When a quota is ended, its dirty lines can be invalidated without write-back, suiting per-frame scratch data such as shadow or normal textures
c-mh-v3-quota-drop.quote: dirty lines of a quota that has ended can simply be dropped by having every line invalidated, so they are not even written back to RAM.

c-mh-v3-slc-driver.text: An SLC driver sets the quotas: device drivers register their memory streams (data stream IDs) and properties with it
c-mh-v3-slc-driver.quote: Based on this information, the SLC Driver determines the quotas (and other options) for the SLC.

c-mh-v3-slc-driver-goal.text: The SLC driver sizes quotas to cut DRAM traffic, in effect energy, using each stream's hits per second per quota line and rebalancing coarsely; Handley thinks a marginal-gain rule would do better
c-mh-v3-slc-driver-goal.quote: it's optimizing for reducing the traffic that has to go to DRAM rather than hitting in the SLC (which is essentially optimizing for energy).

c-mh-v3-slc-purpose.text: The SLC is built mainly for low-energy communication between blocks; the system still uses it as an L3 for the CPU when nothing else needs it
c-mh-v3-slc-purpose.quote: The SLC should be seen primarily as a means to facilitate communication at lower energy.

c-mh-v3-spec-read-2012.text: In the 2012 design a read may enter the memory controller queues during the SLC tag lookup, if it has low-latency QoS, no ordering hazard, few speculative reads ahead of it and a group ID unlikely to hit in the SLC
c-mh-v3-spec-read-2012.quote: while a read request is performing the SLC Tags lookup, the request is also allowed to move to (entry to) the Memory Controller Queues.
c-mh-v3-spec-read-2012.notes: From US9201796B2. The read goes no further down the queues until the SLC miss is confirmed

c-mh-v3-partial-dirty.text: The 2012 SLC keeps partial-line writes in a partial-dirty state, reusing the line's ECC bits as a byte mask; a read that hits such a line forces a merge through DRAM
c-mh-v3-partial-dirty.quote: we re-purpose the ECC bits protecting the line as a bitmask describing which bytes of the line (for a partial dirty line) are valid.
c-mh-v3-partial-dirty.notes: From US20140089602A1. Handley expects newer designs to have explicit mask bits

c-mh-v3-coherency-bypass.text: A read starts down the memory controller pipeline before coherence is resolved, and the SLC tag check runs in parallel with entry to the DRAM queues; the read is killed if either check hits
c-mh-v3-coherency-bypass.quote: once in the Memory Controller we then begin the SLC tag checking in parallel with moving the request on to the Memory Controller DRAM queues.
c-mh-v3-coherency-bypass.notes: From US10802968B2, the third step after the 2012 and 2013 speculative-read patents

c-mh-v3-dt-split.text: The duplicate tags are split into a single-ported tag RAM, mostly read, and a dual-ported state RAM for the frequently changing MOESI bits
c-mh-v3-dt-split.quote: And so what was a single SRAM structure gets split into two parts, each optimized for its particular task.

c-mh-v3-2013-ccu.text: In 2013 the Coherence Point is split by address into two units, CCU A and B, and a modified line passing from one CPU to another goes through it
c-mh-v3-2013-ccu.quote: requests come into the Coherence point and are split (by address) between the two units CCU A and B which look at the Duplicate Tags.
c-mh-v3-2013-ccu.notes: From US20140192801A1; Handley says later designs improve the copyback path

c-mh-v3-cmd-data-pack.text: Commands and data travel on separate wires; a line takes two data beats, and the return arbiter pairs a short command with the second beat of a long one
c-mh-v3-cmd-data-pack.quote: transfer of commands goes down one set of wires, transfer of data down a second set of wires
c-mh-v3-cmd-data-pack.hedge: Perhaps, again at this stage, the standard line length is 64B, and the data fabric width is 32B?

c-mh-v3-line-change.text: Around 2015 the L2 line, and probably the line across the rest of the SoC, changed from 64 B to 128 B
c-mh-v3-line-change.quote: around 2015 I think, the line length for L2 (and I think the rest of the SoC outside the core) changes from 64B to 128B.
c-mh-v3-line-change.notes: He cannot tell whether the data fabric widened to 64 B (two beats per line) or stayed at 32 B (four beats)

c-mh-v3-rowhammer.text: The memory controller detects and handles Rowhammer-style repeated row accesses
c-mh-v3-rowhammer.quote: a modification of the Memory Controller to detect and handle Rowhammer type security attacks

c-mh-v3-phy-calibration.text: The memory controller PHY calibrates its read delay and reference voltage at run time and recalibrates periodically, so DRAM can run at slightly lower voltage or refresh slightly less often
c-mh-v3-phy-calibration.quote: Optimizing this signal detection allows the DRAM either to run at slightly lower voltage, or to go slightly longer before being refreshed.
c-mh-v3-phy-calibration.notes: From US9477259B2 and US10019387B2; earlier designs looked offsets up in tables

c-mh-v3-slc-way-power.text: The SLC tracks how much of its capacity is really in use and powers down ways to match; a later version adds hysteresis and staggered power-up
c-mh-v3-slc-way-power.quote: track how large a fraction of the SLC is “really” being used - limit the number of active ways to match that fraction
c-mh-v3-slc-way-power.notes: From US9218040B2 and US8984227B2. The SLC version predates the similar L2 scheme

c-mh-v3-slc-drowsy.text: SLC SRAMs sit on separate voltage planes at retention voltage when idle; requests to a sleeping region are gathered and served together once enough arrive or enough time passes
c-mh-v3-slc-drowsy.quote: Individual SRAMs are on independent voltage planes and can be powered down to a retention voltage when not being accessed.
c-mh-v3-slc-drowsy.notes: From US8977817B2. Delaying requests is acceptable at this level of cache, not in an L1 or L2

c-mh-v3-slc-drowsy-qos.text: In the later drowsy scheme high-QoS requests are never delayed; each sector wakes on a timer to serve low-QoS requests and returns to retention after an idle interval
c-mh-v3-slc-drowsy-qos.quote: We start with the obvious decision that high QoS requests are not delayed.

c-mh-v3-split-paths.text: Write data is stored once in a buffer at fabric entry and moved once to the SLC or DRAM; only the small control packet, holding a pointer to the data, is routed and arbitrated
c-mh-v3-split-paths.quote: the data payload (which can be large, eg 64B or 128B) is written once to a buffer, then moved once from that buffer to either the SLC or DRAM.
c-mh-v3-split-paths.notes: From US9860841B2, which Handley places at the A9 or A10. IO and CPU data use separate buffers

c-mh-v3-return-no-coherence.text: Most return traffic from the memory controller does not pass through Coherence
c-mh-v3-return-no-coherence.quote: Some simplifications are possible because most of the return packets from the Memory Controller do not need to pass through Coherence.

c-mh-v3-pio-network.text: A second network, the PIO network, carries device-memory and most uncacheable requests; it is not snooped and does not pass through the SLC or memory controller
c-mh-v3-pio-network.quote: there is a whole second network on the SoC, called the PIO network. ... The PIO network is not snooped
c-mh-v3-pio-network.hedge: I think the best way to think of PIO is
