c-mh-v8-a15-adr-rename.quote: ADR/ADRP, used to access global data, made faster (now handled at Rename, like MOV immediate)
c-mh-v8-a15-adr-rename.notes: From Dougall Johnson's list; on the M1 adr and adrp are not eliminated (c-dj-mov-elim)

c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.text: Icestorm, the M1's E core, is four wide; its A15 successor Blizzard widens this to five
c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.quote: Blizzard (the small core) is now 5-wide rather than 4-wide
c-mh-v8-icestorm-4wide.notes: Implied by Dougall Johnson's A15 finding as Handley relays it

c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.text: The A15/M2 E core (Blizzard) is five wide, with a ROB about 33% larger than its predecessor's
c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.quote: Blizzard (the small core) is now 5-wide rather than 4-wide, with a 33% larger ROB
c-mh-v8-a15-blizzard.notes: E core, from Dougall Johnson's list

c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.text: Icestorm's ROB holds about 60 racks, each rack being 7 slots of which one may hold a failable instruction
c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.quote: For the basic ROB rack (unit of 7 slots, one of which can be a failable instruction) we have ... for E cores: about 60 for M1
c-mh-v8-icestorm-rob-60.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings. The same list gives about 330 for the M1 P core, as in retire.groups

c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.text: The A15 P core's ROB holds about 290 racks, against about 330 on the M1
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.quote: for P cores: about 330 for M1, 290 for A15, and 270 for A16
c-mh-v8-a15-rob-290.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings

c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.text: The A16 P core's ROB holds about 270 racks, against about 330 on the M1
c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.quote: for P cores: about 330 for M1, 290 for A15, and 270 for A16
c-mh-v8-a16-rob-270.notes: Handley does not say who measured the rack counts; the section relays Dougall Johnson's findings

c-mh-v8-a15-ecore-rob-75.text: The A15 E core's ROB holds about 75 racks, against about 60 on Icestorm
c-mh-v8-a15-ecore-rob-75.quote: for E cores: about 60 for M1, 75 for A15, and 108 for A16

c-mh-v8-a16-ecore-rob-108.text: The A16 E core's ROB holds about 108 racks, against about 60 on Icestorm
c-mh-v8-a16-ecore-rob-108.quote: for E cores: about 60 for M1, 75 for A15, and 108 for A16

c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.text: Despite the smaller P-core rack counts on the A15 and A16, Dougall Johnson's NOP measurement still gives 7 instructions per rack
c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.quote: Although dougall suggests this is not the case, that NOP measurement still gives a 1:7 ratio
c-mh-v8-a16-rack-7.notes: Handley wonders whether the ROB was split into separate failable and non-failable parts so the total could shrink at the same 1:7 ratio

c-mh-v8-noc-networks.text: Per a 2021 patent, the NoC is split into several independent address+data networks, for example IO (ordered, coherent, high latency), CPU (ordered, coherent, low latency) and GPU/NPU/ISP (relaxed order, non-coherent)
c-mh-v8-noc-networks.quote: Split the existing NoC (which is already multiple networks, for address vs data, with a separate network for IO/interrupts) into multiple “address+data” networks.
c-mh-v8-noc-networks.notes: US20220334997A1; the networks may also differ in topology

c-mh-v8-mc-hash-bits.text: Per a 2021 patent, physical addresses are hashed across the memory controllers so sequential streams spread widely, and each routing step (chip, slice, row, side, then inside the controller) drops the address bits it has used
c-mh-v8-mc-hash-bits.quote: the physical memory address space is hashed then spread over multiple memory controllers ... the address bit(s) that forced that routing decision are dropped

c-mh-v8-mc-shutdown.text: Per the same patent, on-chip logic reports how busy each memory controller is to the OS, which can shut idle controllers down after moving their remaining pages, or leave their DRAM in self-refresh
c-mh-v8-mc-shutdown.quote: certain memory controllers can be shut down (to save energy, of course) in low usage situations

c-mh-v8-power-levels.text: Per a 2021 patent, power is managed at four time scales: clock dithering against undervolt events at about 150 cycles, then frequency from current tracking, then voltage per island, then temperature
c-mh-v8-power-levels.quote: On the fastest time scale (which is still of the order of ~150 cycles) we see that the primary goal is to respond to an undervolt (UVD) event.
c-mh-v8-power-levels.notes: US20220137692A1; the patent lets each level tell the central controller what it plans next

c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.text: Per a 2021 patent, the memory controller's bank selection now weighs each requester's bandwidth QoS as well as its latency QoS, so a requester confined to one bank still gets bandwidth
c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.quote: coupling, to some extent, the bank selection stage to the virtual channel selection stage based not only on an ... latency QoS but also on an ... bandwidth QoS
c-mh-v8-mc-gen4.notes: US20220357879A1 (Memory Bank Hotspotting); Handley calls it a step toward a fourth-generation controller

c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.text: The M3 Pro has about 150 GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, from three memory channels
c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.quote: the M3 Pro has ~150GB/s of DRAM bandwidth, corresponding to three “memory channels”
c-mh-v8-m3pro-dram-150.notes: Handley gives no source for the figure; die shots show two DRAM packages on one side and one on the other

c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.text: Per a 2021 patent, real-time requests get a separate transaction table in the memory controller with their own DRAM bandwidth credits
c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.quote: The separate real time queue comes with separate DRAM bandwidth credits
c-mh-v8-mc-rt-credits.notes: US20230060508A1; Handley guesses the GPUs of the M1 Pro and Max could otherwise hog DRAM bandwidth

c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.text: Two 2023 patents are the first Apple memory-controller patents to handle DRAM ranks, grouping requests by rank and staying on one rank when bandwidth matters
c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.quote: these are the first Apple Memory Controller patents I have seen that reference rank!
c-mh-v8-mc-ranks.notes: US20240095194A1 and US20240094917A1; Handley reads them as a route to larger DRAM capacity

c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.text: The M3 Pro has three SLC and memory-controller units, not four, so addresses must be routed by a factor of three
c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.quote: the M3 Pro now comes with three, not four, SLC’s and memory controllers
c-mh-v8-m3pro-three-slc.notes: A 2023 routing patent (US20240104017A1) shows how to route by multiples of 3 (and 15)

c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.text: Per a 2022 patent, a physical address range can be marked real-time: its lines may be reserved in the L1, L2 and SLC and its NoC transactions get maximum priority
c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.quote: mark some lines in the various caches (L1, L2, SLC) as reserved for realtime lines, and we can give NoC transactions to these addresses maximum priority
c-mh-v8-realtime-lines.notes: US11886340B1; Handley links it to the Vision Pro

c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.text: Per a patent extending one that masks zero bytes on NoC transfers, caches track common data patterns and send a pattern index instead of the data
c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.quote: when such a pattern needs to be transferred, the pattern index can be ... rather than the data
c-mh-v8-zero-pattern.notes: US11442855B2; Handley reads a figure as mapping some addresses into a pattern space, which would give zero-content pages but not zero-content lines

c-mh-v8-slc-states.text: SLC lines need only Invalid, Modified and Valid states; Exclusive and Shared are not needed because no requester inside the SLC modifies data
c-mh-v8-slc-states.quote: cache lines only requires states like Invalid, Modified, and Valid. States like Exclusive or Shared are about some ... within the cache

c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.text: Handley guesses SLC lines are about 512 B, run as a sectored cache with one tag and per-sector valid flags, for example four 128 B sectors
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.quote: SLC cache lines are probably long. My guess is that they perhaps 512B long
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.hedge: My guess is that they perhaps
c-mh-v8-slc-line-512.notes: There is no SLC line param; c-7cpu-slc-line and c-mh-v2-l2-line-128-bw give 128 B for the SLC, which would match one sector here

c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.text: Per a 2021 patent, each SLC half-line has a 3-bit state; a partial state marks invalid granules (say 8 B), and the line is shifted to free room for per-granule valid and modified masks
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.quote: split the cache line into two halves, upper and lower. Each half gets three bits of tag, so eight states are available.
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.hedge: I’m somewhat guessing the exact numbers used by Apple
c-mh-v8-slc-partial-valid.notes: US20220365881A1; Handley thinks the main use is remote atomics executed in the SLC

c-mh-v8-l1d-no-way-mispredict.text: Tests show no L1D way prediction, or else a predictor that stays perfect even on a random stream of accesses
c-mh-v8-l1d-no-way-mispredict.quote: Experimentally there seems to be no way prediction for the L1D (or whatever they are doing seems to be a perfect predictor even when one tries to generate a random stream of accesses!)

c-mh-v8-way-confirm.text: Per a 2021 patent, the way predictor keeps a copy of the predicted way's tag, and a per-line bit cleared on eviction or a TLB change lets a repeat hit skip the cache tag compare
c-mh-v8-way-confirm.quote: so we’ve basically replaced transporting and comparing a tag (multiple bits, perhaps 40 or so) with a single bit
c-mh-v8-way-confirm.notes: US11487667B1; Handley thinks it suits I-caches best

c-mh-v8-l1-plru.text: Apple's L1 replacement is at least pseudo-LRU, possibly full LRU tracking
c-mh-v8-l1-plru.quote: Apple is definitely doing something at least pseudo-LRU-like, possibly fully LRU tracking.
c-mh-v8-l1-plru.notes: No method given. Differs from vol 2's reading that an L1D line's way comes from physical page bits (c-mh-v2-l1d-way-hash)

c-mh-v8-critical-lines.text: Per a 2022 patent, L2 lines carry a criticality field that travels with the line to the L1 and the SLC (where the DSID field is reused); page-table leaves and the heads of the I-fetch and load miss queues are critical
c-mh-v8-critical-lines.quote: lines in the L2 have an additional field that describes how “critical” they are. This field moves around with the line as it travels down to L1 or out to SLC

c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.text: Per the same patent, the L2 uses strict LRU and places new lines at chosen points in the order, keeping critical lines longer and letting non-temporal or unused prefetched lines go first
c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.quote: the L2 uses a strict LRU scheme, but then uses the ideas suggested above to place new lines in an “appropriate” place in the LRU ordering
c-mh-v8-l2-lru-patent.notes: US20230060225A1 (2022). Differs from the random replacement Handley inferred for the M1 L2 (c-mh-v2-l2-random-repl); the patent postdates the M1

c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.text: Per a 2022 patent, one controller watches L1 and L2 metrics (prefetch usefulness, pointer-chase hit rates, thrashing) and adjusts prefetch aggressiveness, L1 write allocation and the L1 insertion policy
c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.quote: We have the sort of total control we have come to expect from Apple, a single controller that’s tracking both L1 and L2 and collecting various metrics.
c-mh-v8-thrash-detect.notes: US11886354B1; when thrashing, writes may go to L2 instead of allocating in L1

c-mh-v8-variable-latency.text: Per a 2022 patent, a large cache can have a hit latency that depends on distance, about one cycle to the nearest blocks and four to the farthest, with far blocks winning return collisions to bound the worst case
c-mh-v8-variable-latency.quote: they suggest that reasonable values for current caches are the nearest blocks are one cycle away, the farthest blocks four cycles away
c-mh-v8-variable-latency.notes: US11893241B1; Handley discusses it as a way to keep a large SLC fast

c-mh-v8-slc-quota.text: The SLC has long enforced per-client quotas; per a 2022 patent, quotas are now adjusted each epoch from usage statistics such as traffic and hit rates
c-mh-v8-slc-quota.quote: track these various statistics over some epoch, and at the end of each epoch adjust quotas to reflect the patterns just seen
c-mh-v8-slc-quota.notes: US11914521B1; the patent says the scheme also applies to L1 and L2

c-mh-v8-age-tracking.text: Per a 2018 patent, scheduler entries hold short age offsets from a base timestamp, and the older-or-younger bitmaps across pipelines needed for a flush are built only when a flush happens
c-mh-v8-age-tracking.quote: a short offset relative to a base timestamp is used for the timestamp of an instruction within the scheduling queue
c-mh-v8-age-tracking.hedge: As far as I can tell

c-mh-v8-writeback-pool.text: Per a 2021 patent, results beyond the register file's write ports go to a temporary pool and drain later instead of stalling; six integer results plus three load pairs would need 12 writes in one cycle
c-mh-v8-writeback-pool.quote: all six integer execution units generate a result, along with three load pair instructions. In theory this means we need to write back 6 + 2*3=12results in one cycle

c-mh-v8-fill-forward.text: Apple cores forward fill data to waiting loads: once a missed line is known to be coming, the load is scheduled and its bytes go to the LSU as the line fills the L1, perhaps two or three cycles sooner
c-mh-v8-fill-forward.quote: the Apple cores implement fill-forwarding. ... This presumably knocks two or three cycles off the latency.
c-mh-v8-fill-forward.notes: Described as a side issue in US20230011446A1 (2021)

c-mh-v8-fadd-m1.text: A chain of dependent FADDs runs at one billion per second on the M1, matching a 3-cycle FADD latency
c-mh-v8-fadd-m1.quote: On M1 the latency of FADD is 3 cycles and frequency is 3GHz, so we expect, and see, 1B instructions per second of this stream.

c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.text: On the M3 the same dependent FADD chain runs at 1.6 billion per second; Handley guesses back-to-back fusion cuts a dependent FADD pair from 6 to 5 cycles, which with the 4:3 clock ratio gives 1.6x
c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.quote: For M3 the performance is 1.6B instructions per second ... reduce the latency for dependent pairs of FADDs from 6 to 5 cycles
c-mh-v8-m3-fadd-fusion.notes: Handley does not say who ran the M3 test; he compares IBM POWER10's back-to-back fusion

c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.text: The M1 has no load-op or op-store fusion
c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.quote: one set of fusions that was missing from M1 was load-op and op-store fusions
c-mh-v8-m1-no-load-op-fusion.notes: Aside with no method; adds to the unfused pairs listed in c-dj-no-fusion

c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.text: Per a 2022 patent, a small ALU in the load/store unit applies an op to the loaded value, fusing loads with ADD, XOR, shifts and rotates, and with CBZ or TBZ but not flag-setting compares
c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.quote: having a small ALU within the load/store unit which can execute the ALU op directly on the loaded value while it’s still in the load/store unit
c-mh-v8-load-op-patent.notes: US12008369B1; branch details sit in a Fusion Table indexed by the unused second-register field of the load-pair encoding

c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.text: In the load-op fusion patent the load and op need only be decoded in the same cycle, not be adjacent, and the fused pair may return both the loaded value and the op result
c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.quote: First the load and op do not need to be adjacent! As long as they are in the same decode group (ie decoded in the same cycle) the fusion will happen.
c-mh-v8-load-op-rules.notes: As of 2024, LLVM's M4 model listed no load-op fusion pattern

c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.text: Per a 2023 patent, TAGE-style load value or address prediction keeps its prediction tables in the front end, read around rename, and its training tables in the load/store unit
c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.quote: One, prediction table, sits in the front end, able to provide values at around Rename time. The other, training table, sits in the Load/Store unit.
c-mh-v8-tage-lvp-patent.notes: US12159142B1; only table indices, not full history, are sent down the pipe

c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.text: The M4 P core still executes at most three loads per cycle
c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.quote: the back end is (still, as of the M4) set up to handle only three loads per cycle
c-mh-v8-m4-three-loads.notes: Aside with no method; the same limit as the M1 (lsu.loads_per_cycle)

c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.text: Per a 2022 patent, a fetch-predictor field lets fetch run through a predicted-taken short forward branch whose target is in the same fetch group, up to about 16 instructions, and drop the skipped instructions
c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.quote: at essentially any length of branch where the branch and the target sit within the same possible Fetch Group (ie are within up to ~16 instructions of each other)
c-mh-v8-sfb-patent.notes: US20240028339A1; skipped instructions are removed between the I-cache and the fetch queue

c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.text: Per the same patent, a short backward loop is duplicated in the fetch queue so one fetch supplies two iterations
c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.quote: We have now duplicated the loop body within the Fetch Queue. Essentially one Fetch has given us two iterations round the loop
c-mh-v8-short-loop-unroll.notes: US20240028339A1; an odd trip count is fixed by the slower predictors without a full flush

c-mh-v8-return-fetch-stack.text: Per the same patent, a Return Fetch Stack, about one entry for now, keeps the instructions after a short call so the return needs no second fetch
c-mh-v8-return-fetch-stack.quote: pretty much a single entry “stack” for now, to be used (again based on data being tracked in the Fetch Predictor Table) only for cases of a short call

c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.text: Before the 2022 return-fetch patents, the trace after a return was not held in the fetch predictor, so fetch after a return assumed the maximum length and discarded the excess
c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.quote: The patent says that the trace following a return is currently not stored in the Fetch Predictor, and so after a return we have to proceed as though the trace is unknown
c-mh-v8-return-trace-not-stored.notes: US11941401B1. Corrects Handley's earlier assumption that the M1 kept return fetch parameters; he guesses the fetch state machine was too complex. See c-mh-v4-nfp-return-table, c-mh-v4-return-bubble

c-mh-v8-return-params.text: Per a 2022 patent, the fetch-predictor entry for the code after a call goes either onto the RAS with the return address (faster) or into a separate table indexed by the return address (less energy)
c-mh-v8-return-params.quote: This stores Return Fetch Parameters in a separate piece of storage that is indexed by the return address.
c-mh-v8-return-params.hedge: if I have the big picture correct
c-mh-v8-return-params.notes: US11941401B1; Handley suggests the faster scheme for P cores and the other for E cores

c-mh-v8-bp-bank-hint.text: Per the same patent, the fetch predictor records which branch-predictor bank holds a branch's data, so only that bank wakes to confirm the branch
c-mh-v8-bp-bank-hint.quote: the Fetch Predictor stores the appropriate bank holding data for this particular branch and sends it to the Branch Predictor, so only that particular bank needs to wake up

c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.text: AMX instructions issue through the store pipelines, at most two per cycle, and wait in the store queue until they are non-speculative and passed to the AMX unit
c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.quote: Instructions are passed through the STORE pipeline (meaning a maximum of two per cycle can be issued) and sit in the store queue until they are shifted to the AMX unit.
c-mh-v8-amx-store-pipe.notes: Matches Johnson's AMX roles for load/store units 7 and 8 (c-dj-ls-units)

c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.text: The AMX unit holds four logical register sets, one for each of the four cores it serves
c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.quote: We have four logical sets of registers in AMX for each of the four client CPUs.
c-mh-v8-amx-reg-sets.notes: Aside with no method; a 2021 patent (US20230095072A1) renames registers of idle clients into a shared pool

c-mh-v8-abandonable-requests.text: Per an Apple patent, each cache request carries an abandonable flag (prefetches, instruction fetches and speculative loads are abandonable), so on an interrupt the cache may drop those requests and the core drains faster
c-mh-v8-abandonable-requests.quote: every load (more precisely every cache request) sent to the cache now has an additional field added which notes whether the request is “abandonable”

c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.text: The L2, L2 TLB, page walkers, LZ engine and AMX are shared by the cores of a cluster, and all cores of a cluster run at one frequency
c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.quote: the shared hardware (L2, L2 TLB, page walkers, LZ engine, AMX, etc) ... all cores in a cluster have to share the same frequency
c-mh-v8-cluster-shared.notes: A firmer statement than c-mh-v2-tlb2-per-cluster and c-mh-v2-tlb2-shared-guess, which lacked direct evidence; no evidence is given here either. The shared clock matches c-mh-v3-cluster-one-freq

c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.text: The M3 Pro and M3 Max have six-core P-clusters
c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.quote: The M3 Pro and Max implement a 6-core P-cluster.
c-mh-v8-m3pro-6core.notes: Aside with no method; the M1 cluster has 4 (pcluster.cores)

c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster.text: The M1 and M2 have one AMX unit per P-cluster; the M1 Pro, with two P-clusters, has two
c-mh-v8-amx-per-cluster.quote: A single unit would represent the same design as M1 and M2

c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.text: Peak large-matrix FP64 DGEMM on one M1 AMX unit is about 300 GFLOPS, twice that on an M1 Pro or Max with two units
c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.quote: Peak DGEMM (FP64) large matrix multiple performance on a single M1 AMX unit is around 300GFLOPS, so twice that on an M1 Pro or Max.
c-mh-v8-amx-m1-dgemm.notes: Handley points to Philip Turner's amx-benchmarks, run on an M1 Max with two AMX units

c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.text: One M2 AMX unit reaches about 350 GFLOPS on large FP64 matrix multiplies
c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.quote: refers to an M2, and has that large matrix multiple performance on a single AMX unit as more like 350GFLOPS
c-mh-v8-m2-amx-350.notes: From slides of a BLIS Retreat 2023 talk (GemmFIP-ExoLang)

c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.text: Code reaching about 600 GFLOPS on an M1 Max reaches about 800 GFLOPS on an M3 Max, about the clock ratio, so the M3 Max has two AMX units, one per P-cluster
c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.quote: code that achieved about 600GLOPS on an M1 Max achieves 800GFLOPS on an M3 Max, which is more or less what we would expect from frequency scaling
c-mh-v8-m3max-amx.notes: The GFLOPS figures come from a Twitter thread by Gabriel Baraldi

c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.text: The M3 Pro has one AMX unit, yet Howard Oakley found small-matrix and FFT Accelerate calls consistently faster on it than on the two-unit M1 Pro
c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.quote: the M3 Pro (which we have concluded has just one AMX unit) was consistently faster than the M1 Pro (two AMX units)
c-mh-v8-m3pro-amx-one.notes: Handley credits AMX improvements outside the outer-product peak, which scales only with clock

c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.text: Used as an outer-product engine, an AMX unit computes a full 8x8 (64-product) outer product each cycle, so its peak grows only with clock
c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.quote: when the AMX unit is used as an outer product engine, calculating a full 8×8→64 outer ... every cycle, it can only scale faster by the GHz ratio
c-mh-v8-amx-outer-8x8.notes: Said of AMX units from the M1 to the M3

c-mh-v8-faster-isb.text: Per a 2022 patent, an ISB can flush and refetch younger instructions once the relevant older work is done, without waiting to reach the head of the ROB
c-mh-v8-faster-isb.quote: we don’t have to wait until the ISB is the first instruction in the ROB before we execute the flush and reload of all subsequent instructions

c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.text: The M1 has no load address prediction: Handley's tests found none, and the SLAP paper reports strided address prediction only from the M2/A15 on
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.quote: my tests were not ideal) that it was not present in the M1 ... Strided Address Prediction has been available since the M2/A15
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.hedge: though possibly my tests were not ideal
c-mh-v8-m1-no-lap.notes: Confirms c-mh-v1-no-addr-prediction and c-mh-v2-no-address-prediction with an outside source (SLAP, Kim et al. 2025)

c-mh-v8-m2-lap.text: The SLAP paper reports strided load address prediction on the P cores from the M2/A15 on, and not on the E cores
c-mh-v8-m2-lap.quote: Strided Address Prediction has been available since the M2/A15 ... this fanciness is reserved for the the P core, and is not present on the E core
c-mh-v8-m2-lap.notes: Dougall Johnson's A15 list also notes better memory latency in some cases, which Handley ties to this

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp.text: The FLOP paper reports load value prediction on the P cores from the M3/A17 Pro on
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp.quote: tells us that Load Value Prediction has been available since the M3/A17 Pro

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.text: Load value prediction tracks up to about 72 distinct load PCs, in what looks like a 4-way table indexed by a hash of the PC
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.quote: up to about 72 different loads (ie distinct PC’s pointing to a load instruction) can be tracked, in what looks like a 4-way associative table indexed by a hash of the PC
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-entries.notes: Handley's reading of the FLOP paper's results

c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.text: About 250 matching loads are needed before a load value is trusted for value prediction
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.quote: It looks like the system required about 250 successful loads before it latches a particular load value as trustworthy
c-mh-v8-m3-lvp-train.notes: Handley thinks the paper's shorter runs (60, 120, 180 loads) come from training-slot reuse in its test code

c-mh-v8-lap-stride.text: Load address prediction needs about 120 to 500 matching loads before it is trusted, and handles strides of about -256 to 256
c-mh-v8-lap-stride.quote: we seem to require about 120..500 successive loads before the predictor is trusted, and the stride can be (something like)between -256 and 256
c-mh-v8-lap-stride.notes: Handley's reading of the SLAP paper's plots; value is the largest stride magnitude

c-mh-v8-m2-lap-train.text: Load address prediction training takes about 120 loads on the M2
c-mh-v8-m2-lap-train.quote: the training time jumped from ~120 for the M2 to ~320 for the M3

c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.text: Load address prediction training takes about 320 loads on the M3, up from about 120 on the M2
c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.quote: the training time jumped from ~120 for the M2 to ~320 for the M3
c-mh-v8-m3-lap-train.notes: Handley wonders whether the M3's shared value and address training table changed the counts

c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.text: Apple's 2019 load address prediction patent suggests a 6-bit confidence counter, so a pattern latches after 62 or 63 matches
c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.quote: The original 2019 patent suggests a 6bit counter, with one or two values having special meaning, so that only 62 or 63 successive matches are required to latch a pattern.
c-mh-v8-lap-patent-6bit.notes: Linked to the predictor found from the M2/A15 on; the M1 has none

c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.text: SLAP found load address prediction on the iPhone 13 mini but not on the iPhone 13, though both use the A15
c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.quote: Load Address Prediction is present in the iPhone 13 Mini but not in the iPhone 13
c-mh-v8-a15-lap-stepping.notes: Handley guesses an early A15 stepping had the feature off or broken

c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.text: All cores of an Apple cluster run at one frequency, apart from sleeping cores, so reaching the L2 or another core never crosses a clock domain; a SoC-wide controller sets each cluster's frequency, voltage and L2 power savings
c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.quote: Apple (at least to the extent they describe things in patents) provide a power budget for a cluster ... The whole reason we run the Apple cluster at a single frequency (apart from sleeping cores)
c-mh-v8-cluster-one-clock.notes: Agrees with c-mh-v3-cluster-one-freq. Said while contrasting Nuvia's per-cluster power controllers.

c-mh-v8-virtual-alloc.text: Apple already appears to give out ordering identifiers at rename and the physical load/store queue slot only at execution
c-mh-v8-virtual-alloc.quote: ordering identifiers (which are just numbers) at Allocate, and allocating the ultimate resource at the point of execution. We've seen that Apple already seem to be doing this with LSU slots

c-mh-v8-three-engines.text: Apple now seems to run instruction prefetch, fetch and full branch prediction as three decoupled address-generation engines
c-mh-v8-three-engines.quote: Apple seem to now be using three decoupled address-generation engines to perform I-fetch/branch prediction.
c-mh-v8-three-engines.notes: Said in a summary written around the Neoverse V2 launch, so no chip is named. The M1 goes only as far as an instruction queue (c-mh-v4-decoupled-iq).

c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.text: Apple's data prefetchers track addresses in virtual space and train on every load and store, in order, at the LSU rather than on the stream of L1 misses
c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.quote: Apple have the same functionality (tracking in virtual space, not physical space; Apple are ahead in capturing all load/stores in order at the LSU
c-mh-v8-prefetch-lsu.notes: Restates c-mh-v2-prefetch-at-lsu. He ranks Apple and Arm's Neoverse V2 about level on prefetch algorithms.

c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.text: Apple's AMPM prefetcher covers the cases of SMS and best-offset prefetching, and its content-directed prefetcher is a stronger form of a correlated miss cache for walking pointer structures
c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.quote: My understanding is that Apple's AMPM scheme handles the same sort of cases as SMS ... and BO (fancy version of a next line prefetcher); and Apple's Content Directed Prefetcher is a more powerful form of CMC
c-mh-v8-prefetch-kinds.notes: Consistent with c-mh-v2-prefetch-kinds, which also lists a large-stride prefetcher.

c-mh-v8-cdp-lsu.text: Training at the LSU lets Apple's prefetching use the values loaded, not only addresses, to spot pointer chasing early; this comes from the 2016 content-directed prefetch patent, whose filtering step seems to need LSU information
c-mh-v8-cdp-lsu.quote: if you do your prefetching based on what you see at the LSU (as Apple does, but apparently no-one else) you can also train on the content of what is loaded

c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.text: After the L2 has been powered down and lost its contents, Apple runs the prefetchers more aggressively once it powers up again
c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.quote: the way Apple runs the prefetchers more aggressively after the L2 cache is powered up after having been powered down and lost its contents
c-mh-v8-prefetch-wake.notes: Given as existing Apple behaviour with no chip named. The deny-list patent repeats it for a CPU waking from sleep with empty caches (c-mh-v8-deny-list-ration).

c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.text: Eyeballing published SPEC2017 results, the M1 and M2 are mostly slightly ahead of Arm's Neoverse V2 on IPC, but not dramatically
c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.quote: Apple is mostly still slightly ahead on IPC (as of M1 and M2), but not dramatically so
c-mh-v8-spec-ipc-v2.notes: Apple results from the TomyLemon Apple-CPU-Benchmarks collection. Large x264 and exchange2 leads he puts down to compilers.

c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.text: Geekbench 6 single-thread scores, averaged over devices, rise 1.62x from M1 to M4 (1.12x, 1.20x and 1.21x per generation); SPEC2017 shows about the same 60% gain
c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.quote: Overall 1.12 1.20 1.21 1.62 ... SPEC2017 numbers basically replicate this pattern of ~60% improvement from M1 to M4.
c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.notes: Mostly iPads, with an iMac for the M3. Pro, Max and Ultra parts run 0.1 to 0.2 GHz higher and, with their larger SLC, score 2 to 3% more.

c-mh-v8-ghz-m1-m4.text: Clock speed rose 1.38x from M1 to M4, by 1.09x to the M2, 1.17x to the M3 and 1.07x to the M4
c-mh-v8-ghz-m1-m4.notes: From the same device averages as c-mh-v8-gb6-m1-m4.

c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.text: About 17% of the M1 to M4 single-thread gain is IPC, roughly 5% per generation, less than the clock contribution
c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.quote: About 17% of the overall improvement has been IPC, so call it about 5% IPC boost per generation.
c-mh-v8-ipc-per-gen.notes: Per-benchmark IPC is mostly flat or rising; object detection gains 2.30x in IPC from M1 to M4, horizon detection none.

c-mh-v8-n3-sram.text: The M1 and M2 are built on N5 and the M3 and M4 on N3, where SRAM density barely improves, so Apple kept its structures at about the same sizes and restructured the pipeline for higher clocks
c-mh-v8-n3-sram.quote: M1 and M2 were on an N5 process, M3 and M4 on an N3 process. ... pivot to retaining the same sorts of structures in the same sorts of sizes, but restructuring the pipeline
c-mh-v8-n3-sram.notes: N3 raises logic density by about 60% but SRAM density by about 5%.

c-mh-v8-m3-width-9.text: The M3 P core is 9 wide
c-mh-v8-m3-width-9.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.

c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.text: The M4 P core is 10 wide
c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.
c-mh-v8-m4-width-10.notes: The trace-cache discussion also calls the current CPU 10 wide.

c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.text: The latest P cores have eight integer execution units, up from six
c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.quote: Thus 9-wide (M3) and 10-wide (M4), along with 8 rather than 6 integer execution units.
c-mh-v8-m4-int-units-8.notes: The sentence does not say whether the M3 already has eight. The M1 has six (eu_int.count).

c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.text: Apple's current P cores still have two load units, one store unit and one ambidextrous load/store unit, where Arm's Cortex-X925 has three load units
c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.quote: compared to Apple's two loads, a store, and an ambidextrous unit
c-mh-v8-m4-ls-pipes.notes: Same layout as on the M1 (c-mh-v2-ls-pipes, lsu.ls_units).

c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.text: Apple's current P cores still have four NEON pipelines
c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.quote: Another version of this for Apple might be to boost the existing four NEON pipelines to handle SVE.
c-mh-v8-m4-neon-4.notes: Same count as on the M1 (eu_fp.count).

c-dj-width.text: Firestorm's pipeline width is eight instructions (uops) per cycle
c-dj-width.quote: Firestorm has a pipeline width of eight instructions per cycle. Uops per cycle: 8
c-dj-width.notes: Johnson gives one pipeline width, not separate fetch/decode/rename widths. Method from #firestorm-pipeline-overview (uops counted with the RETIRE_UOP counter against the 8 uops/cycle limit).

c-dj-taken.text: Firestorm sustains one taken branch per cycle
c-dj-taken.quote: Uops per cycle: 8 Taken branches per cycle: 1
c-dj-taken.notes: The page does not say how this was measured.

c-dj-int-prf.text: The integer physical register file holds about 380 to 394 registers
c-dj-int-prf.quote: Integer physical register file size: ~380-394? ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-int-prf.notes: Johnson gives the range ~380-394 with a question mark; value is the midpoint.

c-dj-fp-prf.text: The FP/SIMD physical register file holds about 432 registers
c-dj-fp-prf.quote: FP/SIMD physical register file size: ~432? ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-flags-prf.text: The flags physical register file holds about 128 registers
c-dj-flags-prf.quote: Flags physical register file size: ~128 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-branches.text: About 144 branches can be in flight
c-dj-branches.quote: In-flight branches: ~144 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool

c-dj-loads.text: About 130 loads can be in flight
c-dj-loads.quote: In-flight loads: ~130 ... These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-loads.notes: The page points to the load/store queue blog post for detail (see c-dj-lsq-lq-130).

c-dj-stores.text: About 60 stores can be in flight
c-dj-stores.quote: In-flight stores: ~60 These numbers mostly come from my M1 buffer size measuring tool
c-dj-stores.notes: The page points to the load/store queue blog post for detail (see c-dj-lsq-sq-60).

c-dj-retire-groups.text: The coalesced retire queue holds about 330 retire groups
c-dj-retire-groups.quote: The coalesced retire queue consists of ~330 such groups.
c-dj-retire-groups.notes: The page names no filler; the LSQ post reaches this limit with ~329 loads or stores under an FSQRT delay (c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329). Group boundaries are c-dj-group-boundaries.

c-dj-group-size.text: A retire group may contain up to seven uops
c-dj-group-size.quote: Firestorm coalesces uops into retire groups, which all retire together. A retire group may contain up to seven uops.
c-dj-group-size.notes: Seven-uop groups are only observed for eliminated instructions (c-dj-group-issuing).

c-dj-nop-window.text: The coalesced retire queue allows an out-of-order window of over 2200 nop instructions
c-dj-nop-window.quote: This allows an out-of-order window of ... or over 2200 nop instructions.

c-dj-issuing-window.text: The coalesced retire queue allows an out-of-order window of just over 1000 contrived instructions that issue
c-dj-issuing-window.quote: This allows an out-of-order window of just over 1000 (contrived) instructions that issue

c-dj-rename-retire.text: The rename retire queue allows up to about 623 renames in flight
c-dj-rename-retire.quote: This is tracked in a separate structure, called the "rename retire queue", which allows for up to ~623 renames.
c-dj-rename-retire.notes: The every-write-needs-an-entry rule is c-dj-rename-cost. Also listed in #other-limits as "In-flight renames: ~623".

c-dj-retire-rate.text: Retirement is measured at up to eight coalesced retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-retire-rate.quote: Retirement-rate is measured at up to eight coalesced retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-retire-rate.notes: The page says "measured" but not how.

c-dj-rename-rate.text: Retirement is measured at up to sixteen rename retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-rename-rate.quote: or up to sixteen rename retire queue entries per cycle
c-dj-rename-rate.notes: The page says "measured" but not how.

c-dj-int-units.text: Firestorm has six integer units (1 to 6), each with ALU and ubfm/sbfm
c-dj-int-units.quote: Integer units: 1: alu + ubfm/sbfm + flags + branch ... 6: alu + ubfm/sbfm + mul + madd + crc + bfm/extr
c-dj-int-units.notes: The page says issues are measured with SCHEDULE_UOP and per-class issue counters. Unit roles are c-dj-int-roles.

c-dj-ls-units.text: Firestorm has four load/store units handling up to 128-bit accesses: unit 7 store and AMX, unit 8 load/store and AMX, units 9 and 10 load only
c-dj-ls-units.quote: Load/store units (up to 128-bit loads and stores ... 7: store + amx 8: load/store + amx 9: load 10: load

c-dj-fp-units.text: Firestorm has four FP/SIMD units (11 to 14)
c-dj-fp-units.quote: SIMD units: 11: fp/simd 12: fp/simd 13: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr 14: fp/simd
c-dj-fp-units.notes: Unit roles are c-dj-fp-roles. For unit 14 the page lists reciprocal and reciprocal-square-root estimates (frecpe, frsqrte, urecpe, ursqrte), not fsqrt.

c-dj-mov-elim.text: 64-bit register moves (mov x0, x1) are usually handled by renaming; mov w0, w1, mov x0, xzr and adr/adrp are not eliminated
c-dj-mov-elim.quote: mov x0, x1 (usually handled by renaming, 64-bit version only) ... not eliminated, including adr/adrp, mov w0, w1 and mov x0, xzr

c-dj-zero-idiom.text: mov x0, #0 (and its 32-bit form) and movi v0.16b, #0 (and other types) are handled by renaming
c-dj-zero-idiom.quote: mov x0, #0 (handled by renaming, as is 32-bit version) ... movi v0.16b, #0 (handled by renaming, including other types)
c-dj-zero-idiom.notes: mov x0, xzr is not eliminated (c-dj-mov-elim).

c-dj-mov-imm.text: Immediate moves (mov x0, #imm, 32- and 64-bit, including bitwise/movz/movn aliases) are handled by renaming at most twice per eight instructions
c-dj-mov-imm.quote: mov x0, #123 (handled by renaming at a max of 2 per 8 instructions, both 32-bit and 64-bit. Includes all tested immediate "mov" aliases e.g. bitwise/movz/movn)

c-dj-fusion.text: Certain consecutive instruction pairs issue as one uop: flag-setting ALU + b.cc, ALU + cbz/cbnz, aese + aesmc, aesd + aesimc, aese/aesd + eor, pmull + eor, and amx + amx
c-dj-fusion.quote: Certain instructions are able to issue as one uop if they appear consecutively in the instruction stream.
c-dj-fusion.value: flag-ALU+b.cc, ALU+cbz/cbnz, aese+aesmc, aesd+aesimc, aes+eor, pmull+eor, amx+amx
c-dj-fusion.notes: Conditions and non-fused pairs: c-dj-fusion-read-limit, c-dj-fusion-cbz, c-dj-fusion-crypto, c-dj-fusion-amx, c-dj-fusion-branch-limits and c-dj-no-fusion.

c-dj-l1d-latency.text: A load's result can feed the base address of another load with 3-cycle latency
c-dj-l1d-latency.quote: Loads may be passed to the base address of other loads with 3c latency (which is nice for linked lists)
c-dj-l1d-latency.notes: The 4c ALU-chain latency is c-dj-load-alu-latency. The page gives no method for latencies.

c-dj-pipeline-flow.text: Instructions decode to one or more uops, which are mapped, renamed and placed in a dispatch queue, then dispatched to a scheduler, issue when their operands are ready, and are marked completed in the reorder buffer, which releases entries in order
c-dj-pipeline-flow.quote: Typically, an instruction is decoded to one or more uops, each uop is mapped and renamed and placed into a dispatch queue. These uops are then dispatched from the queue to a scheduler.

c-dj-issue-counters.text: Issues are counted by the documented SCHEDULE_UOP counter, and three undocumented counters count issues to the integer, load/store and SIMD units separately; uops are counted by RETIRE_UOP
c-dj-issue-counters.quote: can be measured using the documented SCHEDULE_UOP counter. Three undocumented counters measure issues to the integer, load/store, and simd units separately

c-dj-unit-issue-limit.text: Each execution unit accepts one issue per cycle
c-dj-unit-issue-limit.quote: Issues count towards the "execution unit" limits (one issue per unit per cycle)

c-dj-fewer-issues.text: Most instructions issue once per uop, but nop, ldp and fused instructions have fewer issues than uops
c-dj-fewer-issues.quote: most instructions have the same number of issues as uops, but some have fewer (e.g. nop, ldp, and fused instructions)

c-dj-shift-extend-issues.text: ALU operations with an optional shift or extend have more issues than uops
c-dj-shift-extend-issues.quote: some instructions have more issues than uops, e.g ALU operations with an optional shift or extend

c-dj-issue-peak.text: Because shifted/extended ALU ops issue more than once per uop, Firestorm can sustain 11 issues per cycle in contrived cases
c-dj-issue-peak.quote: which allows Firestorm to sustain 11 issues per cycle in contrived cases

c-dj-int-roles.text: All six integer units do ALU and ubfm/sbfm; units 1-3 set flags; 1 and 2 take branches, adr and msr/mrs nzcv; 1 also mrs; 2 indirect branches and pointer authentication; 3 and 4 probably moves from SIMD/FP; 5 and 6 multiply; 5 divide; 6 madd, crc and bfm/extr
c-dj-int-roles.quote: 1: alu + ubfm/sbfm + flags + branch ... indirect branch + ptrauth ... mov-from-simd/fp? ... 5: alu + ubfm/sbfm + mul + div 6: ... mul + madd + crc + bfm/extr
c-dj-int-roles.value: 1-6 alu, ubfm/sbfm; 1-3 flags; 1-2 branch, adr, msr/mrs nzcv; 1 mrs; 2 indirect branch, ptrauth; 3-4 mov-from-simd/fp?; 5-6 mul; 5 div; 6 madd, crc, bfm/extr

c-dj-fp-roles.text: All four SIMD units do FP/SIMD; units 13 and 14 add fcsel and moves to GPRs; unit 14 alone adds fcmp/fcmpe, fdiv, frecpe, frsqrte, fjcvtzs, ursqrte, urecpe and sha
c-dj-fp-roles.quote: 13: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr 14: fp/simd + fcsel + to-gpr + fcmp/e + fdiv + frecpe + frsqrte + fjcvtzs + ursqrte + urecpe + sha
c-dj-fp-roles.value: 11-14 fp/simd; 13-14 fcsel, to-gpr; 14 fcmp/e, fdiv, frecpe, frsqrte, fjcvtzs, ursqrte, urecpe, sha

c-dj-agu-shift.text: Load/store address generation includes register shifts up to LSL #3
c-dj-agu-shift.quote: Load/store units (up to 128-bit loads and stores, including address generation with shifts up to LSL #3)

c-dj-fusion-read-limit.text: Flag-setting ALU ops (adds/subs/ands/cmp/tst) fuse with a following b.cc; fusion is complete only when the fused instructions read no more than 4 registers per 6 instructions
c-dj-fusion-read-limit.quote: adds/subs/ands/cmp/tst + b.cc (complete fusion when fused instructions read no more than 4 registers per 6 instructions)

c-dj-fusion-cbz.text: ALU ops (add/sub/and/orr/eor/bic etc., including flag-setting variants) usually fuse with a following cbz/cbnz when their destination is the cbz operand
c-dj-fusion-cbz.quote: add/sub/and/orr/eor/bic/etc. + cbnz/cbz (usually fused, if destination matches cbz operand. also works with instruction variants that set flags)

c-dj-fusion-crypto.text: aese + aesmc, aesd + aesimc, aese/aesd + eor and pmull + eor usually fuse when the second instruction overwrites the first's destination in a matching operand pattern
c-dj-fusion-crypto.quote: aese + aesmc (usually fused if operands match pattern "A, B ; A, A") ... pmull + eor (usually fused if operands match pattern "A, B, C ; A, A, D" or "A, B, C ; A, D, A")

c-dj-fusion-amx.text: Pairs of AMX instructions fuse, except AMX loads and stores, probably into something like an stp
c-dj-fusion-amx.quote: amx + amx (excluding loads and stores - probably fuses to something like a stp)

c-dj-fusion-branch-limits.text: Branch fusion does not happen with implicit shift or extend, nor with instructions that read flags such as adc
c-dj-fusion-branch-limits.quote: Branch fusion does not work with implicit shift or extend, nor instructions that read flags (like adc)

c-dj-no-fusion.text: adrp + add, mov + movk, mul + umulh and udiv + msub are not fused
c-dj-no-fusion.quote: Other tested patterns are not fused, including adrp + add, mov + movk, mul + umulh, and udiv + msub.

c-dj-vec-mov-elim.text: Full-width vector register moves (mov v0.16b, v1.16b, also v0.8h etc.) are usually handled by renaming; v0.8b moves are not
c-dj-vec-mov-elim.quote: mov v0.16b, v1.16b (usually handled by renaming. Includes other full-width types e.g. v0.8h but not v0.8b)

c-dj-nop-b-no-issue.text: nop and unconditional b never issue
c-dj-nop-b-no-issue.quote: Certain instructions do not need to issue: ... nop (never issues) b (unconditional branch never issues)

c-dj-load-alu-latency.text: When a load is chained with ALU operations instead of feeding another load's base address, its latency is 4 cycles
c-dj-load-alu-latency.quote: Loads may be passed to the base address of other loads with 3c latency ... but chaining with ALU operations gives a latency of 4c.

c-dj-ldp-second-dest.text: The second destination register of an LDP always has 4-cycle latency
c-dj-ldp-second-dest.quote: (Although the second destination register in an LDP always has 4c latency.)

c-dj-index-shift-penalty.text: A load takes one extra cycle when its index register comes from a shift-like instruction; addition and bitwise producers carry no penalty
c-dj-index-shift-penalty.quote: Loads may have an extra 1-cycle of latency when the index register is the output of a shift-like instruction. Addition and bitwise operations do not have this penalty.
c-dj-index-shift-penalty.notes: Johnson says other latency chains had not been tested.

c-dj-madd-acc-latency.text: A MADD result feeds the addend of a following MADD with 1-cycle latency, but has 3-cycle latency into other instructions
c-dj-madd-acc-latency.quote: MADD's output can be passed to its third operand (the addend) with 1c latency, but if it's chained with other instructions it has 3c latency.

c-dj-int-simd-roundtrip.text: An integer-to-SIMD/FP-and-back round trip can take as little as 7 cycles, for example when chaining flags operations
c-dj-int-simd-roundtrip.quote: Integer to SIMD/FP roundtrip latency can be as low as 7c (e.g. when chaining flags operations).

c-dj-rob-model.text: Firestorm's reorder buffer is unconventional: a ~330-entry coalesced retire queue of retire groups plus a ~623-entry rename retire queue
c-dj-rob-model.quote: Firestorm uses an unconventional reorder buffer, which I described as a ~330 entry "coalesced retire queue" and a ~623 "rename retire queue"
c-dj-rob-model.value: coalesced retire queue + rename retire queue

c-dj-reclaim-table.text: Johnson equates the ~623-entry rename retire queue with a Physical Register Reclaim Table
c-dj-reclaim-table.quote: a ~623 "rename retire queue" (equivalent to a "Physical Register Reclaim Table")

c-dj-group-boundaries.text: Uops that can fail before retiring (such as memory accesses) must start a retire group, and uops that can fail after retiring (such as conditional branches) must end one
c-dj-group-boundaries.quote: Uops which can fail before retiring (such as memory accesses) must appear at the start of a group, and uops that can fail after retiring (such as conditional branches) must appear at the end of a group.

c-dj-ooo-commit.text: Non-speculative loads and stores may commit out of order, before retirement; once a store has completed, the architectural state must have advanced past it
c-dj-ooo-commit.quote: loads and stores may commit out-of-order if they are non-speculative. This has some interesting implications. In particular, once a store has "completed", the architectural state must have advanced past that point.
c-dj-ooo-commit.notes: Johnson refers to his load/store queue blog post for the evidence.

c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.text: Load and store queue entries are allocated when the ops issue from the scheduler, not at rename or dispatch
c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.quote: discovered that load and store queue entries are allocated when the ops issue from the scheduler
c-dj-lsq-alloc-issue.notes: Intro, before the first heading. Reasoning in #final-notes: the 58-instruction gap between loads+loads and fsqrts+loads means loads keep entering the scheduler after the queue is full, "So I conclude that the resources are allocated late."

c-dj-lsq-lq-130.text: With two cache-missing loads as the delay, 128 loads fit between them before a stall; counting both delay loads, the load queue holds 130 entries
c-dj-lsq-lq-130.quote: Since the first load, 128 other loads, and the last load are in flight at the same time, I'd call this a load queue size of 130
c-dj-lsq-lq-130.notes: Delay: two independent cache-missing loads; filler: loads. Johnson: "I still believe this to be correct". The FSQRT + dependent-branch probe gives 188 = 130 + 58 (c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188).

c-dj-lsq-store-107.text: With cache-missing loads as the delay, 107 stores fit between them before a stall; Johnson withdrew his earlier reading of this as a 107-entry store queue
c-dj-lsq-store-107.quote: 128 loads or 107 stores could run, without stopping the final long-latency load from executing in parallel ... I incorrectly called this a 107 entry store queue.
c-dj-lsq-store-107.notes: Delay: two cache-missing loads; filler: stores. Explained as 60 store-queue entries plus 47 scheduler entries (c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47); the base-register effect is c-dj-lsq-x29-base.

c-dj-lsq-sched-48.quote: the load/store scheduler has 48 entries ... I found the last point at which an independent load could still fit into the scheduler and run, to find the scheduler size.
c-dj-lsq-sched-48.filler: loads or stores with addresses dependent on the delay
c-dj-lsq-sched-48.notes: Delay: a long-latency chain; filler: loads or stores whose addresses depend on it; probe: one independent load that still runs. Repeated in #fighting-stores-with-square-roots.

c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.text: The load/store dispatch queue in front of the scheduler has 10 entries
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.quote: with a 10 entry dispatch queue ... the number of extra load/stores, once the scheduler was full, that were required to block independent floating-point operations. That gives the dispatch queue size.
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.filler: loads or stores with addresses dependent on the delay
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-10.notes: Delay: a long-latency chain; filler: dependent loads/stores beyond a full scheduler; probe: independent FP ops that get blocked. Mixing op types separates the queues.

c-dj-lsq-dispatch-stall.text: An op that finds both its scheduler and its dispatch queue full stalls the frontend: no further ops enter any dispatch queue until that queue has room
c-dj-lsq-dispatch-stall.quote: But if the scheduler and dispatch queue are full, and we have an op that needs to go to that queue, we stall. This means no more ops can enter any dispatch queues until there is room in that queue.

c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.text: With chains of square roots as the delay, about 329 loads or stores fit between them, the same limit for mixed loads and stores; Johnson attributes it to the coalescing retire queue, not the load/store queues
c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.quote: about 329 loads or stores can run between floating point operations, without forcing the two long-latency chains to run completely in parallel
c-dj-lsq-fsqrt-329.notes: Delay: long-latency FP chains (fsqrt, per the heading and #final-notes); filler: independent loads or stores. Exceeds the 130/60 queue sizes, so queue entries are freed before retirement (c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec).

c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.text: Loads and stores complete, freeing their load/store queue entries but not their retire queue entries, once they are non-speculative
c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.quote: I'm guessing that loads and stores can complete (free their load/store queue entries, but not their retire queue entries) once they are non-speculative.
c-dj-lsq-release-nonspec.notes: Tested by making the loads/stores speculative: one initial load/store whose address depends on the delay, or (in the write-up) a branch dependent on it (c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188).

c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.text: Load/store completion that frees queue entries happens in order relative to other loads and stores
c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.quote: I believe this completion is in-order relative to other loads and stores.
c-dj-lsq-release-in-order.notes: The intro states it as entries "released once they are non-speculative and all earlier loads and stores have been released".

c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.text: With a square-root delay and a branch dependent on it keeping the loads speculative, 188 loads fit before a stall
c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.quote: adding a branch, dependent on the result of the first long-latency operation ... we can run 188 loads or 118 stores without forcing the two long-latency chains to run completely in parallel
c-dj-lsq-branch-loads-188.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent B.cc (chained via FCMP, per #the-data, since FMOV might interfere); filler: loads. 188 = 130 queue + 48 scheduler + 10 dispatch queue.

c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.text: With a square-root delay and a branch dependent on it keeping the stores speculative, 118 stores fit before a stall
c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.quote: This will ensure the loads and stores cannot become non-speculative, and keep their queue entries. In this test we see we can run 188 loads or 118 stores
c-dj-lsq-branch-stores-118.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent B.cc (chained via FCMP); filler: stores. 118 = 60 store queue + 58.

c-dj-lsq-extra-58.text: The 58 entries beyond the queue sizes are the 48-entry load/store scheduler plus its 10-entry dispatch queue: integer and FP work continues while they fill, and the next load/store stalls the machine
c-dj-lsq-extra-58.quote: If the load/store scheduler and dispatch queue are full, the integer and floating point units can continue operating. But if we hit one more load/store, the machine stalls ... This explains the 58 extra entries.

c-dj-lsq-sq-60.text: Subtracting the 58 scheduler and dispatch-queue entries from the 118-store result, the store queue has 60 entries
c-dj-lsq-sq-60.quote: By this logic (subtracting 58 for the size of the scheduler and dispatch queue), the store queue has only 60 entries.
c-dj-lsq-sq-60.notes: Delay: FSQRT chain plus a dependent branch; filler: stores; 118 - 58. Johnson's summary: "130 load queue entries and 60 store queue entries".

c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47.text: The earlier 107-store result is 60 store-queue entries plus 47: a probe load can still enter and issue while the 48-entry scheduler has one free entry, but not once it is full
c-dj-lsq-scheduler-47.quote: So why did we think it had 47 more? Because if the 48 entry scheduler is almost full, but has one free entry, then a load can enter the scheduler, and then issue from the scheduler and execute

c-dj-lsq-x29-base.text: With cache-missing loads as the delay, the store probe gives 60 when the second delay load is based on X29 and the stores on X29 or SP, but 107 when either base register is X3 (same values)
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.quote: I tried to reproduce the "107 entry store queue" result, but the result I got was 60 entries ... Changing either or both registers back to X3 (even though the values did not change) gave me 107 again.
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.hedge: take this section with a grain of salt
c-dj-lsq-x29-base.notes: Delay: two cache-missing loads (second one X29 + variable offset); filler: stores at X29 or SP + constant offset. In a July 2022 update Johnson could not reproduce this section on an M1 Max and suspects hardware or software revisions.

c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.text: Memory dependency prediction appears to special-case X29 (the frame pointer): the load waits until it knows no older store aliases it, which it can check for up to 60 speculative stores but not 61
c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.quote: X29 is typically used as the stack frame base pointer, and I suspect the memory dependency prediction has a special case for this, and makes the load wait until it knows the store doesn't alias it.
c-dj-lsq-x29-prediction.notes: Same M1 Max non-reproduction caveat as c-dj-lsq-x29-base. The intro calls it "a trick for manipulating load/store alias prediction".

c-dj-lsq-mov-counter.text: Apple's PMU has a MEMORY_ORDER_VIOLATION event, described as incorrect speculation between a store and a dependent load
c-dj-lsq-mov-counter.quote: Apple provides a performance counter for this. It's called MEMORY_ORDER_VIOLATION and described as "Incorrect speculation between store and dependent load".

c-dj-lsq-prf-not-late.text: Physical register file probes show no delay-type dependence (int+int vs int+float), so registers are neither allocated late nor freed early
c-dj-lsq-prf-not-late.quote: I do not see this kind of pattern when measuring physical register file sizes (e.g. comparing int+int vs int+float), so I believe they are neither allocated late, nor freed early.

c-dj-ice-lq-30.quote: The same logic works for Icestorm, where we see 30 load queue entries and 18 store queue entries

c-dj-ice-sq-18.quote: The same logic works for Icestorm, where we see 30 load queue entries and 18 store queue entries
c-dj-ice-sq-18.notes: The X29-based probe also measures 18 on Icestorm (#an-uncomfortable-surprising-discovery).

c-dj-ice-sched-ls-18.quote: 18 store queue entries (with an 18 entry scheduler and a 6 entry dispatch queue)

c-dj-ice-dispatch-ls-6.text: Icestorm's load/store dispatch queue has 6 entries
c-dj-ice-dispatch-ls-6.quote: with an 18 entry scheduler and a 6 entry dispatch queue

c-dj-group-issuing.text: Groups of seven uops are only observed for eliminated instructions; issuing uops are limited to roughly four per retire group
c-dj-group-issuing.quote: with issuing uops limited to roughly four per group
c-dj-group-issuing.notes: 330 groups at four issuing uops is ~1,320, not the "just over 1000" issuing window the same paragraph gives; three per group (~990) fits that window

c-dj-rename-cost.text: Every architectural register write takes a rename retire queue entry, eliminated or not: cbz and str take none, add and mov one, adds and ldp two
c-dj-rename-cost.quote: cbz or str do not require entries, add and mov need one entry, and adds or ldp need two entries

c-zhou-ibtb.text: Firestorm's indirect BTB holds 1024 entries and Icestorm's 512; it is a tagged cache, not indexed by branch address
c-zhou-ibtb.quote: which means the size of iBTB is 512 entries on icestorm, 1024 entries on firestorm

retire_groups.name: Coalesced retire groups
retire_groups.description: Uops retire in groups of up to seven; a memory op starts a group and a branch ends one.
retire_groups.detection_rule: NOP knee divided by load, store or branch knee is close to a whole number >= 2

rename_retire_queue.name: Rename retire queue (history file)
rename_retire_queue.description: A second queue of about 620 entries limits instructions that change the register map.
rename_retire_queue.detection_rule: register-writing fillers knee far below the NOP knee and above the physical register count

lsq_at_issue.name: Load/store queue entries allocated at issue
lsq_at_issue.description: Load and store queue entries are taken at issue, not at dispatch.
lsq_at_issue.detection_rule: same filler gives different knees under a miss delay and an ALU delay

register_security_tag.name: Register mapping security tag
register_security_tag.description: Reading a register the process has not written slows integer issue to about 4-wide.
register_security_tag.detection_rule: throughput drop when reading unclaimed registers

decoupled_fetch.name: Decoupled fetch with fetch-directed prefetch
decoupled_fetch.description: Fetch is not fully decoupled from branch prediction on the M1.
decoupled_fetch.detection_rule: I-cache miss cost drops under predictable branches for footprints larger than L1I

streaming_store_nt.name: Automatic non-temporal streaming stores
streaming_store_nt.description: Streaming stores become non-temporal without software hints.
streaming_store_nt.detection_rule: full-line streaming stores show no read-for-ownership traffic, so streaming write bandwidth beats partial-line writes

lsq_early_release.name: Early release of load/store queue entries
lsq_early_release.description: Loads and non-speculative stores give back their queue entries before retiring.
lsq_early_release.detection_rule: the same load or store filler gives a larger knee with no older store pending than with one

path_history_shift_xor.name: Path history register (shift-and-XOR)
path_history_shift_xor.description: The 100-bit history shifts and XORs in branch address bits, not outcomes.
path_history_shift_xor.detection_rule: two paths that differ in one bit of one earlier branch's PC or target give a spy branch with opposite outcomes ~0 % mispredicts while the bit is in the history and ~25 % (3-bit counters) once it has aged out

bpu_isolation.name: Branch predictor context isolation
bpu_isolation.description: The conditional predictor keeps no privilege or process tag.
bpu_isolation.detection_rule: out-of-place mistraining of a victim branch from another privilege level or process, with matching low-32-bit addresses and history, gives the victim ~25 % mispredicts when entries are shared and ~0 % when they are isolated

l1i_coupled_btb.name: Branch targets tied to the L1I
l1i_coupled_btb.description: A branch that misses the first-level BTB takes its target from the L1I, with a two-cycle bubble.
l1i_coupled_btb.detection_rule: taken-branch latency steps with code footprint (branch spacing) more than with branch count

zero_cycle_loads.name: Zero-cycle loads (register-file memory renaming)
zero_cycle_loads.description: A load from a just-stored address is renamed to the register holding the stored value.
zero_cycle_loads.detection_rule: a store and reload through the same base register shortens a load-to-DIV dependency chain; the same address through a different register does not

banked_prf_power.name: Banked register file with bank power gating
banked_prf_power.description: The register file has four banks that power down separately; waking one costs two or three cycles.
banked_prf_power.detection_rule: a small extra delay at the register-exhaustion knee that appears or vanishes when the delay changes by one cycle

dispatch_buffers.name: Two-level dispatch through unordered buffers
dispatch_buffers.description: Rename writes into unordered dispatch buffers that feed one scheduler queue per unit.
dispatch_buffers.detection_rule: after a long run of ADDs, rename-only instructions (MOV, NOP) run free for about buffer size / drain rate cycles; a filler limited to three integer units fills a 12-entry buffer, not 24

paired_sched_queues.name: Paired scheduler queues
paired_sched_queues.description: Scheduler queues are paired; a queue with nothing ready issues from its partner.
paired_sched_queues.detection_rule: a filler that can issue to only one unit of a pair sees about half the queue capacity of one that can issue to both

immediate_regs.name: Immediate register pool written at rename
immediate_regs.description: A MOV of a non-zero immediate completes at rename into a pool of about 36 registers.
immediate_regs.detection_rule: a MOV #imm filler knee lies about 36-38 above the ADD knee, and up to ~36 padded MOV #imm placed before ADDs do not move the ADD knee

l2_cachelets.name: Per-core L2 cachelets (inner and outer L2)
l2_cachelets.description: The 12 MiB L2 behaves as four 3 MiB cachelets, one beside each core.
l2_cachelets.detection_rule: single-core bandwidth sweeps step at ~3 MiB and ~7.5 MiB, short of the 12 MiB L2

dczva_l2_zero.name: DC ZVA zero-allocates lines in L2
dczva_l2_zero.description: DC ZVA allocates zeroed lines directly in the L2.
dczva_l2_zero.detection_rule: a DC ZVA stream beats the plain-store fill rate beyond L1 and shows no L1 writebacks

nt_load_handling.name: Non-temporal loads skip L1 fill
nt_load_handling.description: Non-temporal loads are not prefetched into the L1.
nt_load_handling.detection_rule: LDNPQ vs LDPQ sweep is equal in L1, LDNPQ lower in L2 with a higher L1 miss count, higher in DRAM

dtlb_piggyback.name: Single-ported dTLB with piggyback ports
dtlb_piggyback.description: One dTLB lookup per cycle, shared with queued requests to the same page.
dtlb_piggyback.detection_rule: three loads per cycle to one page run at full rate; spreading them over three pages 16 KiB apart drops to about 2.5 cycles per three loads, and a new page on every access to about one load per cycle

l1d_banked_piggyback.name: Banked L1D with piggybacked loads and buffered stores
l1d_banked_piggyback.description: Sixteen 16 B banks; loads to one element share an access and stores are buffered.
l1d_banked_piggyback.detection_rule: loads stepping by 256 B fall to one per cycle, by 128 B to about 1.7 and by 64 B to about 2.35, while steps up to 32 B keep three per cycle; stores keep two per cycle out to 128 B steps

l1d_way_lookup.name: L1D way selection without visible misprediction
l1d_way_lookup.description: Loads to random ways run as fast as loads to one way; no way misprediction shows.
l1d_way_lookup.detection_rule: loads that pick one of eight 16 KiB-apart pages at random on every access run no slower than loads to a fixed page once bank collisions are removed

lsu_virtual_prefetch.name: LSU-resident virtual-address prefetcher
lsu_virtual_prefetch.description: The prefetcher trains on every load and store virtual address at the LSU.
lsu_virtual_prefetch.detection_rule: a linear pointer chase keeps its L1 latency across page boundaries out to DRAM, and page-strided chains the prefetcher can follow lose the L1 TLB miss cost; a physical-address prefetcher would restart at each page

l1d_hashed_way.name: L1D way chosen from physical page bits
l1d_hashed_way.description: A line's way seems fixed by a hash of physical page bits.
l1d_hashed_way.detection_rule: pointer chases with node spacing 2^k+64 B reach the full L1 line count for some k and about one way per set for others, with no extra-cycle way-mispredict outliers

content_directed_prefetch.name: Content-directed (data memory-dependent) prefetch
content_directed_prefetch.description: Pointer-like values in filled lines are prefetched into the L2.
content_directed_prefetch.detection_rule: loading a line of pointers makes later chases through those pointers faster although no load ever used their addresses

barrier_colors.name: Color-tagged barriers at the L1-L2 boundary
barrier_colors.description: Barriers advance a color tag on memory requests, and ordering is enforced between the L1 and the L2, not in the LSU.
barrier_colors.detection_rule: a DMB between stores that hit in the L1 costs little, while one between stores that miss to the L2 waits for the earlier misses

load_poison_bits.name: Load poison bits for load-load ordering
load_poison_bits.description: A load whose line is modified by another core before it becomes non-speculative is poisoned and replayed or flushed.
load_poison_bits.detection_rule: same-address loads on one core take extra machine clears only when another core writes the line between them

l2_snoop_filter.name: L2 duplicate L1 tags (snoop filter and flush engine)
l2_snoop_filter.description: The L2 keeps duplicate tags of its cores' L1s, filters snoops for them, and drives a flush engine that pulls dirty L1 lines before a core powers down.
l2_snoop_filter.detection_rule: an idle core keeps its L1 contents through the other cores' sharing traffic, and stores to lines no other L1 holds see no snoop delay

l2_way_power.name: L2 way-group sleep and power-down
l2_way_power.description: L2 ways sit in three separately powered groups that sleep after an idle count set by leakage and temperature, or power off when use is concentrated.
l2_way_power.detection_rule: after an idle stretch the first L2 hits take one or two extra cycles, and after long light load the usable L2 capacity drops to two thirds or one third until miss pressure restores it

l2_victim_fill.name: L2 as a selective victim cache for L1 data
l2_victim_fill.description: DRAM fills go to the L1 only; L1 castouts enter the L2 as victims, clean ones only when their set has shown reuse and the L1-L2 path is free.
l2_victim_fill.detection_rule: one pass over a footprint larger than the L1 leaves little for a second pass to hit in the L2, while repeated passes build up L2 hits

l2_insertion_priority.name: L2 insertion position by line history
l2_insertion_priority.description: L2 victims enter at LRU positions chosen by stream, prefetch and trip bits, so streams and unused prefetches cycle through a few ways.
l2_insertion_priority.detection_rule: a streaming pass over many MiB evicts only an eighth to a quarter of a resident L2 working set

slc_victim_fill.name: SLC filled by L2 victims
slc_victim_fill.description: CPU lines move from L1 to L2 to the SLC as each level evicts them, so a CPU miss does not allocate in the SLC.
slc_victim_fill.detection_rule: the cached region seen by one core extends to about the L2 share plus the SLC, not to the larger of the two

coherence_duplicate_tags.name: Coherence point with duplicate tags
coherence_duplicate_tags.description: Before the SLC, a coherence point holds copies of every cache's L2 tags and states, a tag-only pseudo-L3 that orders same-address requests.
coherence_duplicate_tags.detection_rule: a read of a line held modified in the other cluster returns faster than a DRAM access

slc_sticky_quota.name: SLC sticky lines and group quotas
slc_sticky_quota.description: SLC lines carry a group ID and a sticky bit; driver-set quotas cap each group, and replacement skips sticky lines.
slc_sticky_quota.detection_rule: not visible to CPU-only probes; a GPU or media working set within its quota survives a CPU sweep larger than the SLC

slc_speculative_read.name: DRAM read issued alongside the SLC lookup
slc_speculative_read.description: A latency-sensitive read enters the memory controller pipeline while the coherence and SLC tag checks run, and is killed if either hits.
slc_speculative_read.detection_rule: DRAM-miss latency exceeds SLC-hit latency by no more than the memory controller's own DRAM access time

slc_power_gating.name: SLC way power-down and drowsy SRAM
slc_power_gating.description: The SLC powers down ways to match the share in use and holds idle SRAM at retention voltage, batching low-QoS requests until it wakes.
slc_power_gating.detection_rule: SLC-range latency or capacity right after an idle period differs from that after a warm-up sweep of the same footprint

fabric_qos_credits.name: Credit-gated fabric with QoS bands
fabric_qos_credits.description: Requests carry one of five QoS classes in three bands on six virtual channels; credits gate entry to the fabric and memory controller.
fabric_qos_credits.detection_rule: not visible to a single-core probe; under bulk GPU traffic a latency-bound CPU miss slows less than CPU streaming bandwidth falls

pio_network.name: Separate PIO network
pio_network.description: Device-memory accesses and short control messages such as interprocessor interrupts use a flat network that skips coherence, the SLC and DRAM.
pio_network.detection_rule: device register access and interprocessor interrupt latency stay flat while the memory fabric is saturated

coprocessor_ordering_table.name: Coprocessor memory-ordering table
coprocessor_ordering_table.description: CPU loads and stores to a page with outstanding AMX (or LZ) accesses wait until the L2 reports those accesses done.
coprocessor_ordering_table.detection_rule: a CPU load to a page that an in-flight AMX store targets stalls even at a different address in that page, but not when it goes to another page

power_estimator_throttle.name: Digital power estimator throttling
power_estimator_throttle.description: Per-core event counts feed a power estimate and energy credits that block vector or AMX issue for a cycle or two and steer DVFS.
power_estimator_throttle.detection_rule: dense SIMD loops on every core of a cluster show issue bubbles at an unchanged clock that disappear when one core runs the same loop alone

idle_clock_division.name: Divided clock while the core waits
idle_clock_division.description: A core stalled on DRAM or waiting for an event receives one clock pulse in four instead of a frequency change.
idle_clock_division.detection_rule: core cycles counted per unit of wall time fall by about four during long DRAM-bound stalls or WFE waits, with no DVFS change

simd_power_down.name: SIMD unit power-down with state offload
simd_power_down.description: After a long stretch without SIMD work the SIMD registers move to a low-leakage store and the SIMD unit loses power.
simd_power_down.detection_rule: the first SIMD instruction after a long integer-only stretch costs a fixed extra delay that recurs after each idle stretch

scan_on_fill_nfp.name: Scan-on-fill next-fetch predictor
scan_on_fill_nfp.description: Prefetched instruction lines are scanned for branches before their first use.
scan_on_fill_nfp.detection_rule: after a predictor flush, later taken branches in a recently filled line redirect faster than the first

loop_modes.name: Tiered loop modes
loop_modes.description: Loops run from the instruction queue, a loop buffer or an L0 cache.
loop_modes.detection_rule: a loop body shorter than the 8-wide dispatch group sustaining more than one iteration (taken loop-back branch) per cycle would show loop packing

fill_forwarding.name: Fill forwarding to waiting loads
fill_forwarding.description: A load that missed the L1 is woken as its line arrives and takes its bytes during the fill, not by replaying afterwards.
fill_forwarding.detection_rule: a pointer chase whose nodes hit in L2 shows a load-to-use latency two or three cycles below the L2 hit latency plus an L1 hit
